Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 1:

Page 3
(Sūrat Yūnus)
Makkiyyah, except verses 40, 94, 95 and 96, which are Madaniyyah. Its verses number 109. It was revealed after the Isra' (the Night Journey).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: this surah is Makkiyyah, except His saying: ﴿And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it. And your Lord knows best the corrupters.﴾ That is Madaniyyah, and it was revealed concerning the Jews.

His saying, exalted is His majesty, ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read ﴿Ra﴾ with a fatha on the ra, in tafkhim (emphatic pronunciation). Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Yahya from Abu Bakr read it with a kasra on the ra, in imalah (inclination toward the i-sound). It is also narrated from Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hammad from 'Asim that it is between the fatha and the kasra. Know that all of these are valid dialects. al-Wahidi said: the original rule is to leave imalah in such words as ma and la, because their alifs do not derive from a ya'. As for the one who uses imalah, it is because these expressions are names of the particular letters, so by using imalah he intends to draw attention to the fact that they are names and not particles.

The second issue: They agreed that His saying ﴿Ra﴾ alone is not a verse, and they agreed that His saying ﴿Ta Ha﴾ alone is a verse. The difference is that ﴿Ra﴾ does not match the endings of the verses that follow it, unlike ﴿Ta Ha﴾, which does match the endings of the verses that follow it.

The third issue: A full discussion of the interpretation of this type of word has already preceded at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, but we mention here also some of what has been said. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿Ra﴾ means: I am Allah, the All-Seeing. It has been said: I am the Lord, there is no lord besides Me. It has also been said: ﴿Ra﴾, (Ha Mim) and ﴿Nun﴾ are the name of the Most Gracious.

His exalted saying: ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾ On this there are two issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿These (tilka)﴾ may be a reference to the verses in this surah, and it may be a reference to the verses of the Qur'an preceding this surah. Likewise, "the Wise Book" may mean the Qur'an, and it may mean other than the Qur'an, namely the Book that is stored and hidden with Allah, from which every book was copied, as He, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an, in a Book well-guarded﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77, 78], and He said: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet﴾ [al-Buruj: 21, 22], and He said: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 4], and He said: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and confirms, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39].

When you know the possibilities we have mentioned, four possible interpretations arise here:

The first possibility: it is said that the word ﴿tilka﴾ refers to the verses present in this surah, so the meaning is: these verses are the verses of the Wise Book, which is the Qur'an. This is because He, exalted, promised His Messenger, peace be upon him, that He would send down to him a Book which water cannot erase and the passing of ages cannot change. So the meaning is that these verses found in the surah of ﴿Ra﴾ are the verses of that firm Book which water cannot erase.

The second possibility: it is said that the meaning is that these verses present in this surah are the verses of the Book stored and hidden with Allah.

Know that according to these two opinions, the reference in our words ﴿tilka﴾ is to the verses of this surah, and there is a difficulty in this: ﴿tilka﴾ is used to point to the absent, whereas the verses of this surah are present. How then is it appropriate to point to them with the word ﴿tilka﴾?

Know that this question has already been raised together with its answer in the explanation of His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1, 2].

The third and fourth possibilities: it is said that the word ﴿tilka﴾ refers to the verses of the Qur'an preceding this surah, and the meaning is that these are the verses of the Wise Qur'an, and the meaning is that they are the verses of that hidden, stored Book with Allah, exalted. There are two other opinions regarding the verse:

One of them: that by ﴿the Wise Book﴾ is meant the Torah and the Gospel. The meaning is that the narratives mentioned in this surah are the same as the narratives mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel, while Muhammad, peace be upon him, had no knowledge of the Torah and the Gospel. So this agreement is possible only if Allah, exalted, specially granted Muhammad the sending down of revelation to him. The second, which is the view of Abu Muslim: that His saying ﴿Ra﴾ refers to the letters of the alphabet, so His saying ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book﴾ means: these letters are the things that were made into signs and indications of this Book by which the challenge occurred. For if this Book were not distinguished from the speech of people by its inimitable quality, it would be impossible for it to be specific to this composition, to the exclusion of all other people who are able to pronounce these letters.

Second issue: Regarding the description of the Book as being "wise," there are several opinions:

First: the Wise (al-Hakim) is one possessing wisdom, in the sense that the Book contains wisdom.

Second: the intended meaning is to describe the speech by the attribute of the one who spoke it. al-A'sha said:

"And a strange (ode) that comes to kings, wise; I have composed it so that it may be said, who is the one who composed it?"

Third: most scholars said that ﴿al-Hakim﴾ means "the one who judges" (al-hakim), with fa'il in the sense of fa'il-as-hakim, its proof being His saying, exalted: ﴿And He sent down with them the Book in truth, that it might judge between people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213]. Thus the Qur'an is like a judge in beliefs, distinguishing their truth from their falsehood, and in actions, distinguishing their correctness from their error, and like a judge concerning the fact that Muhammad is truthful in his claim to prophethood, because the greatest miracle of our Messenger, peace be upon him, is none other than the Qur'an.

Fourth: ﴿al-Hakim﴾ means "the one made firm" (al-muhkam). Ihkam means protection from corruption, so the meaning is that water does not erase it, fire does not burn it, and the ages do not change it. Or the meaning is its freedom from falsehood and contradiction.

Fifth: al-Hasan said: He described the Book as wise because He, exalted, judged in it with justice and goodness and giving to close relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing and oppression, and He judged in it with Paradise for whoever obeys Him and with Hell for whoever disobeys Him. According to this, ﴿al-Hakim﴾ means "the one in which judgment is made" (al-mahkum fihi).

Sixth: In the original language, ﴿al-Hakim﴾ is an expression for one who does wisdom and what is correct, so describing the Qur'an with it is figurative. The basis of the figure is that it indicates wisdom and correctness, and insofar as it indicates these meanings it becomes as though it were itself the wise one.

**Issue 1:** The disbelievers of Quraysh were amazed that God had singled out Muhammad (ﷺ) for prophethood and revelation, and God rebuked them for that amazement. As for showing that the disbelievers were amazed at this singling out, it can be established in several ways:

The first is the words of God: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Surely this is a strange thing!﴾ and ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, saying: "Walk on and be steadfast to your gods. Surely this is a thing that is intended."﴾ [Sad: 5-6]. When they reached such ignorance that they wondered at God, the Exalted, being one, it is not far-fetched that they would also wonder at God, the Exalted, singling out Muhammad with revelation and prophethood.

The second is that the people of Makkah used to say: God did not find a messenger for His creation except the orphan of Abu Talib.

The third is that they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. In summary, this amazement allows two interpretations:

One of them is that they were amazed that God would make a human being a messenger, as He relates of the disbelievers when they said: ﴿Has God sent a human being as a messenger?﴾ [al-Isra': 94].

The other is that they were not amazed at that in itself, but were amazed at God singling out Muhammad, peace be upon him, with revelation and prophethood while he was poor and an orphan. This shows that the disbelievers were amazed at that. As for showing that God rebuked them for this amazement, it is His words in this verse: ﴿Is it a wonder to the people that We have revealed to a man from among them...﴾. His words ﴿Is it a wonder to the people?﴾ are in the form of a question, but their meaning is a denial that this should be a wonder.

The denial of this amazement is necessary for several reasons:

The first is that He, the Exalted, is the Owner of creation and its King. The owner and the king is the one who has command, prohibition, permission and restriction. These obligations must be conveyed to those who are obligated by means of some of the servants. When this is the case, sending a messenger is not an impossible matter; rather, it is permissible according to reason.

The second is that He, the Exalted, created creation to occupy itself with worship, as He said: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]; and He said: ﴿Indeed We created man from a drop of mingled fluid, that We might try him﴾ [al-Insan: 2]; and He said: ﴿He who purifies himself has succeeded, and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾ [al-A'la: 14-15]. Then He, the Exalted, perfected their minds and enabled them to distinguish good from evil. Then God, the Exalted, knew that His servants would not occupy themselves with what they were obligated to do unless He sent to them a messenger and a reminder. At this point, out of the requirement of grace, generosity and mercy, He must send that messenger to them. And if that is obligatory, how can it be a wonder?

The third is that sending messengers is a matter in which God, the Exalted, never left any period of the existence of the obligated without it, as He said: ﴿We did not send before you any except men to whom We revealed﴾ [Yusuf: 109]. So how can it be a wonder when its like has already preceded it? This is confirmed by His words: ﴿We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 59], and by the rest of the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them.

The fourth is that He, the Exalted, sent to them only a man whose lineage they knew, and whom they knew to be trustworthy, far from all kinds of accusations and falsehoods, constant in truthfulness and chastity. Moreover, he was unlettered, did not mix with the people of the religions, and never read a book at all. Yet, despite that, he recites to them their stories and informs them of their events. This indicates that he is truthful and confirmed by God, and it removes the amazement. This is from His words: ﴿It is He who raised among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 2], and He said: ﴿You did not recite any book before it, nor did you write it with your right hand﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48].

The fifth is that a similar amazement existed at the sending of every messenger, as in His words: ﴿And to 'Ad, their brother Hud﴾ [al-A'raf: 65], ﴿And to Thamud, their brother Salih﴾ [al-A'raf: 73], up to His words: ﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 63].

The sixth is that this amazement is either at God sending a messenger from among humans, or they concede that there is no amazement in that, and they were only amazed at God singling out Muhammad, peace be upon him, with revelation and messengership.

As for the first, it is far-fetched, because reason testifies that once obligation is established, there must be a reminder and a messenger who informs them of everything they need in their religion, such as the acts of worship and others.

Having established this, we say: it is better that one from their own kind be sent to them, so that their settling with him is more complete and their familiarity with him is stronger, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [al-An'am: 9], and He said: ﴿Say: "If there were angels walking calmly on the earth, We would have sent down to them from heaven an angel as a messenger."﴾ [al-Isra': 95].

As for the second, it is also far-fetched, because Muhammad, peace be upon him, was described with the qualities of goodness, piety and trustworthiness, and they did not reproach him except for being an orphan and poor. This is extremely far-fetched, because He, the Exalted, is free of need from the worlds, so poverty should not be a cause of diminishment of one's standing with Him, nor should wealth be a cause of perfection of one's standing with Him, as He said: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children will bring you near to Us in nearness﴾ [Saba': 37]. Thus it is established that the disbelievers' amazement at God singling out Muhammad with revelation and messengership is a corrupt statement.

**Issue 2:** The hamzah in His words ﴿Is it...?﴾ (أكان) is for denying the amazement, and for the sake of marveling at this amazement. The phrase ﴿that We revealed﴾ (أن أوحينا) is the ism of kana (the subject of the verb "was"), and ﴿a wonder﴾ (عجبا) is its khabar (predicate). Ibn 'Abbas read (عجب) as the ism, which is indefinite, and ﴿that We revealed﴾ as its khabar, which is definite, like the saying: "its mixture is honey and water." The better view is that kana is complete (tammah, meaning it does not need a predicate), and ﴿that We revealed﴾ is a badal (substitute/apposition) for ﴿a wonder﴾.

**Issue 3:** He, the Exalted, said ﴿Is it a wonder to the people?﴾ and did not say "Is it a wonder in the sight of the people?" The difference is that His words ﴿a wonder to the people﴾ mean that they made it for themselves a marvel at which they wonder, and they appointed and designated it as the object of omen-taking, mockery and amazement. This meaning is not present in the phrase "Is it a wonder in the sight of the people?"

* * *

**Issue 4:** The particle (أن) with the verb in His words ﴿that We revealed﴾ is, in estimation, a verbal noun (masdar), which is the ism of kana, and its khabar is His words ﴿a wonder﴾. The predicate was placed before the subject here because they put the more important first, and the intended object of denial in this verse is indeed their amazement. As for (أن) in His words ﴿that warn the people﴾, it is explanatory (mufassirah, i.e., it explains the preceding revelation), because revelation in it carries the meaning of saying. It may also be lightened from the heavy form (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and its original form is: "that he warned the people," in the sense that the matter is our saying: "Warn the people."

**Issue 5:** When He, the Exalted, made clear that He revealed to His messenger, He then made clear the detail of what was revealed to him, which is warning and good tidings. As for warning, it is for the disbelievers and the wicked, so that they may refrain because of that warning from doing what is not fitting. As for good tidings, it is for the people of obedience, so that their desire for it may increase. He placed warning before good tidings because clearing away is prior to adornment, and removing what is not fitting is prior in rank to doing what is fitting.

**Issue 6:** His words ﴿a sure standing (qadama sidq)﴾ (قدم صدق) have views from the lexicographers and views from the exegetes. As for the views of the lexicographers, al-Wahidi in *al-Basit* transmitted several meanings. Al-Layth and Abu al-Haytham said: qadam means precedence, and the meaning is that they have had a prior good standing with God. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"You are a man of the house of Dhu'aybah, to them is a known precedence and glories."

Ahmad ibn Yahya said: qadam is everything good that you have put forward. Ibn al-Anbari said: qadam is a metaphor for the deed in which one goes ahead, and in which there is no delay or slowness.

Know that the reason for applying the word qadam to these meanings is that striving and precedence are achieved only by the foot, so the effect was named by the name of the cause, just as blessing was called a hand, because it is given by the hand.

If it is said: what is the benefit of attributing qadam to sidq in His words "a qadam of sidq"?

We say: the benefit is to draw attention to the increase of excellence, and that it is among the great precedences. Some said: what is meant is a station of truthfulness.

As for the exegetes, they have views. Some understood "qadam sidq" as righteous deeds, some understood it as reward, and some understood it as the intercession of Muhammad, peace be upon him. Ibn al-Anbari preferred this last view and recited:

"Pray to the Lord of the Throne and take a qadam, which will save you on the day of stumbling and slipping."

**Issue 7:** When a messenger from among them came to the disbelievers, warned them and gave them good tidings, and brought them from God, the Exalted, what is most fitting to His wisdom and grace, they said in amazement: ﴿Surely this is clearly a sorcerer﴾, meaning: this one who claims that he is a messenger is a sorcerer. The beginning with His words ﴿The disbelievers said﴾ is on the estimate: "When he warned them, the disbelievers said: Surely this is clearly a sorcerer." Al-Qaffal said: omitting (idmar) such a phrase is not rare in the Qur'an.

**Issue 8:** Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿Surely this is a sorcerer﴾ (إن هذا لساحر), and what is meant by it is Muhammad (ﷺ). The rest read (لسحر), "surely this is sorcery," and what is meant by it is the Qur'an.

Know that the disbelievers' description of the Qur'an as sorcery indicates the great status of the Qur'an in their eyes, that it is miraculous, and that they were unable to produce a counterpart to it, so they resorted to this statement.

Know also that their boldness in describing the Qur'an as sorcery may be understood as said in the context of blame, or it may be understood as said in the context of praise. For this reason the exegetes differed about it. Some said: they meant that it is an ornamented speech, fine in appearance, but false in reality, with no substance. Others said: they meant that because of its perfect eloquence and the impossibility of its like, it works like sorcery.

Know that since this statement is extremely corrupt, its refutation was not mentioned. We say it is extremely corrupt because the Prophet (ﷺ) was one of them, grew up among them, was not absent from them, and did not associate with anyone other than them. Mecca was not a city of scholars and clever people such that one could say he learned sorcery or learned many sciences from them and was thus able to bring the like of this Qur'an. Since this is the case, understanding the Qur'an as sorcery is an extremely corrupt statement, and for this reason its refutation was left out.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days and then established Himself above the Throne, arranging the affair. There is no intercessor except after His permission. That is Allah, your Lord, so worship Him. Will you not then remember?﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, related of the disbelievers that they marvelled at the revelation, the sending of a messenger and the prophethood, He then removed that wonder by showing that it is by no means far-fetched that the Creator of creation should send to them a messenger who gives them glad tidings of reward for righteous deeds and warns them of punishment for corrupt and false deeds. This answer is only complete and perfect by establishing two matters. The first: establishing that this world has a God who is dominant, all-powerful, whose judgment prevails through command, prohibition and obligation. The second: establishing the Gathering, the Resurrection, the Raising and the Final Hour, so that the reward and punishment, of which the prophets informed, come to pass. Therefore, He, glory be to Him, has mentioned in this place that which indicates the realisation of these two aims.

As for the first, which is establishing divinity, it is by His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾.

As for the second, which is establishing the Return, the Gathering and the Raising, it is by His saying: ﴿To Him is your return, all of you; the promise of Allah is true﴾ [Yunus: 4]. Thus it is established that this arrangement is in the utmost beauty and the furthest perfection. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: We have mentioned in this book and in the rational books that the proof indicating the existence of the Creator, exalted is He, is either possibility (imkan) or origination (huduth), and both of these are either in essences (dhawat) or in attributes (sifat). Thus the totality of the methods indicating the existence of the Creator is four: possibility of essences, possibility of attributes, origination of essences, and origination of attributes. These four are considered at times in the upper world, which is the world of the heavens and the stars, and at times in the lower world. The majority of the proofs mentioned in the divine books rely on the possibility and origination of attributes, at times in the states of the upper world and at times in the states of the lower world. What is mentioned in this place is reliance on the possibility of the celestial bodies in their magnitudes and attributes, and its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: that the bodies of the spheres are without doubt composed of indivisible parts, and whenever this is so, they are necessarily in need of a Creator and a Determiner.

As for the explanation of the first stage: the bodies of the spheres are without doubt capable of imaginary division, and we have demonstrated in the rational books

that everything capable of imaginary division is composed of parts and portions. We have demonstrated that what the philosophers say, that the body is divisible but is in itself one thing, is a corrupt and false statement. It has thus been established by what we have mentioned that the bodies of the spheres are composed of indivisible parts. Once this is established, it is necessary that they require a Creator and a Determiner. That is because, when they were composed, some of those parts came to be within that body and some came to be on its surface, and those parts are equal in nature, quiddity and reality. The philosophers have conceded to us the soundness of this premise when they said that they are simples, and it is impossible that they be composed of parts of differing natures.

Once this is established, we say: the occurrence of some of them in the interior and the occurrence of some of them in the exterior is a matter that is possible to occur and permissible to be established. It is permissible that the outer become inner and the inner become outer. When the matter is so, these parts, at the time of their composition, necessarily require a governing and dominant agent, which assigns some of them to the interior and some of them to the exterior. This indicates that the spheres, in their composition, their shapes and their attributes, require a powerful, knowing, wise Determiner.

The second aspect in arguing from the attributes of the spheres to the existence of the all-powerful God is that we say: the motions of these spheres have a beginning, and whenever this is so, these spheres in their motions require a powerful mover and disposer.

As for the first stage: the proof for its soundness is that motion is an expression for change from one state to another, and this quiddity requires being preceded by the state transitioned from, and eternity negates being preceded by something else. Therefore combining motion and eternity is impossible. Thus it is established that the motions of the spheres have a first. Once this is established, it must be said: these celestial bodies were non-existent in eternity, or if they were existent, they were at rest and still and were not moving. In either case, their motions have a first and a beginning.

As for the second stage: since the matter is so, it is necessary that they require a powerful disposer. The proof for it is that the initiation of these bodies in motion at that specific time, rather than before it or after it, must have an assigner of specification and a bestower of preference. That preferring agent cannot be one that acts by essential necessity, for otherwise that motion would have occurred before that time, because the cause of that motion was already present before that time. Since this has been invalidated, it is established that that preferring agent is an agent who chooses, and that is what was to be proven.

The third aspect in arguing from the attributes of the spheres to the existence of the choosing God is that the parts of one sphere are located in it and not in the other sphere, and the parts of the other sphere are located in it and not in the first sphere. The specification of each of them with those parts is a possible matter, and it must have a preferrer, and the first explanation returns to it. This is the explanation of this proof which God, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse. In the verse there are questions:

The first question: the word ﴿alladhi﴾ (who) is a word established to indicate a single thing when attempting to define it by a known proposition, as when it is said to you: "Who is Zayd?" and you say: "The one whose father is departing." This definition is only apt if the fact that his father is departing is a known matter to the hearer. Here, when He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾, this is only apt if His, glory be to Him and exalted is He, being the creator of the heavens and the earth in six days is a known matter to the hearer, and the Arabs were not aware of that. So how is this definition apt?
Page 10
Its answer: it is said that this statement is well known among the Jews and the Christians, because it is mentioned at the beginning of what they claim to be the Torah. Since that was well known among them, and the Arabs used to mix with them, it is apparent that they also heard it from them, and for this reason the definition is apt.

The second question: what is the benefit in stating the days in which Allah created them?

The answer: He, exalted is He, is capable of creating the entire world in less than the twinkling of an eye. The proof for this is that the world is composed of indivisible parts, and an indivisible part cannot be brought into existence except at once. For if we suppose that its bringing into existence occurs over a time, that time is necessarily divided into successive instants. Then either something of that bringing into existence occurred in the first instant or it did not. If nothing of it occurred in the first instant, then it is outside the duration of the bringing into existence. And if in that instant the bringing into existence of something occurred, and in the second instant the bringing into existence of something else occurred, then if these two are parts of that indivisible part, the indivisible part becomes divisible, which is impossible. And if it is something other, then the bringing into existence of the indivisible part cannot occur except in one instant, in a single push. The same is said of the bringing into existence of all the parts. Thus it is established that He, exalted is He, is capable of bringing the entire world into existence in one push. Also, there is no doubt that He, exalted is He, is capable of bringing it into existence and forming it gradually.

Once this is established, we say: here there are two doctrines:

The first: the doctrine of our companions, which is that whatever He wills is good for Him, and none of His acts is ascribed to any wisdom or interests. On this view, the question of one who says: "Why did He create the world in six days and not in a single moment?" falls away, because we say: whatever He does without a cause for its making, none of His rulings or acts is ascribed to a cause, so this question falls.

The second: the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, who say that God's acts must necessarily include interest and wisdom. On this basis, al-Qadi said: it is not far-fetched that God's creation of the heavens and the earth in this specific period was for the sake of consideration with regard to some of the accountable. Then al-Qadi said:

If it is said: "Who is the one considered, and what is the manner of consideration?" Then he answered and said: As for the one considered, it is that there must be an accountable or non-accountable living being, which God created before His creation of the heavens and the earths, or together with them, otherwise their creation would be in vain.

If it is said: "Why could He not create them for the sake of an animal He would create later?"

We say: God does not fear missing out, so it is not permissible for Him to bring forward the creation of what no one benefits from for the sake of an animal that will come into being afterward. Such a thing is only conceivable for us in preliminary matters, because we fear missing out and fear incapacity and deficiency. He said: once this is established, what was related in the report is sound, that the creation of the angels preceded the creation of the heavens and the earth.

If it is said: "Those angels must have a place, and before the creation of the heavens and the earth there was no place, so how can they exist without a place?"

We say: He who is able to keep the Throne, the heavens and the earth in their places, how could He be unable to keep those angels in their spaces by His power and wisdom? As for the manner of consideration in this: since there was a considered one there, it is not impossible that his consideration, by what he witnesses state after state, is stronger. The proof of this is that what comes to be in this manner indicates that it proceeds from a wise agent, whereas what is created all at once does not indicate that.
Page 11

The third question: are these days like the days of this world, or, as has been related from Ibn Abbas, that he said: they are six days of the days of the Hereafter, each day of which is a thousand years of what you count?

The answer: al-Qadi said: the apparent meaning in this is that it is an informing to His servants of the duration of His creating them, and it is not permissible that this be an informing unless the duration is these known days.

One may say: since the definition occurred by the days mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel, and what was mentioned there were the days of the Hereafter and not the days of this world, that does not detract from the soundness of the definition.

The fourth question: these days are measured according to the rising and setting of the sun, and this meaning did not exist before their creation, so how is this definition conceivable?

The answer: the definition is achieved by the fact that, had the occurrence of the heavens and the earth taken place over a period, and had there been revolving spheres, a sun and a moon there, that period would have been equal to six days.

One may say: this entails the existence of a period before the creation of the world, in which the occurrence of the world took place, and that necessitates the eternity of the period.

Its answer: that period is not existent but is supposed and imagined. The proof of this is that that specific period is originated, and its origination does not require another period, otherwise it would entail positing periods without end, and that is impossible. So whatever they say about the origination of the period, we say about the origination of the world.

The fifth question: "day" may be meant as the day together with its night, and it may be meant as the daytime alone. Which of the two is meant in this verse?

The answer: in the language, the predominant usage is that "day" means the day with its night.

* * *

The second issue: as for His saying: ﴿then established Himself above the Throne﴾, there are discussions in it:

The first point is that this implies He, exalted is He, is settled upon the Throne. The full discussion of this is mentioned at the beginning of surah Ta-Ha, but here we will suffice with a brief statement. We say: this verse cannot be taken according to its apparent meaning, and the following points prove it.

The first point: istiwa' ('alā al-'arsh (establishing or rising over the Throne)) means that He is leaning upon it and settled on it, such that were it not for the Throne, He would fall and descend, just as when we say that so-and-so is seated upon his throne, this meaning is understood from it. However, affirming this meaning requires that He be in need of the Throne, and that were it not for the Throne He would fall and descend. That is impossible, because the Muslims agree that Allah, exalted is He, is the One who holds up the Throne and preserves it, and no one says that the Throne holds up Allah, exalted is He, and preserves Him.

The second: His saying ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ indicates that before that He was not settled upon it, and this indicates that He, exalted is He, changes from state to state, and whoever changes is originated, and that is by consensus false.

The third: since the establishment occurred at this time, this requires that before this time He, exalted is He, was agitated and moving, and all of that is among the attributes of originated things.

The fourth: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that He, exalted is He, established Himself upon the Throne only after He created the heavens and the earth, because the word (thumma) requires delay. This indicates that before creating the Throne He, exalted is He, was independent of the Throne. When He created the Throne, it is impossible that His reality and essence would change from independence to need. Therefore it is necessary that after creating the Throne He remain independent of the Throne, and whoever is so is impossible to be settled upon the Throne. Thus it is established by these points that this verse cannot be taken according to its apparent meaning by consensus, and if that is the case, it is impossible to use it as evidence for establishing place and direction for Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

The third issue: the Muslims agree that above the heavens there is a great body, which is the Throne.

Having established this, we say: is the Throne mentioned in this verse that one, or something else? There are two opinions.

The first opinion, which was chosen by Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, is that it is not meant that one. Rather, what is meant by His saying ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ is that when He created the heavens and the earth, He leveled them and raised their height. Every building is called 'arsh (throne), and its builder is called 'arish (one who builds). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And of the trees and of what they build (ya'rishūn)﴾ [al-Nahl: 68], meaning: what they construct. And He said describing a town: ﴿so it lies in ruins upon its roofs ('urūshihā)﴾ [al-Hajj: 45], and what is meant is that town was emptied of its people while its structures remained intact and its roofs standing. And He said: ﴿And His throne was upon the water﴾ [Hud: 7], meaning: His building. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that because it is more wondrous in terms of power. The builder constructs a building far from the water on solid ground so that it does not collapse, while Allah, exalted is He, built the heavens and the earth upon the water so that the intelligent would know His power and the perfection of His majesty. And istiwa' upon the throne is rising over it by dominance, and the evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He has made for you of the ships and cattle that which you ride﴾ ﴿so that you may sit firmly upon their backs and then remember the favor of your Lord when you are seated upon them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 12, 13]. Abu Muslim said: So it is established that the wording allows this which we have mentioned. We say: it is obligatory to interpret the wording by it, and it is not permissible to interpret it as the Throne that is in the sky. The evidence for this is that the inference toward the existence of the Creator, exalted is He, must be achieved through a known, observable thing, and the Throne that is in the sky is not like that, whereas the bodies of the heavens and the earths are observable and perceptible. So inferring from their conditions to the existence of the wise Creator is permissible, correct, and good. Then he said: What further confirms this is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ refers to the creation of their essences, and His saying ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ refers to their leveling and shaping with forms suited to their benefits. On this interpretation, this verse agrees with His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Are you more difficult to create or is the heaven? He constructed it﴾ ﴿He raised its height and proportioned it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27, 28]. He first mentioned that He built it, then secondly mentioned that He raised its height and proportioned it. Likewise here. By His saying ﴿He created the heavens and the earth﴾ He mentioned that He created their essences, then by His saying ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ He mentioned that He intended to raise their structure, level them, and shape them with forms suited to them.

The second opinion, which is the well-known opinion of the majority of the exegetes, is that what is meant by the Throne mentioned in this verse is the great body that is in the sky. These said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ cannot mean that He created the Throne after creating the heavens and the earths, by the evidence that He, exalted is He, said in another verse: ﴿And His throne was upon the water﴾ [Hud: 7], and that indicates that the formation of the Throne precedes the creation of the heavens and the earths. Rather, this verse must be interpreted in other ways. That is, what is meant is: then He manages the affair while He is established upon the Throne.

The third opinion: what is meant by the Throne is dominion (mulk). It is said: so-and-so has taken over his throne, meaning his dominion. So His saying ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ means that when He, exalted is He, created the heavens and the earth, and the spheres and the stars revolved, and by their revolution He made the four seasons and the various conditions of minerals, plants, and animals, then at that time the existence of these creatures and beings came about. The summary is that the Throne is an expression for dominion, and Allah's dominion is an expression for the existence of His creatures, and the existence of His creatures came about only after the creation of the heavens and the earth. Therefore it is correct to place the particle (thumma), which indicates delay, before the establishment upon the Throne. And Allah knows best His intent.

* * *

The fourth issue: as for His saying ﴿He manages the affair﴾, its meaning is that He decrees and determines according to what wisdom requires, and does what the one who is right in his actions does, looking at the outcomes and consequences of affairs, so that nothing unfitting enters into existence. What is meant by ﴿the affair﴾ is the matter, that is: He manages the conditions of creation and the conditions of the dominion of the heavens and the earth.

If it is said: what is the position of this sentence?

We say: by being the Creator of the heavens and the earth in six days and by being established upon the Throne, He indicated the utmost greatness and the highest majesty. Then He followed them with this sentence, to show that nothing occurs in the upper world or the lower world, no matter nor any occurrence, except by His decree, His management, His judgment, and His rule. Thus this becomes evidence of the utmost power, wisdom, knowledge, comprehensiveness, and management, and that He, glorified is He, is the originator of all possible beings, and to Him all needs lead.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

The first opinion, which is the well-known one, is that what is meant is that His management of things and His making of them does not occur through the intercession of an intercessor or the management of a manager. No one dares to intercede with Him for anything except after His permission, because He, exalted is He, knows best the place of wisdom and correctness, so it is not permissible for them to ask Him for what they do not know to be correct and beneficial.

If it is said: how is it fitting to mention the intercessor in relation to the attribute of the origin of creation, when mention of him is only fitting in relation to the conditions of the Resurrection?

The answer has several aspects:

The first aspect is what al-Zajjaj mentioned: that the disbelievers who were addressed by this verse used to say: the idols are our intercessors with Allah. So what is meant by it is a refutation of them in this statement, and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits﴾ [al-Naba': 38].

The second aspect, which can be said: when He, exalted is He, showed that He is the God of the world, independent in managing it without partner or opponent, He showed the matter of the origin by His saying ﴿He manages the affair﴾, and showed the state of the return by His saying ﴿There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾.

The third aspect: it can also be said that He, exalted is He, placed the management of affairs at the beginning of the creation of the world in the best ways and closest to caring for benefits, even though there was no intercessor there interceding for the pursuit of obtaining benefits. This indicates that the God of the world is watchful over His servants, beneficent to them, desiring good and kindness for them, and there is no need, in His being so, for the presence of an intercessor who intercedes with Him.

The second opinion regarding the interpretation of this intercessor is what Abu Muslim al-Isfahani mentioned. He said: the intercessor here is the second, and it is taken from the even (shaf') which is opposed to the odd (witr), as it is said: the pair and the single. So the meaning of the verse: He created the heavens and the earth alone, with no living being with Him and no partner to help Him. Then He created the angels, the jinn, and humans. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿except after His permission﴾, that is: no one came into being or entered existence except after He said to him: "Be," and so he was and came to be.

Know that when He, exalted is He, had clarified these proofs and explained these conditions, He concluded them afterward with His saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; so worship Him﴾, making clear by that that worship is suitable only for Him, and alerting that He, glorified is He, is the one deserving of all acts of worship, because He is the one who bestows all the blessings that He mentioned and described.

Then He said after it: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾, indicating by that the obligation of reflection upon those manifest and dazzling proofs. This indicates that reflecting upon the creatures of Allah, exalted is He, and inferring from them His majesty, might, and greatness, is the highest of ranks and the most complete of degrees.

This is the commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 4 (part 1 of 5):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him is your return, all of you. The promise of Allah is true. Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it, that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice. And those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, mentioned the proofs indicating the establishment of the origin (al-mabda'), He followed them with what indicates the soundness of the doctrine of the return (al-ma'ad). In this are several issues:

The first issue: a demonstration that denying resurrection (al-hashr wa'l-nashr) is not among the self-evident (badihi) sciences, and there are several proofs for this:

The first: rational people have disagreed over its occurrence and non-occurrence. A group of people, who are the majority of the adherents of the religions (al-milal wa'l-adyan), held that it is possible. And what is known to be impossible by self-evidence cannot be the subject of disagreement.

The second: when we return to our sound intellects and present to them that one is twice two, and we also present to them this proposition, we do not find this proposition to be as strongly impossible as the first proposition.

The third: we either affirm the existence of the rational soul (al-nafs al-natiqah) or we do not. If we affirm it, the difficulty is entirely removed, for just as it is not impossible for this soul to be attached to the body the first time, it is not impossible for it to be attached to the body a second time. And if we deny the doctrine of the soul, the possibility still stands, because it is not far-fetched to say that He, glorified be He, assembles those scattered parts into a second composition, and creates the first human being once more.

The fourth: He, glorified be He, has mentioned many examples indicating the possibility of resurrection, and we shall gather them here.

The first example: we see the earth humbled in the autumn, and we see dryness dominating it because of the intense heat in summer. Then He sends down rain upon it in winter and spring, and after that it becomes adorned with wondrous blossoms and strange lights, as He, exalted, said: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and bring to life thereby the earth after its death. Thus will be the resurrection﴾ [Fatir: 9].

The second: His saying, exalted: ﴿And you see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], up to His saying: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead﴾ [al-Hajj: 6].

The third: His saying, exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky and makes it flow as springs in the earth, then brings out thereby crops of varying colours, then it withers and you see it turning yellow, then He makes it into debris? Indeed in that is a reminder for people of understanding﴾ [al-Zumar: 21].

What is meant is that it is an alert to the matter of the return.

The fourth: His saying: ﴿Then He caused him to die and buried him. Then, when He wills, He will raise him up again. No indeed! He has not fulfilled what He commanded him. Let man look at his food﴾ [Abasa: 21-24]. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "When you see the spring, then increase your remembrance of the resurrection." The likeness between the spring and the resurrection arises only from the aspect we have mentioned.

The second example: what each one of us finds in himself of increase and growth through fattening, and of decrease and wasting through emaciation, and then it may return to its former state through fattening.

Having established this, we say: whatever allows the formation of a part of it does not make the formation of the whole impossible either. And once this is established, it becomes clear that re-creation is not impossible. To this refers His saying, exalted: ﴿And We will make you into what you do not know﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 61], meaning: since He, glorified be He, is capable of originating your essences first, and then of originating your parts during your life, second, gradually, without you knowing the time of their coming into being or the time of their decline, it is therefore necessary to affirm with certainty that it is not impossible for Him, glorified be He, to restore you after decay in the graves for the gathering of the Day of Resurrection.

The third example: since He, exalted, is capable of creating us at the beginning without any prior model, He is all the more capable of bringing us into being a second time when the first bringing into being has preceded. This argument He established in many verses, among them this verse, namely His saying: ﴿Indeed He originates creation and then repeats it﴾.

Second: His saying, exalted, in Surah Ya Sin: ﴿Say: He will give them life who brought them into being the first time﴾ [Ya Sin: 79].

Third: His saying, exalted: ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation, so will you not remember?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 62].

Fourth: His saying, exalted: ﴿Were We then wearied by the first creation? Nay, but they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15].

Fifth: His saying, exalted: ﴿Does man think he will be left neglected? Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36-37], up to His saying: ﴿Is not that One able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40].

Sixth: His saying, exalted: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], up to His saying: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is capable of all things. And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will raise those who are in the graves﴾ [al-Hajj: 6-7]. In this verse He invoked, for the soundness of the gathering, several matters. The first: He argued from the first creation to the possibility of the second creation, namely His saying: ﴿If you are in doubt about the resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. It is as though He, exalted, said: since the first creation was achieved through these bodies passing from one state to other states, why should the second creation not be achieved after many changes and successive variations?

The second: that He, exalted, likened it to the reviving of the dead earth.

The third: that He, exalted, is the Truth, and He would be so only if He were of complete power, perfect knowledge and wisdom. These are the aspects derived from this verse concerning the possibility of the soundness of the gathering and the resurrection.

The seventh verse in this category is His saying, exalted: ﴿Say: Be stones or iron, or a creation of what is greater in your breasts. They will say: Who will restore us? Say: He who brought you into being the first time﴾ [al-Isra: 50-51].

The fourth example: since He, exalted, is capable of fashioning what is greater than the bodies of people, how can it be said that He is unable to restore them? For whoever finds the harder act easy, the easier and lowlier act is all the more easy for him. This meaning is mentioned in many verses, among them His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ [Ya Sin: 81].

Second: His saying: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33].

Third: ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is the heaven He built?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27].

The fifth example: the argument from the occurrence of waking after sleep to the permissibility of gathering and resurrection. For sleep is the brother of death, and waking resembles life after death. He, exalted, said: ﴿And it is He who takes your souls by night and knows what you have earned by day﴾ [al-An'am: 60]. Then after it He mentioned the matter of death and resurrection, saying: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He sends over you guardians, until when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail. Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [al-An'am: 61-62]. And in another verse He said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], up to His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3]. What is meant by it is the argument from the occurrence of these states to the soundness of resurrection and gathering.

The sixth example: revival after death is considered strange only in that an opposite follows another opposite. Yet this is not strange in the power of God, exalted, for since the occurrence of death after life is permissible, how can the occurrence of life again after death be deemed remote? For the ruling on opposites is one. He, exalted, said establishing this meaning: ﴿We have decreed death among you, and We are not to be outdone﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 60]. Also we find fire, with its heat and dryness, produced from green trees with their coolness and moisture. He said: ﴿He who made for you fire from the green tree, and behold, you kindle from it﴾ [Ya Sin: 80]. So it is here too. This is the sum of the discussion on showing that the doctrine of the return, and the occurrence of gathering and resurrection, is not far-fetched to the intellects.

* * *

The second issue: establishing the proof that the return is true and obligatory.

Know that the community is of two groups. Among them are those who say: it is necessary by reason that the God of the world be merciful and just, free from inflicting pain and harm except for greater and more magnificent benefits. And among them are those who deny this principle and say: nothing at all is obligatory upon God, exalted; rather He does what He wills and decrees what He desires. As for the first group, they argued for the existence of the return from several aspects:

The first argument: He, exalted, created creatures and gave them intellects by which they distinguish between good and evil, and gave them powers by which they are able to do good and evil. When this is established, it is obligatory, in the wisdom and justice of God, exalted, that He prevent creatures from reviling God and speaking of Him with evil, and that He prevent them from ignorance and lying and from harming His prophets, His friends and the righteous among His creatures. And it is obligatory in His wisdom that He encourage them toward obedience, good deeds and virtues, for if He did not restrain them from those vices and did not encourage these goods, this would impugn His being benevolent, just, and regarding His servants. And it is known that encouragement toward obedience is not possible except by tying reward to performing it, and restraint from vices is not possible except by tying punishment to performing them. Yet the reward promised as an incentive and the punishment threatened as a deterrent are not realized in the abode of this world. Therefore there must be another abode in which this reward and this punishment are realized, and that is what is sought; otherwise it would follow that He is a liar, and that is false. This is what is meant by the verse we are discussing, His saying: ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾.

If it is said: why can it not be said that it suffices for encouraging good deeds and deterring wrongs that God has placed in intellects the perception of the goodness of good and the ugliness of wrongs, and that with this there is no need for promise and threat? And granting that promise and threat are necessary, why can it not be said that their purpose is merely encouragement and warning, so that the order of the world may be achieved thereby, as He, exalted, said: ﴿With this Allah makes His servants fear. O My servants, fear Me﴾ [al-Zumar: 16]? Then either He does this, so what is the proof of it? As for the claim that if He did not fulfil what He informed of as promise and threat, His speech would become false, we say: do you not specify most of the general statements of the Qur'an because of the existence of evidence obliging that specification? If this were a lie, then in those specifications you judge by, it would necessarily be a lie too? Granting that God, exalted, must do this, why can it not be said that that reward and punishment are an expression of what reaches a person of kinds of comforts and pleasures, and of kinds of pains and sicknesses, and categories of anxieties and sorrows?

The answer to the first question: although reason calls to doing good and abandoning evil, the self and the desire call a person to indulge in bodily appetites and physical pleasures. When this conflict arises, there must be a strong preponderating factor and a complete support, and that is nothing other than arranging promise and threat, reward and punishment, upon the doing and the abandoning.

The answer to the second question: when a person permits the occurrence of falsehood regarding God, exalted, then in that case no desire arises from the promise, nor fear from the threat, because the listener allows that it may be a lie.

The answer to the third question: as long as a servant's life is in this world, he is like a hired worker engaged in labour. A hired worker, while he is working, may not be paid his full wage, because if he takes it he will not exert himself in the work. But when the place where the wage is received is the Hereafter, striving in the work becomes greater and more complete. Moreover, we see in this world that the most ascetic and most knowledgeable of people are afflicted with various kinds of grief, worry and sorrow, while the most ignorant and most sinful enjoy pleasures and delights. So we know that the abode of recompense cannot be this abode, and there must be another abode and another life in which recompense takes place.

The second argument: clear reason requires, in the wisdom of the Wise, that He distinguish between the one who does good and the one who does evil, and that He not place the one who disbelieves in Him or denies Him in the same position as the one who obeys Him. Since this distinction must be made manifest, its occurrence is either in the abode of this world or in the abode of the Hereafter. The first is false, because we see the disbelievers and the sinners in this world in the greatest comfort, and we see the scholars and the ascetics in the opposite condition. For this very meaning God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community, We would have given to those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 33]. Thus it is established that after this abode there must be another abode, and this is the meaning of the verse we are explaining: ﴿That He may recompense those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾. It is also the meaning of His saying in Surat Taha: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Taha: 15], and of His saying in Surat Sad: ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on earth? Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28].

If it is said: Do you not deny that one might say that He, exalted is He, does not distinguish between the one who does good and the one who does evil in reward and punishment, just as He did not distinguish between them in beauty of form and abundance of wealth?

The answer: What you have mentioned actually strengthens our proof, for it is established by clear reason that the distinction is obligatory, and sense perception shows that this distinction did not occur in this world; rather, the matter is the opposite. We see the scholar and the ascetic in the greatest trials, and we see the disbeliever and the sinner in the greatest blessings. So we know that there must be another abode in which this disparity will become manifest. Also, it is not far-fetched to say that He, exalted is He, knew that if this ascetic worshipper were given what was given to the disbelieving sinner, he would transgress, rebel, and prefer the worldly life; and that if that disbelieving sinner were further restricted, he would increase in evil. To this the saying of God, exalted is He, refers: ﴿And if God were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 27].

[p. 18]

The third argument: God, exalted is He, has obligated His servants to worship Him, saying: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. When a Wise one commands His servant to do something, He must make him free of mind and orderly in his circumstances, so that he is able to occupy himself with fulfilling those obligations. But people are created with the disposition of seeking pleasures and acquiring comforts for themselves. So if they had no restraint from fear of the Return, disorder and confusion would multiply, and tumults would become great, and then the obligated person would not be free to occupy himself with performing acts of worship. Therefore it is necessary to affirm with certainty the existence of the abode of reward and punishment, so that the affairs of the world may be ordered and the obligated person may be able to occupy himself with performing servitude.

If it is said: Why is it not permissible to say that the awe of kings and their governance suffices for the preservation of the order of the world? Also, the rabble know that if they ruled by permitting disorder and confusion, the matter would turn against them, and others would be able to kill them and seize their wealth; so for this reason they avoid inciting strife.

The answer: Mere awe of rulers does not suffice for this. That is because the ruler either has reached such a degree of power and strength that he does not fear his subjects, or he fears them. If he does not fear his subjects, while having no fear of the Return, then he will proceed to oppression and harm in the most abominable ways, because the psychic motive is present, and there is no deterrent for him in this world or in the Hereafter. As for if he fears his subjects, then the subjects do not fear him intensely, so that fear does not become a deterrent for them from ugly deeds and oppression. Thus it is established that the order of the world is not completed and perfected except by desire for the Return and fear of it.

The fourth argument: When a dominant ruler has a number of servants, some of whom are strong and some weak, it is obligatory upon that ruler, if he is merciful, attentive and compassionate towards them, that he do justice to the oppressed weak one against the oppressive strong one. If he does not do so, he is content with that oppression, and contentment with oppression does not befit the merciful, attentive, benevolent one.

Having established this, we say: He, glorified is He, is a dominant, powerful, wise Sovereign, free from oppression and vanity. So it is necessary that He do justice for His oppressed servants against His oppressive servants. This justice has not been realised in this abode, because the oppressed may remain in utmost humiliation and abasement, and the oppressor may remain in utmost honour and power. So there must be another abode in which this justice and this fairness will become manifest. This argument can serve as an explanation of this verse which we are explaining.

If they say: Since He enabled the oppressor to oppress in this abode, and did not render him incapable of it, this shows that He is content with that oppression.

We say: Enabling one to oppress is the very same as enabling one to do justice and obedience. For if He had not enabled him to oppress, He would have rendered him incapable of doing good deeds and acts of obedience, and that does not befit the Wise. So it is required by reason that He enable him to both oppression and justice. Then He, exalted is He, avenges the oppressed against the oppressor.

The fifth argument: God, exalted is He, created this world and created every human being in it. Either it may be said that He created them for no benefit and no purpose, or it may be said that He created them for a purpose and a benefit. The first befits the Merciful, the Generous. The second, namely that it be said He created them for an aim, a benefit and a good, then that good and benefit either occurs in this world or in another abode. The first is false for two reasons. The first: the pleasures of this world are physical, and physical pleasures have no reality except the removal of pain, and the removal of pain is a negative matter, and this negation was present while each of the creatures was non-existent; and then there would be no benefit in creating. The second: the pleasures of this world are mixed with pains and trials; indeed, the world is overflowing with evils, calamities, trials and tribulations, and the pleasure in it is like a drop in the sea. So we know that the abode in which creation reaches those desired comforts is another abode apart from the abode of this world.

If they say: Does He not cause the people of the Fire to suffer the severest punishment, not for the sake of any benefit or wisdom? Why then is it not permissible to say that He creates creatures in this world not for a benefit or a wisdom?

We say: The difference is that that harm is harm deserved for their evil deeds, whereas the harm occurring in this world is not deserved. So it is necessary that it be followed by great goods and benefits that compensate for those past harms; otherwise it would follow that the Agent is evil and harmful, and that contradicts His being the Most Merciful of the merciful and the Most Generous of the generous.

The sixth argument: If a human being did not have a return, then the human being would be lower in rank and nobility than all the animals. The consequent is false, so the antecedent is likewise false. The explanation of the implication: the harms that befall a human being in this world are more numerous than the harms that befall all animals. For the rest of the animals, before falling into pains and diseases, are free of mind and content in soul, because they have no thought or reflection. As for the human being, by means of the intellect he has, he constantly reflects on past and future circumstances. So through most past circumstances he acquires kinds of sorrow and regret, and through most future circumstances he acquires kinds of fear, because he does not know how circumstances will come about. Thus it is established that the intellect's presence in the human being is a cause of great harms in this world and of intense and powerful psychic pains. As for physical pleasures, they are shared between humans and the rest of the animals, because dung tastes pleasant to the dung beetle, just as the sweet called lawzinaj tastes pleasant to the human.

Having established this, we say: If a human being had no return through which his state is completed and his felicity becomes manifest, then it would be necessary that the perfection of the intellect be a cause of increased worries, griefs and sorrows without any remedy that compensates for them. And it is known that whatever is like this is a cause of increased lowliness, baseness, wretchedness and fatigue devoid of benefit. Thus it is established that, were it not for the attainment of otherworldly felicity, the human being would be the lowliest of animals, even below beetles and worms. Since that is certainly false, we know that there must be the Hereafter, that the human being was created for the Hereafter and not for this world, and that by his intellect he acquires the causes of otherworldly felicities. For this reason the intellect is noble.

The seventh argument: God, exalted is He, is able to bestow blessings upon His servants in two ways. One is that the blessings be mixed with afflictions and sorrows. The second is that they be free of these. Since God, exalted is He, has bestowed blessings in this world in the first degree, it is necessary that He bestow upon us the second degree in another abode, to manifest the perfection of power, mercy and wisdom. There He bestows favours upon the obedient, pardons the sinners, and removes griefs, worries, desires and doubts. What strengthens this and establishes this discourse is that the human being, when he was an embryo in his mother's womb, was in the narrowest place and the most foul and corrupt. Then when he emerges from his mother's womb, the second state is better and more noble than the first. Then he is placed in the cradle and tightly bound; then after a time he leaves the cradle, runs to the right and left, and moves from taking milk to taking good foods. This third state is undoubtedly better than the second. Then after a time he becomes a commander with authority over creation, or a scholar elevated over the realities of things. Undoubtedly this fourth state is better and more noble than the third. Once this is established, it is necessary by the force of this inductive reasoning to say: the state that comes after death will be more noble, higher and more joyful than the physical pleasures and bodily goods.

The eighth argument: the method of precaution. For if we believe in the Return and prepare for it, then if this doctrine is true, we are saved and the denier is ruined; and if it is false, this belief does not harm us. The most that can be said is that these physical pleasures will escape us. But we say: it is obligatory upon the intelligent person not to care about losing them, for two reasons. One: they are of the utmost baseness, because they are shared with beetles, worms and dogs. Two: they are cut off and quick to vanish. Thus it is established that precaution lies only in belief in the Return. For this reason the poet said:

The astrologer and the physician both said: "The dead will not be raised." I said to you both:
"If your saying is true, I am not a loser; but if my saying is true, then the loss is upon you both."

[The text ends here]

**The Ninth Argument:** Know that as long as an animal is alive, if something is cut from it, such as a nail, a hoof, or hair, that thing grows back; and if it is wounded, the wound heals, while the blood flows through its veins and organs the way water flows through the roots and branches of a tree. Then, when it dies, these conditions are reversed: if something is cut from its hair or nail, it does not grow back; and if it is wounded, it does not heal or knit together, and you see the blood congealing in its veins. Eventually its condition comes to decay and dissolution. Then, when we looked at the earth, we found it similar to this description. We see that in the season of spring its springs gush forth, its hills swell, and water is drawn up into the branches and roots of the trees, while water in the earth is in the position of the blood flowing in the body of an animal. Then its blossoms, flowers and fruits emerge, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and produces every lovely kind of growth﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. If something is cut from its plants, it is replaced and another like it grows in its place; if a branch of a tree is cut, it is replaced; and if it is wounded, it heals. These conditions are similar to the conditions we described for the animal. Then, when winter comes and the cold grows intense, its springs dry up, its moisture dries away, and its herbs decay; and if we cut a branch from a tree, it is not replaced. These conditions are thus similar to death after life. Then we see the earth return to that life in the second spring. So if we understand these meanings in one of the two cases, why should we not understand the same in the second case? Indeed, we say: there is no doubt that man is more noble than the rest of the animals, the animal is more noble than the plant, and the plant is more noble than the inanimate. So if these conditions occur in the earth, why should it not be possible for them to occur in man?!

If they say: the bodies of animals are scattered and torn apart by death, but the earth is not like that.

The answer: man is a term for the rational soul, which is a subsisting substance; or, if we do not hold this view, then he is a term for original parts that remain from the first moment of the embryo's formation to the end of life, which flow through the body, and those parts remain. Thus this objection is removed.

**The Tenth Argument:** There is no doubt that the body of an animal is generated only from the semen, and this semen is gathered from the entire body, as evidenced by the fact that when the semen is separated, weakness and lassitude occur throughout the whole body. Then the substance of that semen is generated from the foods eaten, and those foods are generated from the elemental parts, and those parts were scattered in the eastern and western regions of the earth, and it happened that they came together and from them an animal or a plant was produced, which a human ate; from it blood was generated, and that blood was distributed among his organs, and from it subtle parts were generated. Then, when desire is aroused, a certain quantity of those moisture escapes, which is the semen, and it pours into the mouth of the womb, and from it this human is generated. Thus it is established that the parts from which the human body was generated were scattered in the seas, the mountains and the heights of the air; then they came together by the aforementioned way, and from them this body was generated; and when it dies, those parts are scattered again in the manner of the first scattering.

Since this is established, we say: it is also certain that it is not impossible for them to come together again in the manner of the first gathering. Furthermore, when that semen fell into the mother's womb, it was a small drop; then the human body was generated from it, and the soul was attached to it while that body was in extreme smallness. Then there is no doubt that this body is in extreme moistness, and there is no doubt that many parts of it dissolve because of the operation of the innate heat within it. Also, those bodily parts that remain perpetually throughout the length of life are in a state of dissolution; were it not so, hunger would not occur, and the need for nourishment would not arise. Moreover, we are certain that this aged human is the very same person who was in his mother's belly, then separated and was a child, then a youth. Thus it is established that the bodily parts are constantly dissolving, and that the human is the very same person. Therefore it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the human is either a separate, pure substance, or a subtle luminous body that remains despite the dissolution of this body. If this is so, then under either supposition it is not impossible for it to return to the body again, and this returning human will be the very same as the first human. Thus it is established that the doctrine of the resurrection is true.

**The Eleventh Argument:** What God the Exalted mentioned in His saying: ﴿Does not man see that We created him from a drop of semen, and then he is a manifest adversary?﴾ Know that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿We created him from a drop of semen﴾ [Ya-Sin: 77] points to what we mentioned in the tenth argument, that those parts were scattered in the eastern and western regions of the earth, and God gathered them and created this animal from their composition. What strengthens this is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ ﴿Then We made him a drop in a firm place﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12, 13]. The interpretation of this verse is only correct in the way we have mentioned: that from the extract of clay a plant is produced, and then man eats that plant, and from it blood is generated, and then the blood turns into semen; in this way the apparent meaning of this verse is consistent. Then, after mentioning this meaning, He, glorified is He, related the words of the denier, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: Who will give life to the bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78]. Then He, exalted is He, clarified the possibility of this doctrine.

Know that establishing the possibility of a thing is conceivable only by two methods. One is to say: its like is possible, so this too must be possible. The second is to say: that which is greater than it and higher in status is also possible. Then He, exalted is He, first mentioned the first method, saying: ﴿Say: He who produced them the first time will give them life, and He is Knowing of every creation﴾ [Ya-Sin: 79]. Then there is a subtle point in it: His saying ﴿Say: He will give them life﴾ points to the perfection of power, and His saying ﴿and He is Knowing of every creation﴾ points to the perfection of knowledge. The deniers of the Gathering and Resurrection deny it only out of ignorance of these two principles; for at times they say that He, exalted is He, acts by necessity of His essence, and that which acts by necessity of its essence cannot intentionally bring about creation; and at other times they say that it is impossible for Him to be knowing of particulars, so it is impossible for Him to distinguish the parts of Zayd's body from the parts of 'Amr's body. Since the doubts of the philosophers are derived from these two principles, it is inevitable that whenever God the Exalted mentions the question of the resurrection, He follows it with the affirmation of these two principles. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned after that the second method, which is inference from the higher to the lower. Its explanation is in two respects. The first: life is not produced except by heat and moisture, while dust is cold and dry, so there is opposition between them. However, we say: fiery heat is stronger in the quality of heat than innate heat. So since the generation of fiery heat from the green tree is not impossible, despite the complete opposition between them, how can the occurrence of innate heat in the substance of dust be impossible? The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81], meaning: since you have conceded that He, exalted is He, is the creator of the bodies of the spheres and the stars, how can you then deny His power to effect the Gathering and Resurrection? Then He, exalted is He, cut off the source of doubts by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40]. The meaning is that His fashioning and creating do not depend on the availability of instruments, tools, the father's semen, or the mother's womb. The proof of this is that He created the first father not from a previous father, which shows that He, glorified is He, is independent in creation, origination and bringing into being from intermediaries and instruments.
