The first issue: concerning the interpretation of this "expectation" (raja'), there are two views.

The first view, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and al-Kalbi, is that its meaning is: they do not fear the resurrection (ba'th). The meaning is that they do not fear it because they do not believe in it. The evidence for interpreting "expectation" here as "fear" is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45], and His saying: ﴿and they are apprehensive of the Hour﴾ [al-Anbiya': 49]. Interpreting "expectation" as "fear" is permissible, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not expect dignity from God?﴾ [Nuh: 13]. The Hudhali poet said:

When the bee stings him, he does not expect its sting [i.e., he does not fear it].

The second view: interpreting "expectation" as "hope" (ta'mma). So His saying ﴿do not expect to meet Us﴾ means: they do not hope for Our reward. This expectation is then the one whose opposite is despair, as He said: ﴿They have despaired of the Hereafter as the disbelievers have despaired﴾.

Know that carrying "expectation" on "fear" is far-fetched, because interpreting an opposite as its opposite is not permissible. And there is no obstacle here to taking "expectation" in its plain meaning at all. The evidence for this is that "meeting God" either means the manifestation of God's majesty to the servant and the shining of the light of His greatness upon his spirit, or it means arriving at God's reward and His mercy. If it is the first, it is the greatest of ranks, the most noble of felicities and the most perfect of goods, so how could the intelligent person not hope for it, and how could he not wish for it? If it is the second, it is likewise, because everyone hopes from God, exalted is He, that He will bring him to His reward and the stations of His mercy. Given this, everyone who believes in God hopes for His reward, and everyone who does not believe in God or in the Last Day has himself nullified this hope. Therefore it is rightly good to make the absence of this hope a metonym (kinaya) for the absence of belief in God and the Last Day.

The second issue: "meeting" (liqa') is arriving at a thing. This is impossible with regard to God, exalted is He, since He is exalted above limit and finitude, so it must be taken as a metaphor for "seeing" (ru'ya). This is a clear metaphor, for it is said: "I met so-and-so" when one sees him. Taking it to mean "meeting God's reward" requires adding an extra ellipsis, which goes against the evidence.

Know that it has been established by certain proofs that the happiness of the soul after death lies in the manifestation within it of the knowledge of God, exalted is He, its illumination being perfected and its radiance strengthened. That is the vision (ru'ya), and it is among the greatest felicities. Whoever is heedless of seeking it, turning away from it, content after death with finding the sensory pleasures of eating, drinking and sexual intercourse, is among the misguided.

The second attribute of these disbelievers is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and are content with the life of this world﴾.

Know that the first attribute indicates the emptiness of his heart from seeking spiritual pleasures and its vacancy from seeking the felicities attained through divine knowledges. As for this second attribute, it indicates his absorption in seeking bodily pleasures, his contentment with them, and his immersion in seeking them.

The third attribute is His saying: ﴿and are at rest in it﴾, and concerning it there are two issues:

The first issue: the attribute of the happy is that they experience some kind of trembling and fear at the mention of God, as He said: ﴿Those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned﴾ [al-Anfal: 2]. Then, when this state grows strong, tranquility (tuma'nina) in the remembrance of God arises, as He said: ﴿Their hearts find rest in the remembrance of God; indeed, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28]. The attribute of the wretched is that they attain tranquility in loving the world and in occupying themselves with seeking its pleasures, as He said in this verse: ﴿and are at rest in it﴾.

Page 33

The reality of tranquility is that trembling is removed from their hearts. So when they hear warning and intimidation, their hearts do not tremble, and they become like dead things at the mention of God, exalted is He.

The second issue: the grammatical expectation of the language would be to say "wa-tma'annu ilayha" (and they are at rest toward it). However, prepositions may appropriately stand in place of one another, and for this reason He said: ﴿and are at rest in it﴾.

The fourth attribute is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and those who are heedless of Our signs﴾. The meaning is that in turning away from seeking the meeting with God, exalted is He, they have become like one who is heedless of a thing that never occurs to his mind throughout his life. In sum, these four attributes indicate the extent of his distance from seeking to attain felicity through the otherworldly, spiritual felicities, and the extent of his absorption in seeking these bodily goods and worldly felicities.

Know that when God, exalted is He, described them with these four attributes, He said: ﴿Those, their refuge is the Fire because of what they used to earn.﴾ Concerning it there are two issues:

The first issue: fires are of kinds. There is the fire which is a sensible, luminous, burning body that rises by its nature, and affirming it is obligatory, because it has been established by the proofs mentioned that affirming Paradise and Hell is true.

The second kind: the spiritual, intellectual fire. Its explanation is that whoever loves something intensely, and then that thing is lost to him such that he cannot reach it, his heart and inner being burn. Every intelligent person says: "So-and-so is heartbroken and burning inwardly because of separation from that beloved." The pain of this fire is far greater than the pain of the sensible fire.

Knowing this, we say: the souls that were absorbed in love of bodily things and were heedless of love of the spiritual realm, when that person dies, separation occurs between that soul and its objects of love and desire, which are the states of this world. It has no knowledge of that world and no familiarity with its people. Its likeness is that of one who is removed from the company of his beloved and cast into a dark well with which he has no familiarity and about whose conditions he has no knowledge. This person will be in extreme loneliness and the soul's anguish. So it is here. But if one was averse to these bodily things, aware of their ugliness and defects, and very eager to grasp the firmest handhold, greatly loving God, his likeness is that of one imprisoned in a dark, foul prison filled with harmful insects and deadly calamities, and then it happened that the prison door was opened, he was brought out and presented in the assembly of the greatest sultan together with his beloved and friends, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are with those whom God has blessed of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous; and excellent are those as companions﴾ [al-Nisa': 69]. This is the indication of the definition of the spiritual Fire and the spiritual Paradise.

The second issue: the "bi" in His saying ﴿because of what they used to earn﴾ indicates that their former deeds are what effect the attainment of this punishment. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because of what your hands have sent forth, and because God is not unjust to the servants﴾ [al-Hajj: 10].

[Page 34]

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them by their faith. Rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ ﴿Their call therein will be: "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein will be: "Peace." And the last of their call will be: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had described the condition of the deniers and disbelievers in the previous verse, He mentioned in this verse the condition of the true believers. Know also that He, exalted is He, first mentioned their attributes, then mentioned the lofty conditions and elevated ranks that they have. As for their conditions and attributes, they are in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. There are several interpretations of this:

The first interpretation: The human soul has two powers:
The theoretical power, whose perfection lies in knowing things, and whose chief and sovereign is the knowledge of Allah.
The practical power, whose perfection lies in doing good deeds and acts of obedience, and whose chief and sovereign is the service of Allah. So His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ points to the perfection of the theoretical power through knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and His saying ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ points to the perfection of the practical power through the service of Allah, the Exalted. And since the theoretical power precedes the practical power in honour and rank, it is necessarily mentioned first.

The second interpretation of this verse: Al-Qaffal said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ means: they affirmed with their hearts, then they realised that affirmation through righteous action, which the prophets and the books from Allah, the Exalted, brought.

The third interpretation: ﴿Those who believe﴾ means they occupied their hearts and spirits with acquiring knowledge. ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾ means they occupied their limbs with service. Thus their eyes are occupied with reflection, as He said: ﴿So take warning, O people of vision﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]. Their ears are occupied with hearing the speech of Allah, the Exalted, as He said: ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 83]. Their tongues are occupied with the remembrance of Allah, as the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, remember Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 41]. Their limbs are occupied with the light of obedience to Allah, as He said: ﴿Why do they not prostrate to Allah, who brings out what is hidden in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Naml: 25].

* * *

Know that when He, exalted is He, described them with faith and righteous deeds, He then mentioned the degrees of their honours and the levels of their felicities, and these are four.

The first rank is His saying: ﴿Their Lord will guide them by their faith. Rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Concerning His saying ﴿their Lord will guide them by their faith﴾ there are several interpretations:
The first: He, exalted is He, guides them to Paradise as a reward for their faith and their righteous deeds. What indicates the soundness of this interpretation are several points, one of which is His saying: ﴿On the Day you will see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and on their right﴾ [al-Hadid: 12].
The second: What has been narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, when the believer comes out of his grave, his deed is presented to him in a beautiful form, and it says to him: 'I am your deed.' So it becomes for him a light and a guide to Paradise. And when the disbeliever comes out of his grave, his deed is presented to him in an evil form, and it says to him: 'I am your deed,' so it takes him away until it brings him into the Fire."
The third: Mujahid said: The believers will have a light that walks with them to Paradise.
The fourth, which is the rational interpretation: Faith is an expression for a light that has been connected to them from the world of holiness. That light is like a thread connecting the heart of the believer with that holy world. If this luminous thread is obtained, the servant is able to follow that light and return to the world of holiness. But if this luminous cord is not found, he wanders in the darkness of the world of misguidance, we seek refuge in Allah from it.

[Page 35]

The second interpretation: Ibn al-Anbari said: Their faith guides them to special qualities in knowledge, excellences in expressions, and flashes of light by which their hearts are illuminated, and through which doubts and misgivings are removed from them, as in His saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad: 17]. These increases, additions, and excellences may be attained in this world before death, and may be attained in the Hereafter after death. Al-Qaffal said: If we take the verse according to this interpretation, the meaning is: "Their Lord will guide them by their faith, and rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss," except that the conjunction "and" has been omitted, and His saying "flow" has been made a new, separate statement, disconnected from what precedes it.

The third interpretation: The discussion of this verse must be preceded by premises.

The first premise: Knowledge is light and ignorance is darkness. Clear reason bears witness that the matter is so. What confirms this is that if you put a noble and important question to two persons, and one of them understands it while the other does not, you will see the face of the one who understands radiant, bright and shining, and the face of the one who does not understand gloomy, dark and contracted. For this reason, the custom of the Qur'an is to express knowledge and faith by light, and ignorance and disbelief by darkness.

The second premise: The spirit is like a tablet, and knowledges and cognitions are like engravings inscribed upon that tablet. Here there is a subtle point: when a physical tablet has physical engravings drawn upon it, the presence of some engravings on that tablet prevents the presence of the rest of the engravings on it. But the tablet of the spirit is of the opposite nature: when the spirit is empty of engravings of cognitions and knowledges, it becomes difficult for it to acquire cognitions and knowledges. Then, when it strives and acquires some of them, the acquisition of what it has acquired helps it to acquire the rest more easily, and the more it has acquired, the easier the acquisition of the remainder becomes. So physical engravings, some of them prevent the acquisition of the rest, while spiritual engravings, some of them aid in the acquisition of the rest. This indicates that the conditions of the spiritual world are the opposite of the conditions of the physical world.

The third premise: Righteous deeds are the deeds that lead the soul to abandon this world and seek the Hereafter, while blameworthy deeds are the opposite of that.

Having known these premises, we say: When a person believes in Allah, his spirit is illuminated by the light of this knowledge. Then, when he persists in righteous deeds, there comes to be in him a firm disposition toward turning to the Hereafter and turning away from this world. And the more complete these states are, the stronger the soul's readiness to acquire the rest of the knowledges becomes. And the stronger and more complete the readiness, the more the ascending stages of knowledge become, and the stronger their radiance and shining. And since the degrees of knowledge and intellectual lights have no end, there is necessarily no end to the degrees of this guidance indicated by His saying: ﴿their Lord will guide them by their faith﴾.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿Rivers will flow beneath them﴾. What is meant by it is that they will be sitting on raised couches in gardens, and the rivers will flow from in front of them. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Your Lord has made beneath you a stream﴾ [Maryam: 24], where "beneath" was the ground on which she was sitting, but the meaning is "in front of you." Likewise His saying: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 51], meaning "in front of me." So it is the same here.

[Page 36]

The third issue: Faith is knowledge, and the guidance that follows from it is also of the kind of knowledges. Then, He, exalted is He, did not say "their Lord will guide them to their faith," but said: ﴿their Lord will guide them by their faith﴾. This indicates that knowing the two premises does not necessarily produce knowing the conclusion; rather, knowing the two premises is a cause for the arising of a complete readiness in the soul to receive the conclusion. Then, when this readiness has arisen, the bringing-into-being comes from the Real, glorified and exalted is He. This is the meaning of the saying of the philosophers that the absolute Bestower and the True Giver is none other than Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

* * *

The second rank of their felicities and the degrees of their perfections is His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Their call therein will be: "Glory be to You, O Allah"﴾. On this there are issues:

The first issue: Concerning "their call" there are several interpretations:
The first: The call here means supplication. It is said: "He called (da'a), calls, a call (du'a') and a calling (da'wa)," just as it is said: "He complained (shaka), complains, a complaint (shika'ah) and a complaint (shakwa)." Some exegetes said: "Their call" means their supplication. And He said concerning the people of Paradise: ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they ask for﴾ [Ya-Sin: 57], and He said in another verse: ﴿They call therein for every fruit, in security﴾ [al-Dukhan: 55]. What strengthens that the meaning of "call" here is supplication is that they said: "O Allah," and this is an address to Allah, glorified and exalted is He. The meaning of their saying: ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ is: "We glorify You," like the saying of the one who stands in prayer in the supplication of qunut: "O Allah, You alone we worship."
The second: The supplication may be meant as worship. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and what you call upon besides Allah﴾ [Maryam: 48], meaning "what you worship." So the meaning of the verse is that there is no worship for the people of Paradise except that they glorify Allah and praise Him, and their occupation with that remembrance is not by way of obligation, but by way of delight in the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted.
The third: Some said: It is not far-fetched that what is meant by "call" is the very claim that one party makes against another. The meaning is that the people of Paradise call, in this world and in the Hereafter, to the glorifying of Allah, the Exalted, from every fault, and to acknowledging His divinity. Al-Qaffal said: The origin of this is also from supplication, because the litigant calls his adversary to one who will judge between them.
The fourth: Muslim said: "Their call" means their saying, their acknowledgement and their crying out, and that is their saying: ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾.
The fifth: Al-Qadi said: What is meant by His saying ﴿their call﴾ is their way of glorifying Allah, the Exalted, and sanctifying Him, and their custom and practice. The proof that this is what is meant is that His saying ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ is neither a supplication nor a claim, but the one who claims something is constantly mindful of it, so He made the word "call" a metaphor for that constancy and perpetual adherence. Since the people of Paradise were constant in this remembrance, the word "call" was therefore applied to it.
The sixth: Al-Qaffal said: It has been said concerning His saying ﴿and for them is whatever they call for﴾ [Ya-Sin: 57] that it means "what they wish for." The Arabs say: "Call for whatever you want against me," meaning: "wish." Ibn Jurayj said: I was informed that His saying ﴿Their call therein is: Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ means that when a bird passes by them which they desire, they say: "Glory be to You, O Allah," and the angel brings them that desired thing. So the interpretation of the verse has come out, from this aspect, as meaning that when they desire something they say: "Glory be to You, O Allah," so the meaning of their call is what arises in their hearts of wishing. In this interpretation there is another aspect, which is better and more noble than what preceded, namely that the meaning is that their wish in Paradise is to glorify Allah, the Exalted, i.e., their wish for what they wish for is nothing but glorifying Allah, the Exalted, and sanctifying Him and declaring Him free of imperfection.
The seventh: Al-Qaffal also said: It is possible that the meaning of "call" is what they used to call out to in the world during their times of war, to those in whom they took refuge and whose help they sought, such as their saying: "O family of so-and-so." So Allah, the Exalted, informed that their intimacy in Paradise is in remembering Allah, the Exalted, their tranquillity is in praising Allah, and their delight is in glorifying Allah, the Exalted.

[Page 37]

The second issue: His saying ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ has two aspects:

The first view: those who say that the people of Paradise made this remembrance a sign of seeking desirable things. Ibn Jurayj said: when a bird passes by them and they desire it, they say, "Glory be to You, O Allah," and it is brought to them; and when they have attained their desire from it, they say, ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. Al-Kalbi said: their saying ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ is a signal between the people of Paradise and the servants, so when they hear it from them, they bring them what they desire. Know that this view is, in my opinion, very weak, and its clarification is from several aspects:

The first: the upshot of this statement comes back to the claim that the people of Paradise made this lofty, sanctified remembrance a sign for seeking food, drink, and spouses, and this is in utmost baseness.

The second: He, exalted is He, said concerning the people of Paradise: ﴿And for them is whatever they desire﴾. So when they desire the eating of that bird, they have no need to seek it; and when they have no need to seek, this statement collapses.

The third: this requires turning the speech away from its noble, lofty outward meaning toward a base interpretation to which the wording gives no indication, and this is false.

The second interpretation of this verse is that we say: what is meant is the occupation of the people of Paradise with the sanctification of Allah, glorified is He, and the praise of Him, because their happiness lies in this remembrance, their delight in it, their joy in it, and the perfection of their state comes only from it. This view is the correct one from which there is no escape. Then, on this basis, there are several aspects to the verse. The first: al-Qadi said: He, exalted is He, promised the God-fearing a great reward, as He mentioned at the beginning of this surah in His saying: ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾. So when the people of Paradise enter Paradise and find those great blessings, they know that Allah, exalted is He, was truthful in His promise to them of those blessings; at this point they say: ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾, meaning: we glorify You above breaking promises and lying in speech.

The second: we say: the ultimate happiness of the happy and the final stage of the ranks of the prophets and the saints is their being made happy by the levels of knowledge of the Majesty.

Know that knowing the essence of Allah, exalted is He, and comprehending the reality of His true nature is something no path lies open to creation for; rather, the highest attainment is knowing His negative attributes or His relational attributes. As for the negative attributes, they are called the attributes of Majesty (jalal), and as for the relational attributes, they are called the attributes of Bounty (ikram). Therefore the perfection of the lofty remembrance is confined to these, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Bounty﴾ [al-Rahman: 78]. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "Persist in calling upon Owner of Majesty and Bounty." And since negations are prior in rank to relations, therefore the mention of Majesty precedes the mention of Bounty in wording. And since it is established that the ultimate happiness of the happy lies only in these two stations, He, exalted is He, mentioned their being constant in this lofty, sanctified remembrance. And since there is no end to the ascents of the Majesty of Allah, nor any limit to the stages of His divinity, His bounty, and His beneficence, likewise there is no end to the ranks of the ascent of sanctified souls in these lofty divine stations.

The third: the nearest angels were, before the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, occupied with this remembrance. Do you not see that they said: ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. So the Real, glorified is He, inspired the happy among the children of Adam until they uttered this glorification and praise, to show that what the nearest angels uttered before the creation of the world is from the lofty remembrance, and the very same was uttered by the happy among the children of Adam, peace be upon him, after the passing away of the world. And since this remembrance contains this lofty honor, therefore a report has come of its recitation at the beginning of the prayer: when the one praying says the takbir, he says: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You, Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god besides You."

* * *

The third level of the stations of the happiness of the people of Paradise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and their greeting therein is peace﴾. The commentators said: the greeting of some of them to others is by peace, and the greeting of the angels to them is by peace, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying], "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23–24]. And the greeting of Allah, exalted is He, to them is also by peace, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. Al-Wahidi said: on this interpretation, this is an idafa of the verbal noun to its object. But in my view there is another aspect: that their constancy in mentioning this word indicates that they were in the world in a place of calamities and in a position of fears; so when they are brought out of the world and reach the honor of Allah, exalted is He, they have become safe from calamities, secure from fears and deficiencies. Allah, exalted is He, has informed of them that they mention this meaning in His saying: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us [all] sorrow. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative. [He] who has settled us in the home of settlement by His bounty; there touches us not therein fatigue, and there touches us not therein weariness"﴾ [Fatir: 34–35].

* * *

The fourth level of their stations of happiness is His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And the last of their call will be: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ Concerning it there are questions:

The first question: We have mentioned that a group of the commentators took these lofty, sanctified words to refer to the states of the people of Paradise with respect to eating and drinking. They said: when the people of Paradise desire something, they say, "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You"; and when they have eaten and are finished, they say, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds." But this speaker's gaze has not risen, in his worldly life or his next life, above food and drink, and such a person deserves to be counted among the herd of beasts. As for the genuine verifiers, they have abandoned that, and they have views on it. Al-Hasan al-Basri narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The people of Paradise are inspired with praise and glorification just as you are inspired with your breaths." Al-Zajjaj said: in my view on this matter there are other aspects:

The first of them: that when the people of Paradise were made happy by the remembrance "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You," and beheld what they were in of safety from calamities and fears, they knew that all these exalted states and sanctified stations were made easy only by the goodness, bounty, and favor of the Real, glorified is He; therefore they were necessarily occupied with praise and commendation, and they said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ The conclusion of this speech came about because their occupation with glorifying and extolling Allah, exalted is He, is among the greatest of the blessings of Allah upon them; and occupation with thanking for a blessing comes after seeing that blessing, and for this reason this word was made the conclusion.

The second: that every person has, according to his strength, a ladder of ascent; at times he descends from that ladder, and at times he ascends to it. The ladder of the knowers who are truthful is the knowledge of Allah, the glorifying of Allah, and the praising of Allah; so when they say ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ they are in the very midst of the ladder; and when they descend from it to the world of created beings, the outcome of that descent is the overflow of goodness upon all who are in need, and to this the saying refers: ﴿and their greeting therein is peace﴾. Then again they ascend to their ladder, and upon ascending they say: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ So these lofty words are an indication of the variation of the servant's states through descent and ascent.

The third: we say: our saying "Allah" is a name for the essence of the Real, glorified is He. At times the servant looks to the attributes of Majesty, which are indicated by His saying ﴿Glory be to You﴾; then he seeks to ascend from them toward the presence of the Majesty of the essence, an ascent befitting human capacity, which is indicated by His saying "O Allah." Then, when he moves on from that place, and passes through the first of those lights, he returns to the world of Bounty, which is indicated by His saying ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ These are words that occurred to the mind and turned in the imagination; if they are correct, then the success is from Allah, exalted is He, and if they are not so, then reliance is upon the mercy of Allah, exalted is He.

The second question: Al-Wahidi said: the "an" in His saying ﴿an al-hamdu lillah﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy (anna), and for this reason it does not govern, since by lightening it has departed from resemblance to the verb, as in the line of verse: "Verily, every one who goes barefoot and wears sandals is perishing," meaning that he is perishing. The author of al-Nazm said: the "an" here is superfluous, and the sense is: "And the last of their call is: Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds." But this view is worth nothing. Some of them read "anna al-hamda" with the heavy form and the accusative "al-hamda."

[Page 34]

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them by their faith. Rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ ﴿Their call therein will be: "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein will be: "Peace." And the last of their call will be: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had described the condition of the deniers and disbelievers in the previous verse, He mentioned in this verse the condition of the true believers. Know also that He, exalted is He, first mentioned their attributes, then mentioned the lofty conditions and elevated ranks that they have. As for their conditions and attributes, they are in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. There are several interpretations of this:

The first interpretation: The human soul has two powers:
The theoretical power, whose perfection lies in knowing things, and whose chief and sovereign is the knowledge of Allah.
The practical power, whose perfection lies in doing good deeds and acts of obedience, and whose chief and sovereign is the service of Allah. So His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ points to the perfection of the theoretical power through knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and His saying ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ points to the perfection of the practical power through the service of Allah, the Exalted. And since the theoretical power precedes the practical power in honour and rank, it is necessarily mentioned first.

The second interpretation of this verse: Al-Qaffal said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ means: they affirmed with their hearts, then they realised that affirmation through righteous action, which the prophets and the books from Allah, the Exalted, brought.

The third interpretation: ﴿Those who believe﴾ means they occupied their hearts and spirits with acquiring knowledge. ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾ means they occupied their limbs with service. Thus their eyes are occupied with reflection, as He said: ﴿So take warning, O people of vision﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]. Their ears are occupied with hearing the speech of Allah, the Exalted, as He said: ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 83]. Their tongues are occupied with the remembrance of Allah, as the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, remember Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 41]. Their limbs are occupied with the light of obedience to Allah, as He said: ﴿Why do they not prostrate to Allah, who brings out what is hidden in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Naml: 25].

* * *

Know that when He, exalted is He, described them with faith and righteous deeds, He then mentioned the degrees of their honours and the levels of their felicities, and these are four.

The first rank is His saying: ﴿Their Lord will guide them by their faith. Rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Concerning His saying ﴿their Lord will guide them by their faith﴾ there are several interpretations:
The first: He, exalted is He, guides them to Paradise as a reward for their faith and their righteous deeds. What indicates the soundness of this interpretation are several points, one of which is His saying: ﴿On the Day you will see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and on their right﴾ [al-Hadid: 12].
The second: What has been narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, when the believer comes out of his grave, his deed is presented to him in a beautiful form, and it says to him: 'I am your deed.' So it becomes for him a light and a guide to Paradise. And when the disbeliever comes out of his grave, his deed is presented to him in an evil form, and it says to him: 'I am your deed,' so it takes him away until it brings him into the Fire."
The third: Mujahid said: The believers will have a light that walks with them to Paradise.
The fourth, which is the rational interpretation: Faith is an expression for a light that has been connected to them from the world of holiness. That light is like a thread connecting the heart of the believer with that holy world. If this luminous thread is obtained, the servant is able to follow that light and return to the world of holiness. But if this luminous cord is not found, he wanders in the darkness of the world of misguidance, we seek refuge in Allah from it.

[Page 35]

The second interpretation: Ibn al-Anbari said: Their faith guides them to special qualities in knowledge, excellences in expressions, and flashes of light by which their hearts are illuminated, and through which doubts and misgivings are removed from them, as in His saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad: 17]. These increases, additions, and excellences may be attained in this world before death, and may be attained in the Hereafter after death. Al-Qaffal said: If we take the verse according to this interpretation, the meaning is: "Their Lord will guide them by their faith, and rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss," except that the conjunction "and" has been omitted, and His saying "flow" has been made a new, separate statement, disconnected from what precedes it.

The third interpretation: The discussion of this verse must be preceded by premises.

The first premise: Knowledge is light and ignorance is darkness. Clear reason bears witness that the matter is so. What confirms this is that if you put a noble and important question to two persons, and one of them understands it while the other does not, you will see the face of the one who understands radiant, bright and shining, and the face of the one who does not understand gloomy, dark and contracted. For this reason, the custom of the Qur'an is to express knowledge and faith by light, and ignorance and disbelief by darkness.

The second premise: The spirit is like a tablet, and knowledges and cognitions are like engravings inscribed upon that tablet. Here there is a subtle point: when a physical tablet has physical engravings drawn upon it, the presence of some engravings on that tablet prevents the presence of the rest of the engravings on it. But the tablet of the spirit is of the opposite nature: when the spirit is empty of engravings of cognitions and knowledges, it becomes difficult for it to acquire cognitions and knowledges. Then, when it strives and acquires some of them, the acquisition of what it has acquired helps it to acquire the rest more easily, and the more it has acquired, the easier the acquisition of the remainder becomes. So physical engravings, some of them prevent the acquisition of the rest, while spiritual engravings, some of them aid in the acquisition of the rest. This indicates that the conditions of the spiritual world are the opposite of the conditions of the physical world.

The third premise: Righteous deeds are the deeds that lead the soul to abandon this world and seek the Hereafter, while blameworthy deeds are the opposite of that.

Having known these premises, we say: When a person believes in Allah, his spirit is illuminated by the light of this knowledge. Then, when he persists in righteous deeds, there comes to be in him a firm disposition toward turning to the Hereafter and turning away from this world. And the more complete these states are, the stronger the soul's readiness to acquire the rest of the knowledges becomes. And the stronger and more complete the readiness, the more the ascending stages of knowledge become, and the stronger their radiance and shining. And since the degrees of knowledge and intellectual lights have no end, there is necessarily no end to the degrees of this guidance indicated by His saying: ﴿their Lord will guide them by their faith﴾.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿Rivers will flow beneath them﴾. What is meant by it is that they will be sitting on raised couches in gardens, and the rivers will flow from in front of them. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Your Lord has made beneath you a stream﴾ [Maryam: 24], where "beneath" was the ground on which she was sitting, but the meaning is "in front of you." Likewise His saying: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 51], meaning "in front of me." So it is the same here.

[Page 36]

The third issue: Faith is knowledge, and the guidance that follows from it is also of the kind of knowledges. Then, He, exalted is He, did not say "their Lord will guide them to their faith," but said: ﴿their Lord will guide them by their faith﴾. This indicates that knowing the two premises does not necessarily produce knowing the conclusion; rather, knowing the two premises is a cause for the arising of a complete readiness in the soul to receive the conclusion. Then, when this readiness has arisen, the bringing-into-being comes from the Real, glorified and exalted is He. This is the meaning of the saying of the philosophers that the absolute Bestower and the True Giver is none other than Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

* * *

The second rank of their felicities and the degrees of their perfections is His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Their call therein will be: "Glory be to You, O Allah"﴾. On this there are issues:

The first issue: Concerning "their call" there are several interpretations:
The first: The call here means supplication. It is said: "He called (da'a), calls, a call (du'a') and a calling (da'wa)," just as it is said: "He complained (shaka), complains, a complaint (shika'ah) and a complaint (shakwa)." Some exegetes said: "Their call" means their supplication. And He said concerning the people of Paradise: ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they ask for﴾ [Ya-Sin: 57], and He said in another verse: ﴿They call therein for every fruit, in security﴾ [al-Dukhan: 55]. What strengthens that the meaning of "call" here is supplication is that they said: "O Allah," and this is an address to Allah, glorified and exalted is He. The meaning of their saying: ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ is: "We glorify You," like the saying of the one who stands in prayer in the supplication of qunut: "O Allah, You alone we worship."
The second: The supplication may be meant as worship. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and what you call upon besides Allah﴾ [Maryam: 48], meaning "what you worship." So the meaning of the verse is that there is no worship for the people of Paradise except that they glorify Allah and praise Him, and their occupation with that remembrance is not by way of obligation, but by way of delight in the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted.
The third: Some said: It is not far-fetched that what is meant by "call" is the very claim that one party makes against another. The meaning is that the people of Paradise call, in this world and in the Hereafter, to the glorifying of Allah, the Exalted, from every fault, and to acknowledging His divinity. Al-Qaffal said: The origin of this is also from supplication, because the litigant calls his adversary to one who will judge between them.
The fourth: Muslim said: "Their call" means their saying, their acknowledgement and their crying out, and that is their saying: ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾.
The fifth: Al-Qadi said: What is meant by His saying ﴿their call﴾ is their way of glorifying Allah, the Exalted, and sanctifying Him, and their custom and practice. The proof that this is what is meant is that His saying ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ is neither a supplication nor a claim, but the one who claims something is constantly mindful of it, so He made the word "call" a metaphor for that constancy and perpetual adherence. Since the people of Paradise were constant in this remembrance, the word "call" was therefore applied to it.
The sixth: Al-Qaffal said: It has been said concerning His saying ﴿and for them is whatever they call for﴾ [Ya-Sin: 57] that it means "what they wish for." The Arabs say: "Call for whatever you want against me," meaning: "wish." Ibn Jurayj said: I was informed that His saying ﴿Their call therein is: Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ means that when a bird passes by them which they desire, they say: "Glory be to You, O Allah," and the angel brings them that desired thing. So the interpretation of the verse has come out, from this aspect, as meaning that when they desire something they say: "Glory be to You, O Allah," so the meaning of their call is what arises in their hearts of wishing. In this interpretation there is another aspect, which is better and more noble than what preceded, namely that the meaning is that their wish in Paradise is to glorify Allah, the Exalted, i.e., their wish for what they wish for is nothing but glorifying Allah, the Exalted, and sanctifying Him and declaring Him free of imperfection.
The seventh: Al-Qaffal also said: It is possible that the meaning of "call" is what they used to call out to in the world during their times of war, to those in whom they took refuge and whose help they sought, such as their saying: "O family of so-and-so." So Allah, the Exalted, informed that their intimacy in Paradise is in remembering Allah, the Exalted, their tranquillity is in praising Allah, and their delight is in glorifying Allah, the Exalted.

[Page 37]

The second issue: His saying ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ has two aspects:

The first view: those who say that the people of Paradise made this remembrance a sign of seeking desirable things. Ibn Jurayj said: when a bird passes by them and they desire it, they say, "Glory be to You, O Allah," and it is brought to them; and when they have attained their desire from it, they say, ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. Al-Kalbi said: their saying ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ is a signal between the people of Paradise and the servants, so when they hear it from them, they bring them what they desire. Know that this view is, in my opinion, very weak, and its clarification is from several aspects:

The first: the upshot of this statement comes back to the claim that the people of Paradise made this lofty, sanctified remembrance a sign for seeking food, drink, and spouses, and this is in utmost baseness.

The second: He, exalted is He, said concerning the people of Paradise: ﴿And for them is whatever they desire﴾. So when they desire the eating of that bird, they have no need to seek it; and when they have no need to seek, this statement collapses.

The third: this requires turning the speech away from its noble, lofty outward meaning toward a base interpretation to which the wording gives no indication, and this is false.

The second interpretation of this verse is that we say: what is meant is the occupation of the people of Paradise with the sanctification of Allah, glorified is He, and the praise of Him, because their happiness lies in this remembrance, their delight in it, their joy in it, and the perfection of their state comes only from it. This view is the correct one from which there is no escape. Then, on this basis, there are several aspects to the verse. The first: al-Qadi said: He, exalted is He, promised the God-fearing a great reward, as He mentioned at the beginning of this surah in His saying: ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾. So when the people of Paradise enter Paradise and find those great blessings, they know that Allah, exalted is He, was truthful in His promise to them of those blessings; at this point they say: ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾, meaning: we glorify You above breaking promises and lying in speech.

The second: we say: the ultimate happiness of the happy and the final stage of the ranks of the prophets and the saints is their being made happy by the levels of knowledge of the Majesty.

Know that knowing the essence of Allah, exalted is He, and comprehending the reality of His true nature is something no path lies open to creation for; rather, the highest attainment is knowing His negative attributes or His relational attributes. As for the negative attributes, they are called the attributes of Majesty (jalal), and as for the relational attributes, they are called the attributes of Bounty (ikram). Therefore the perfection of the lofty remembrance is confined to these, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Bounty﴾ [al-Rahman: 78]. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "Persist in calling upon Owner of Majesty and Bounty." And since negations are prior in rank to relations, therefore the mention of Majesty precedes the mention of Bounty in wording. And since it is established that the ultimate happiness of the happy lies only in these two stations, He, exalted is He, mentioned their being constant in this lofty, sanctified remembrance. And since there is no end to the ascents of the Majesty of Allah, nor any limit to the stages of His divinity, His bounty, and His beneficence, likewise there is no end to the ranks of the ascent of sanctified souls in these lofty divine stations.

The third: the nearest angels were, before the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, occupied with this remembrance. Do you not see that they said: ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. So the Real, glorified is He, inspired the happy among the children of Adam until they uttered this glorification and praise, to show that what the nearest angels uttered before the creation of the world is from the lofty remembrance, and the very same was uttered by the happy among the children of Adam, peace be upon him, after the passing away of the world. And since this remembrance contains this lofty honor, therefore a report has come of its recitation at the beginning of the prayer: when the one praying says the takbir, he says: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You, Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god besides You."

* * *

The third level of the stations of the happiness of the people of Paradise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and their greeting therein is peace﴾. The commentators said: the greeting of some of them to others is by peace, and the greeting of the angels to them is by peace, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying], "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23–24]. And the greeting of Allah, exalted is He, to them is also by peace, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. Al-Wahidi said: on this interpretation, this is an idafa of the verbal noun to its object. But in my view there is another aspect: that their constancy in mentioning this word indicates that they were in the world in a place of calamities and in a position of fears; so when they are brought out of the world and reach the honor of Allah, exalted is He, they have become safe from calamities, secure from fears and deficiencies. Allah, exalted is He, has informed of them that they mention this meaning in His saying: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us [all] sorrow. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative. [He] who has settled us in the home of settlement by His bounty; there touches us not therein fatigue, and there touches us not therein weariness"﴾ [Fatir: 34–35].

* * *

The fourth level of their stations of happiness is His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And the last of their call will be: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ Concerning it there are questions:

The first question: We have mentioned that a group of the commentators took these lofty, sanctified words to refer to the states of the people of Paradise with respect to eating and drinking. They said: when the people of Paradise desire something, they say, "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You"; and when they have eaten and are finished, they say, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds." But this speaker's gaze has not risen, in his worldly life or his next life, above food and drink, and such a person deserves to be counted among the herd of beasts. As for the genuine verifiers, they have abandoned that, and they have views on it. Al-Hasan al-Basri narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The people of Paradise are inspired with praise and glorification just as you are inspired with your breaths." Al-Zajjaj said: in my view on this matter there are other aspects:

The first of them: that when the people of Paradise were made happy by the remembrance "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You," and beheld what they were in of safety from calamities and fears, they knew that all these exalted states and sanctified stations were made easy only by the goodness, bounty, and favor of the Real, glorified is He; therefore they were necessarily occupied with praise and commendation, and they said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ The conclusion of this speech came about because their occupation with glorifying and extolling Allah, exalted is He, is among the greatest of the blessings of Allah upon them; and occupation with thanking for a blessing comes after seeing that blessing, and for this reason this word was made the conclusion.

The second: that every person has, according to his strength, a ladder of ascent; at times he descends from that ladder, and at times he ascends to it. The ladder of the knowers who are truthful is the knowledge of Allah, the glorifying of Allah, and the praising of Allah; so when they say ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ they are in the very midst of the ladder; and when they descend from it to the world of created beings, the outcome of that descent is the overflow of goodness upon all who are in need, and to this the saying refers: ﴿and their greeting therein is peace﴾. Then again they ascend to their ladder, and upon ascending they say: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ So these lofty words are an indication of the variation of the servant's states through descent and ascent.

The third: we say: our saying "Allah" is a name for the essence of the Real, glorified is He. At times the servant looks to the attributes of Majesty, which are indicated by His saying ﴿Glory be to You﴾; then he seeks to ascend from them toward the presence of the Majesty of the essence, an ascent befitting human capacity, which is indicated by His saying "O Allah." Then, when he moves on from that place, and passes through the first of those lights, he returns to the world of Bounty, which is indicated by His saying ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ These are words that occurred to the mind and turned in the imagination; if they are correct, then the success is from Allah, exalted is He, and if they are not so, then reliance is upon the mercy of Allah, exalted is He.

The second question: Al-Wahidi said: the "an" in His saying ﴿an al-hamdu lillah﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy (anna), and for this reason it does not govern, since by lightening it has departed from resemblance to the verb, as in the line of verse: "Verily, every one who goes barefoot and wears sandals is perishing," meaning that he is perishing. The author of al-Nazm said: the "an" here is superfluous, and the sense is: "And the last of their call is: Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds." But this view is worth nothing. Some of them read "anna al-hamda" with the heavy form and the accusative "al-hamda."

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 10, verse 11:

God's words: ﴿If Allah were to hasten for people the evil as they hasten the good, their term would surely have been decreed for them. So We leave those who do not expect to meet Us in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾

On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** In my considered opinion, the beginning of this surah deals with the doubts of those who deny prophethood, together with the answers to them.

The first doubt was that the people were amazed that God had singled out Muhammad (peace be upon him) for prophethood. God removed this amazement with His words: ﴿Is it a wonder for people that We revealed to a man from among them...﴾ (10:2). Then He mentioned the proofs of monotheism and the proofs of the truth of the Resurrection. The essence of the answer is that He is saying: "I have only come to you with monotheism and the affirmation of the Resurrection, and I have proven their truth. So there remains no meaning in your amazement at my prophethood."

The second doubt of the people was that they would always say: "O God, if what Muhammad says is true in his claim to be a messenger, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment." God answered this doubt with what He mentioned in this verse. This is the discussion of the manner of the arrangement (*nazm*) of the verse. Some people have mentioned other aspects:

The first: al-Qadi said: When God clarified, in what came before, the promise and the threat, He followed it with what shows that it is right for these two to be postponed beyond this worldly life, because their occurrence in this world would be like an obstacle to the continuation of moral responsibility (*taklif*).

The second is what al-Qaffal mentioned: When God described the disbelievers as those who do not hope to meet Allah, who are content with and at rest in the life of this world, and who are heedless of the signs of Allah, He made clear that among their heedlessness is that whenever the Messenger warns them, they hasten the punishment out of ignorance and foolishness.

**The second issue:** In many verses God has informed us that these polytheists, whenever they were warned of the descent of punishment in this world, hastened that punishment, as they said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾ (8:32). And He said: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that will surely befall﴾ (70:1), and so on. Then, when they were threatened with the punishment of the Hereafter in this verse, namely His words: ﴿Those—their refuge is the Fire, for what they used to earn﴾, they hastened that punishment and said: "When will that happen?" As God said: ﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it﴾ (42:18). He also said, in this surah after this verse: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ (10:48), up to His words: ﴿Now? And you used to seek to hasten it!﴾ (10:51). He said in Surah al-Ra'd: ﴿And they seek to hasten you toward evil before good, though precedents of punishment have already passed before them﴾ (13:6). Thus God made clear that they have no benefit in hastening the arrival of evil upon them, because if God brought that punishment upon them, they would die and perish, since their constitution in this world cannot bear that. There is no benefit in causing their death. Perhaps they would believe afterward, and perhaps from their loins there would come forth one who is a believer. This requires that He not hasten the arrival of that evil upon them.

**The third issue:** There is a difficulty in the wording of the verse, namely: How did He pair *ta'jil* (hastening/causing to hasten) with *istic'jal* (seeking to hasten), when the expected formulation would have been to pair *ta'jil* with *ta'jil* and *istic'jal* with *istic'jal*?

Its answer has several aspects:

The first: The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: The original of this speech is: "If Allah were to hasten for people the evil in the manner of His hastening the good for them." But He placed their seeking to hasten the good (*istic'jaluhum bil-khayr*) in the position of His hastening the good for them, to indicate the swiftness of His response and His granting of their request, so that their seeking the good is, as it were, a hastening for them.

The second: Some have said: The true meaning of your saying "I hastened so-and-so" is: "I sought his haste." Likewise, "I hastened the matter" means: "I brought it quickly," as if you sought haste in it. *Istic'jal* is more well-known and more apparent in this sense. In this aspect the meaning of the verse becomes: "If God willed the haste of evil for people as they willed the haste of good for themselves, their term would have been decreed for them." The proponent of this aspect said: On this reading there is no need to depart from the apparent meaning of the verse.

The third: Everyone who hastens something has sought its hastening. If that is so, then everyone who is causing haste is also seeking haste. So the sense becomes: "If Allah sought haste for people in evil, as they sought haste in good." However, He described Himself as bringing about haste and described them as seeking it, because what befits Him, exalted is He, is bringing into being, and what befits them is seeking.

**The fourth issue:** God called the punishment "evil" (*sharr*) in this verse, because it is harm to the one who is punished and something hateful to him, just as He called it "bad deed" (*sayyi'a*) in His words: ﴿And they seek to hasten you toward the bad deed before the good﴾ (13:6), and in His words: ﴿The recompense for a bad deed is a bad deed like it﴾ (42:40).

**The fifth issue:** Ibn 'Amir recited *"la-qada"* with a fatha on the lam and the qaf, and *"ajalahum"* with the accusative, meaning: "Allah would have decreed." The recitation of 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), *"la-qada ilayhim ajalahum"*, supports this. The rest of the readers recited with a damma on the qaf, a kasra on the dad, and a fatha on the ya' (*"qudiya"*), with *"ajaluhum"* in the nominative, as a passive construction (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluh*, the form whose agent is not named).

**The sixth issue:** What is meant by the seeking of good by these polytheists is that when severe calamities descended upon them, they would call upon God to remove them. God has related this about them in many verses, such as His words: ﴿Then, when harm touches you, to Him you cry out for help﴾ (16:53), and His words: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us﴾ (39:49).

**The seventh issue:** A questioner may ask: How is His words ﴿So We leave those who do not expect to meet Us﴾ connected to what came before, and what is its meaning?

The answer is that His words ﴿If Allah were to hasten for people﴾ contain the meaning of the negation of hastening, as if it were said: "He does not hasten evil for them, nor does He decree their term; so He leaves them in their transgression," that is, He gives them respite despite their transgression, as a means of establishing the proof against them.

**The eighth issue:** Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: When God has ruled against them that they are in transgression and blind wandering, it is impossible that they not be as such, for otherwise His true report would turn into a falsehood, His knowledge into ignorance, and His judgment into invalidity. All of this is impossible. Then, despite this, He imposed moral obligations upon them, and this would be like imposing a obligation to combine two opposites.

[p. 40] [p. 41]

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 10, verse 12:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿When harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing. But when We remove his harm from him, he passes on as though he had never called upon Us to remove a harm that touched him. Thus is made attractive to the wasteful what they used to do.﴾

Concerning it there are several issues:

The First Issue: Regarding the manner of the arrangement (nazm) there are two views. The first: when Allah, in the previous verse, explained that if He sent down punishment upon the servant in this world he would perish and be finished, He then explained in this verse what shows the utmost of his weakness and the extremity of his incapacity, so that this would confirm what He had mentioned, that if punishment were sent down upon him he would die. The second: Allah related about them that they were hastening the descent of the punishment, then He explained in this verse that they are lying in that request and haste, because if even a trivial thing that he dislikes and that harms him befalls man, he humbles himself before Allah the Exalted seeking its removal from him and its repulsion from him, and that indicates that he is not sincere in this request.

The Second Issue: The purpose of this verse is to show that man has little patience when trial descends, and little gratitude when he finds blessings and favours. When harm touches him, he turns to supplication and entreaty, lying down, standing or sitting, striving in that supplication, asking Allah the Exalted to remove that affliction and replace it with blessing and favour. When Allah the Exalted removes that from him by well-being, he turns away from gratitude, does not remember that harm, does not recognise the measure of the bounty, and becomes like one who never called upon Allah to remove his harm. This indicates the weakness of human nature and the strength of heedlessness and desire's dominion over him. Allah the Exalted mentioned this only as a warning that this way is blameworthy; rather, it is obligatory upon the intelligent person to be patient when trial descends and grateful when he attains blessings, and it is proper for him to be abundant in supplication and entreaty in times of ease and comfort, so that he is answered in times of distress. From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever would like to be answered in times of distress and hardships, let him increase supplication in times of ease."

Know that when the believer is tested with an affliction and a trial, it is obligatory for him to observe several matters. The first of them: that he be content with the decree of Allah the Exalted, not objecting to it in heart or tongue. It is obligatory upon him to do so because He, the Exalted, is the Owner absolutely and the King by right. So He may do in His dominion and His possession whatever He wills as He wills. And because He, the Exalted, is Wise absolutely, and He is far removed from doing falsehood or futility, so whatever He does is wisdom and rightness. When that is so, then he knows that if Allah the Exalted leaves that trial upon him, it is justice, and if He removes it from him, it is grace; and at that point it is obligatory upon him to be patient, to keep silent, and to abandon anxiety and agitation. The second: if at that time he occupies himself with the remembrance of Allah the Exalted and praise of Him instead of supplication, it is better, because of the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him), relating from the Lord of Majesty: "Whoever is preoccupied with My remembrance from asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give those who ask." And because occupation with remembrance is occupation with the Truth, while occupation with supplication is occupation with seeking the portion of the self, and there is no doubt that the first is better. Then, if he occupies himself with supplication, it is necessary that he stipulate in it that its removal be good for his religion; in general, it is obligatory that religion be weightier in his sight than this world. The third: when He, glorified be He, removes that affliction from him, it is obligatory upon him to strive greatly in gratitude, and not to be free of that gratitude in ease and hardship, in states of adversity and comfort. This is the correct path at the descent of trial. Here there is another station higher and more excellent than what we have mentioned: the people of realization have said that whoever, at the time of finding a blessing, is occupied with the blessing and not with the Benefactor, will at the time of affliction be occupied with the affliction and not with the One who afflicts. Such a person is always in affliction: at the time of trial there is no doubt that he is in trial, and at the time of the attainment of blessing, his fear of its loss is the most severe kind of trial, for the more perfect, sweeter, stronger and more excellent a blessing is, the more harmful the fear of its loss and the more intense the sense of desolation. Thus it is established that whoever is occupied with the blessing is always in the depths of affliction. As for whoever, at the time of the blessing, is occupied with the Benefactor, it follows that at the time of trial he is occupied with the One who afflicts; and when the Benefactor and the Afflicter are one, his gaze is always upon one object of seeking, and his object is exempt from change and sanctified from alteration. Whoever is like this, at the time of trial and at the time of blessing, is drowned in the sea of felicities, reaching the furthest of perfections. This kind of exposition is a sea without shore, and whoever wishes to reach it, let him be among those who arrive at the Essence, not among those who only hear the report.

The Third Issue: They differed concerning (al-insan, man) in His saying: ﴿When harm touches man﴾. Some of them said: it is the disbeliever. Among them was one who exaggerated and said: every place in the Qur'an where mention of al-insan occurs, what is meant is the disbeliever. This is false, because His saying: ﴿O man, indeed you are labouring towards your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him﴾ and ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6-7] — there is no doubt that the believer is included in it; likewise His saying: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time?﴾ [al-Insan: 1], and His saying: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12], and His saying: ﴿And We have created man and know what his soul whispers to him﴾ [Qaf: 16]. So what they said is far-fetched. Rather, the truth is that we say: the singular noun with the definite article (al-) has the rule that if there is a previously known referent, it is directed to it; and if there is no previously known referent, it must be taken as encompassing all, to preserve it from vagueness and nullity. The word (al-insan) here is fitting for the disbeliever, because the action mentioned does not at all befit the Muslim.

* * *

The Fourth Issue: Regarding His saying: ﴿he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing﴾ there are two views:

The first view: what is meant is mention of the states of supplication. So His saying: ﴿lying on his side﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), as evidenced by the conjunction of the two other states to it. The implied meaning is: he calls upon Us lying down, or sitting, or standing.

If they say: what is the benefit of mentioning these states?

We say: its meaning is that the one afflicted does not cease calling, does not slacken in supplication until the harm is removed from him, whether he is lying down, sitting, or standing.

The second view: these three states are an enumeration of the states of the harm, and the implied meaning is: when harm touches man, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing, he calls upon Us. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. The first is more correct, because mention of the supplication is closer to these states than mention of the harm, and because the claim that these states are states of supplication implies man's exertion in supplication; then, if he abandons supplication altogether and turns away from it, that is more astonishing.

The Fifth Issue: Regarding His saying: ﴿passes on (marra)﴾ there are several meanings:

The first: what is meant is that he went on in his former course before the touch of harm and forgot the state of distress.

The second: he passed on from the station of entreaty and humbling himself, not returning to it, as though he had no covenant with it.

The Sixth Issue: His saying, exalted be He: ﴿as though he had never called upon Us to remove a harm that touched him﴾. Its estimation: as though he had not called upon Us. Then the pronoun was dropped from it for the sake of lightness. A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿as though they had not lingered﴾ [Yunus: 45]. Al-Hasan said: he forgot what he had called Allah about and what Allah did for him in removing that affliction from him.

The Seventh Issue: The author of "al-Nazm" said: His saying: ﴿When harm touches man﴾, (idha) is laid down for the future, then He said: ﴿So when We removed﴾, and this is for the past. So this arrangement indicates that the meaning of the verse is that it was thus in the past, and thus it will be in the future. Thus what the verb in the future tense in the verse indicates is the future meaning in it, and what the verb in the past tense indicates is the past meaning in it. I say: rational proof supports this meaning, because man is created with weakness, incapacity and little patience, and is also created with arrogance, wantonness, forgetfulness, rebellion and insolence. When affliction befalls him, his weakness and incapacity drive him to much supplication, entreaty, showing humility and submission; and when the affliction is removed and he falls into ease, forgetfulness overcomes him, so he forgets Allah the Exalted's kindness to him, and falls into transgression, tyranny, denial and ingratitude. These states are the results of his nature and the necessary consequences of his creation. In sum, these wretched ones are excused, and yet they have no excuse.

The Eighth Issue: Regarding His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Thus is made attractive to the wasteful what they used to do﴾ there are several discussions:

The First Discussion: whether this one who makes it attractive is Allah the Exalted, or the self, or Satan. This is a branch of the question of compulsion and predestination, which is well known.

The Second Discussion: concerning the explanation of the cause for which Allah, glorified be He, named the disbeliever "wasteful". There are several views:

The first view: Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: the disbeliever is wasteful towards himself and towards his wealth, and wastes both. As for himself, because he made it a slave to the idol; and as for wealth, because they used to waste their wealth in the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham.

The second view: al-Qadi said: whoever's habit is that at the descent of affliction he is abundant in entreaty and supplication, and at the removal of affliction and the descent of blessings he turns away from the remembrance of Allah, heedless of Him, not occupied with thanking Him, he is wasteful in the matter of his religion, exceeding the limit in heedlessness of Him. There is no doubt that just as a person may be wasteful in spending, so too he may be wasteful in what he leaves of obligation or what he undertakes of ugliness, when he exceeds the limit in it.

The third view: and this is what came to mind at this time: the wasteful is the one who spends much wealth for a base aim. It is known that the pleasures and goods of this world are extremely base in comparison with the felicities of the Abode of the Hereafter. Allah the Exalted gave him the senses, the intellect, understanding and the power to acquire those great felicities. So whoever expends these noble instruments in order to attain these base bodily felicities has spent great and numerous things for the sake of attaining trivial and base things, and so he must be among the wasteful.

The Third Discussion: The kaf in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Thus﴾ is for comparison. The meaning: just as this disbeliever was made to find this ugly, reprehensible action attractive, so were the wasteful made to find attractive what they used to do of turning away from the remembrance and following desires.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 13–14:

﴿Indeed, We destroyed the generations before you when they did wrong, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they were not going to believe. Thus do We recompense the criminal people.﴾ ﴿Then We made you successors in the land after them, that We might see how you would act.﴾

Regarding the verse, there are several issues:

The first issue: explaining the manner of the arrangement (nazm). Know that when God related of them that they used to say: ﴿O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], He then answered them by mentioning that there is no good in answering their supplication. Then He showed that they were lying in this request, because if a calamity befell them, they would begin to plead with God to remove it and to lift it from them. In this verse He stated what serves as a warning: that God may indeed send upon them the punishment of annihilation and not remove it from them. The purpose of this is that it should be a deterrent for them from their saying: "If this is the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky." For whenever they hear that God may answer their supplication and send upon them the punishment of annihilation, and then they hear from the Jews and Christians that this has happened many times, this becomes a deterrent for them and a restraint from mentioning that statement. This is a good and acceptable explanation of the arrangement.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "lamma" is a temporal adverb governing ﴿ahlaknā﴾ ("We destroyed"), and the "wa" in His saying ﴿wa-jā'at-hum﴾ ("and their messengers came to them") is for the circumstantial clause, meaning: they did wrong by denying. Their messengers had come to them with the proofs and evidences of their truthfulness, which are the miracles. His saying ﴿wa-mā kānū li-yu'minū﴾ ("but they were not going to believe") may be a conjunction upon ﴿ẓalamū﴾ ("they did wrong") or may be a parenthetical insertion; the "lām" serves to emphasize the negation. God had known of them that they would persist in disbelief. This indicates that He destroyed them only because of their denial of the messengers, and thus He recompenses every criminal. It is a warning to the people of Makkah for their denial of the Messenger of God. It has also been read as ﴿yajzī﴾ with the "ya" (third person). His saying ﴿Then We made you successors﴾ addresses those to whom Muhammad, peace be upon him, was sent, meaning: We made you successors in the land after the generations whom We destroyed, ﴿that We might see how you would act﴾, whether good or evil, and We shall deal with you according to your deeds. Two questions remain concerning the verse:

The first question: How is it permissible to attribute "seeing" (naẓar) to God, when it carries the meaning of encountering (muqābala)?

The answer: The word "seeing" has been borrowed to mean true knowledge, which admits no doubt, and this knowledge has been likened to the seeing of the one who looks and the sight of the one who witnesses.

The second question: His saying ﴿Then We made you successors in the land after them, that We might see how you would act﴾ implies that God was not knowing of their circumstances before their existence.

The answer: What is meant by it is that God treats His servants in the manner of one who seeks knowledge of what will come from them, so that He may recompense them according to it, as in His saying: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud: 7]. Similar examples of this have already passed. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, the world is green and sweet, and indeed God makes you successors in it, and He watches how you act." Qatadah said: "God our Lord has spoken truly; He made us successors only so that He might look at our deeds. So show God good deeds from yourselves, by night and by day."

The third issue: Al-Zajjaj said: The position of "kayfa" (how) is accusative, governed by "ta'malūn" (you do), because it is an interrogative particle, and an interrogative does not take what precedes it as its governor. If you said: "that We might see good you do or evil," the governing word for "khayr" and "sharr" (good and evil) would be "ta'malūn."
