First issue: Most readers recited (matā'u) with a raised ʿayn (ʿayn being the letter ع, i.e., the vowel on it), and Hafs from ʿAsim recited ﴿matā'a﴾ with a fatha on the ʿayn. As for the nominative reading, there are two ways of understanding it. The first: that His saying, ﴿your transgression is against yourselves﴾, is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying, "(matā'u al-ḥayāt al-dunyā)" (the enjoyment of worldly life), is the predicate (khabar). What is meant by His saying, ﴿your transgression is against yourselves﴾, is the transgression of some of you against others, as in His saying, ﴿so kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54]. The meaning of the statement is that the transgression of some of you against others is the enjoyment of worldly life, and it has no permanence. The second: that His saying, ﴿baghyukum﴾, is the subject, His saying, ﴿ʿalā anfusikum﴾, is its predicate, and His saying, "(matā'u al-ḥayāt al-dunyā)", is the predicate of an elided subject, the estimate being: it is the enjoyment of worldly life. As for the reading with the accusative, its explanation is that we say: His saying, ﴿baghyukum﴾, is the subject, His saying, ﴿ʿalā anfusikum﴾, is its predicate, and His saying, ﴿matā'a al-ḥayāt al-dunyā﴾, is in the position of an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid), the estimate being: you enjoy the enjoyment of worldly life.

Second issue: Baghy is among the most reprehensible of sins. The prayer and peace of Allah be upon him said: "The swiftest of good in reward is the joining of ties of kinship, and the swiftest of evil in punishment is baghy and a false oath." It is also narrated: "Two things Allah hastens in this world: baghy and disobedience to one's parents." And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: Were a mountain to transgress against a mountain, the transgressor would be crushed. Al-Ma'mun used to recite these two verses concerning his brother:
O possessor of baghy, indeed baghy is a downfall, so refrain; the best of a person's deeds is the most just of them.
Were a mountain one day to transgress against a mountain, its heights and its depths would be crushed.
And from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi: Three qualities, whoever has them, they will be upon him: baghy, breaking covenants, and deceit. The Exalted said: ﴿Your transgression is only against yourselves﴾.

Third issue: The summary of the statement of the Exalted, ﴿O mankind, your transgression is only against yourselves﴾, is: it is not possible for you to commit transgression against one another except for a few days, which is the duration of your life, despite its brevity and swift passing. ﴿Then to Us is your return; then We will inform you of what you used to do﴾ in the world. The informing (al-inba') is the telling, and in this place it is a threat of punishment, like a man's saying to another: "I will inform you of what you did."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the example of the worldly life is like rain which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, [vegetation] of which men and livestock eat, until, when the earth takes on its adornment and is beautified, and its people think they have power over it, Our command reaches it by night or by day, and We make it a harvested stubble as if it had not flourished yesterday. Thus do We detail the signs for a people who give thought.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, your transgression is only against yourselves; [it is but] the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾, He followed it with this wondrous parable which He struck for one who transgresses on the earth and is deceived by the world, whose clinging to it grows firm, and whose turning away from the matter of the Hereafter and preparation for it grows strong. So He said: ﴿Indeed, the example of the worldly life is like rain which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it﴾. This statement admits of two meanings. The first is that the meaning is: the vegetation of the earth mingled with it by means of this water descending from the sky, because when rain falls, many kinds of plants grow by its means, and these kinds are mixed together; and this concerns what had not been growing before the rain fell. The second is that what is meant is that which has grown but has not yet flourished or become lush; rather, it is at the first emergence from the earth and the beginning of its existence. When rain falls upon it and mingles with that rain, that is, each of them joins the other, that vegetation stirs, grows, becomes goodly, reaches completion, and clothes itself in the perfection of freshness and adornment. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until, when the earth takes on its adornment and is beautified﴾. This is because zukhruf (adornment) denotes the perfection of a thing's beauty. The earth is described as taking on its adornment by way of comparison to a bride when she wears fine garments of every color and adorns herself with all the colors possible in adornment: red, green, yellow, gold, and white. There is no doubt that whenever the garden becomes in this state and with this quality, its owner rejoices in it, his hope of benefiting from it greatly increases, and his heart becomes absorbed in it. Then He, exalted is He, sends upon this wondrous garden a great calamity all at once, by night or by day, whether frost, wind, or flood, so that those trees and crops become void and destroyed, as if they had never existed at all. There is no doubt that the grief of the owner of that garden becomes great and his sorrow intensifies. Likewise is the one who sets his heart upon the pleasures and good things of this world; when those things escape him, his sorrow and anguish over them become great.

Know also that the comparison of the worldly life to this vegetation admits of aspects which al-Qadi (may God have mercy on him) summarized:

The first aspect: the outcome of this worldly life, which a person spends in the affairs of this world, is like the outcome of this vegetation, which, at the time when hope in benefiting from it had greatly increased, falls into despair; for generally, whoever clings to the world, when he sets his heart upon it and his desire for it grows great, death comes upon him. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until, when they rejoice in what they were given, We seize them suddenly, and they are then in despair﴾ [al-An'am: 44] — losing the world, having spent their lives in it, and losing the Hereafter, while they were turned toward it.

The second aspect of the comparison: He, exalted is He, made clear that just as that crop attained no praiseworthy outcome, so too the one deceived by the world who loves it attains no praiseworthy outcome.

صفحة ٦٠

The third aspect: that the aspect of comparison is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23]. When the striving of this farmer became void due to the occurrence of destructive causes, so too is the striving of the one deceived by the world.

The fourth aspect: that the owner of that garden, when he developed it with exertion of the self and toil of the spirit, and attached his heart to benefiting from it, then when that destructive cause occurred, the severe hardship he bore in the past became the cause of severe misery for him in the future, namely what he suffers in his heart of regrets. Likewise is the state of one who sets his heart upon the world and wearies himself in acquiring it; when he dies and loses all that he gained, the hardship he bore in acquiring the means of the world becomes the cause of great misery for him in the Hereafter.

The fifth aspect: perhaps He, exalted is He, struck this parable only for one who does not believe in the Return, because we see that the crop which has reached the utmost limit in cultivation has reached the limit of adornment and beauty, then a calamity befalls the earth adorned by it, so that this beauty disappears entirely, and then that earth becomes described by that adornment once again. So He mentioned this example to show that whoever is able to do that is able to restore living beings in the Hereafter, to recompense them for their deeds: if good, then good; if evil, then evil.

Second issue: "al-mathal" (the parable, example) is a statement by which the condition of the second is likened to the first; it is also permissible that what is meant by al-mathal is the attribute. The implied sense is: indeed the attribute of the worldly life is... As for His saying ﴿wa-izzayyanat﴾ (and is beautified), al-Zajjaj said: it means tazayyanat (adorned itself); the ta' was assimilated into the zay and the zay was made quiescent, so an alif of connection (hamzat al-wasl) was brought for it. This is like what we mentioned concerning His saying ﴿fa-iddarra'tum﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72] and ﴿iddaraku﴾ [al-A'raf: 38].

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and its people think they have power over it﴾, Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) said: it means that the people of that land are able to harvest it and gather its fruits. The verification is that although the pronoun apparently refers back to the earth, it actually refers back to the vegetation present in the earth. As for His saying ﴿Our command reaches it﴾, Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) said: it means Our punishment. The verification is that the meaning is: Our command reaches it with its destruction. As for His saying ﴿and We make it harvested stubble﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: nothing remains in it; al-Dahhak said: it means the reaped. On this view, by al-hasid (the harvested) is meant the earth whose growth has been reaped; and it is also permissible that by al-hasid is meant the vegetation. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-hasid means uprooted; others said: al-hasid means cut or uprooted. As for His saying ﴿as if it had not flourished yesterday﴾, al-Layth said: it is said of a thing when it has perished: "as if it had not flourished yesterday", i.e., as if it had not existed, from the saying of the people: "ghaniya al-qawm fi darihim" (the people dwelt in their abode) when they stayed there; on this view this is an attribute of the vegetation. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: as if it had not been inhabited yesterday; on this view what is meant is the earth. As for His saying ﴿Thus do We detail the signs﴾, i.e., We mention one of them after another in sequence, so that their succession and abundance may be a cause of the strengthening of certainty and an occasion for the removal of doubt and dubiety.

**[Page 61]**

Allah says: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace, and guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾ There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue: the manner of its composition (naẓm, the arrangement of the discourse).** Know that when Allah, the Exalted, had repelled the heedless from inclining toward this world through the earlier parable, He encouraged them toward the Hereafter through this verse. The basis of the encouragement toward the Hereafter is what has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "My example and your example is like a master who built a house, set out a feast, and sent a caller. Whoever answers the caller enters the house, eats from the feast, and the master is pleased with him. Whoever does not answer does not enter, does not eat, and the master is not pleased with him. The Master is Allah, the house is the abode of Islam, the feast is Paradise, and the caller is Muhammad (peace be upon him)." And he (ﷺ) also said: "There is no day on which the sun rises except that two angels are beside it calling out, audible to all creation except the two weighty ones (jinn and humankind): 'O people, come to your Lord! Allah calls to the Abode of Peace.'"

**The second issue:** There is no doubt that the Abode of Peace means Paradise. However, they differed about the reason for which this name was given, in several views:

*The first view:* Peace (al-Salām) is Allah, the Exalted, and Paradise is His abode. Here it is necessary to explain the benefit of naming Allah, the Exalted, as "Peace," and there are several points on this:

One of them: since He is wājib al-wujūd (the one whose existence is necessary in Himself), He is free from extinction and change, and free from needing anything else in His essence or attributes. This quality belongs to none but Him, the Glorified, as He said: ﴿And Allah is the Rich, and you are the poor﴾ [Muhammad: 38], and He said: ﴿O people, you are the poor toward Allah﴾ [Fāṭir: 15].

The second: He, the Exalted, is described as Peace in the sense that creation is safe from His injustice. He said: ﴿And your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 46]. Moreover, all that is other than Him belongs to His dominion and possession, and the action of an agent in his own possession is not injustice. Also, injustice arises only from one who is incapable, ignorant, or needy, and since all of these are impossible for Allah, the Exalted, injustice is impossible with respect to Him.

The third: Al-Mubarrad said: He, the Exalted, is described as Peace in the sense that He is Dhū al-Salām (the Possessor of Peace), i.e., the One who none but Him can grant peace. Salām is an expression for delivering the helpless from hardships and calamities. Thus the Truth, the Exalted, is the One who covers the faults of the faulty, the One who answers the call of those in distress, and the One who brings justice to the wronged against the wrongdoers. Al-Mubarrad said: According to this interpretation, salām is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of salima (to be safe).

*The second view:* Salām is the plural of salāmah (safety), and the meaning of Abode of Peace is: the abode whoever enters it is safe from calamities. Thus salām here means salāmah, like riḍā' means riḍā'ah (nursing). For a person there is safe from all calamities: death, sickness, pain, misfortunes, the incitements of Satan, disbelief, bidʿah (innovation), toil, and fatigue.

*The third view:* Paradise was called the Abode of Peace because Allah, the Exalted, greets its people with peace. He said: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 58]. The angels also greet them with peace, as He said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate. "Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured"﴾ [al-Raʿd: 23–24]. They also greet one another with peace, as He said: ﴿Their greeting therein is "Peace"﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 23]. Furthermore, their greeting reaches the blessed among the people of this world, as He said: ﴿And if he is of the companions of the right, then "Peace be upon you from the companions of the right"﴾ [al-Wāqiʿah: 90–91].

**The third issue:** Know that the perfection of Allah's generosity, the perfection of His power, and the perfection of His mercy toward His servants are known. His calling of His servants to the Abode of Peace indicates that in that abode there is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. For when the Great one magnifies something, encourages toward it, and emphasizes that encouragement greatly, this indicates the perfection of that thing's state, especially since Allah has filled this Holy Book with descriptions of Paradise, such as His saying: ﴿Then rest and provision and a Garden of Bliss﴾ [al-Wāqiʿah: 89]. Here we will mention a general discourse to establish this point, so we say: a person strives in his today for his tomorrow, and every person has two tomorrows: a tomorrow in this world and a tomorrow in the Hereafter. We say: the tomorrow of the Hereafter is better than the tomorrow of this world in four respects.

**[Page 62]**

The first of them: a person may not attain the tomorrow of this world, but he will certainly attain the tomorrow of the Hereafter.

The second: even if he attains the tomorrow of this world, he may not be able to benefit from what he has gathered, either because that wealth is lost from him, or because a sickness occurs in his body that prevents him from benefiting from it. As for the tomorrow of the Hereafter, whatever a person has earned for that day will certainly benefit him.

The third: even if he finds the tomorrow of this world and is able to benefit from his wealth, those benefits are mixed with harms and hardships, since the felicities of this world are not free from calamities but are mingled with afflictions, and induction (istiqrāʾ) indicates this. For this reason the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever seeks what has not been created, tires himself, and he will not be provided with it." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, and what is that?" He said: "A day's joy in its entirety." As for the benefits of the tomorrow of the Hereafter, they are free from grief, sorrow, and sadness, and safe from every repellent thing.

The fourth: even if a person reaches the tomorrow of this world and benefits from it, and that benefit is free of the mixture of calamities, it must still be terminated. The benefits of the Hereafter are lasting and free from termination. Thus it is established that the felicities of this world are tainted by these four defects, and the felicities of the Hereafter are free from them. For this reason Paradise is the Abode of Peace.

**The fourth issue:** Our companions (the Ashʿarīs) argued from this verse that disbelief and faith occur by the decree of Allah, the Exalted. They said: He, the Exalted, explained in this verse that He called all creation to the Abode of Peace, then explained that He did not guide but some of them. This specific guidance must be different from that general call. There is also no doubt that empowerment, enablement, the sending of messengers, and the revelation of books are general matters, so this specific guidance must be different from all these things. And what that is, is nothing but what we have mentioned: that He specified it with knowledge and recognition to the exclusion of others.

Know that this verse is problematic for the Muʿtazila (the Rationalist school), and they could not produce many objections to it. The summary of what al-Qāḍī ('Abd al-Jabbār) mentioned is in two aspects. The first: that the meaning is "and Allah guides whomever He wills to answer that call," in the sense that whoever answers the call, obeys, and fears God, Allah will guide him to it. The second: that the intended meaning of this verse is the favours (alṭāf, sing. lutf). Our companions answered these two aspects with a single point: that in their view it is obligatory upon Allah to perform this guidance, and what is obligatory cannot be contingent upon His will, whereas this is contingent upon His will, so it is impossible to interpret it in the way they stated.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 26:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For those who have done good is the best (reward) and more.﴾ ﴿Neither darkness nor humiliation shall cover their faces.﴾ ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

Know that when He, Exalted is He, called His servants to the Abode of Peace, He mentioned the felicities that they would attain therein, saying: ﴿For those who have done good is the best (reward) and more.﴾ So it is necessary to explain these three words.

As for the first word, which is His saying ﴿for those who have done good﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is: for those who said the word "There is no god but Allah." Al-Asamm said: its meaning is: for those who did good in everything they were worshipped in, and its meaning is that they performed what was commanded as it should be, and avoided what was forbidden in the manner in which it became forbidden.

The second opinion is closer to the truth, because high ranks are only attained by the people of acts of obedience.

As for the second word, which is ﴿the best﴾, Ibn al-Anbari said: al-husna (the best) in the language is the feminine of al-ahsan (the best), and the Arabs apply this word to a beloved state and a desired quality; for this reason it is not made emphatic, nor is it qualified by anything. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the intended meaning is "the best reward." A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Is the recompense for good anything but good?﴾ [al-Rahman: 60].

As for the third word, which is al-ziyadah (the "more"): we say that this word is ambiguous, and for this reason people differed in its interpretation, and the essence of their statements returns to two opinions:

The first opinion: that what is intended by it is the sight of Allah, Exalted is He. They said: the evidence for it is both transmission and reason.

As for transmission: it is the authentic hadith reported concerning it, namely that "the best" is Paradise and "the more" is the gazing upon Allah, Exalted is He.

As for reason: the word al-husna is a singular noun to which the definite article has been attached, so it refers to the previously known referent, which is the Abode of Peace. What is well known among Muslims and established among the people of Islam by this term is Paradise and what it contains of benefits and honour. Once this is established, it is necessary that what is meant by "the more" be something different from everything in Paradise of benefits and honour, otherwise repetition would follow. Everyone who has said this has said that it is none other than the sight of Allah, Exalted is He. This indicates that what is meant by this "more" is the sight. Two things confirm this. The first: He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22-23]. So He affirmed for the people of Paradise two matters: the first, radiance of the faces, and the second, looking toward Allah, Exalted is He. The verses of the Qur'an explain one another, so it is necessary to interpret "the best" here as radiance of the faces, and "the more" as the sight of Allah, Exalted is He. The second: He, Exalted is He, said to His Messenger ﷺ: ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great dominion﴾ [al-Insan: 20]. He affirmed for him bliss and the sight of a great dominion, so it is necessary here to interpret "the best" and "the more" as these two matters.

The second opinion: that it is not permissible to interpret this "more" as the sight. The Mu'tazilah said: several things indicate this. The first: rational proofs have shown that the sight of Allah, Exalted is He, is impossible. The second: the "more" must be of the same kind as that which it is added to, and the sight of Allah, Exalted is He, is not of the kind of the bliss of Paradise. The third: the report on which you rely in this matter is what is narrated, that the "more" is the gazing at the Face of Allah, Exalted is He, and this report necessitates anthropomorphism, because gazing is an expression for turning the pupil toward the direction of the thing seen. That requires the seen thing to be in a direction, since "face" is the name of a particular organ, and this too necessitates anthropomorphism. Thus it is established that this word cannot be interpreted as the sight, so it must be interpreted as something else. At this point al-Jubba'i said: "the best" is an expression for the reward that is due, and "the more" is what Allah, Exalted is He, adds to this reward of His bounty. He said: what indicates its soundness is the Qur'an and the statements of the exegetes.

As for the Qur'an: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That He may pay them their wages in full and increase them of His bounty﴾ [Fatir: 30].

As for the statements of the exegetes: it is reported from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "the more" is a single chamber of a pearl. And from Ibn 'Abbas that "the best" is the good deed, and "the more" is ten times its like. And from al-Hasan: ten times its like up to seven hundred fold. And from Mujahid: "the more" is Allah's forgiveness and His good pleasure. And from Yazid ibn Samurah: "the more" is that a cloud passes over the people of Paradise and says: "What do you want me to rain upon you?" They do not want anything except that it rains it upon them.

Our companions answered these points. They said: as for your statement that rational proofs have shown the impossibility of seeing Allah, Exalted is He, this is disputed, because we have explained in the books of usul that those proofs are extremely weak and utterly feeble. When the intellect contains nothing that prevents the sight of Allah, Exalted is He, and sound reports have come affirming the sight, it is necessary to apply them to their apparent meanings. As for your statement that the "more" must be of the same kind as that which it is added to: we say that when the thing added to is determined by a specific measure, the addition to it must be different from it.
An example of the first: a man says to another, "I gave you ten mudd of wheat and more." Here the addition must be of wheat.

An example of the second: his saying, "I gave you wheat and more." Here the addition must be other than wheat. What is mentioned in this verse is the word "the best," which is Paradise, and it is unrestricted, not determined by a specific measure. So the addition to it must be something different from everything in Paradise. As for your statement that the report mentioned in this matter includes the word "gazing" and the affirmation of a "face" for Allah, Exalted is He, and both of these necessitate anthropomorphism: we say that this report conveys the affirmation of the sight and also conveys the affirmation of corporeality. Then proof has been established that He is not a body, and proof has not been established that His sight is impossible. So it is necessary to abandon only what proof has shown to be corrupt. Moreover, we have explained that the wording of this verse indicates that the "more" is the sight, without any need that would conflict with the establishment of that report. And Allah knows best.

Know that when He, Exalted is He, explained the felicities that the people of Paradise attain, He then explained the afflictions from which Allah, by His bounty, protected them, saying: ﴿Neither darkness nor humiliation shall cover their faces.﴾ The meaning: no darkness shall cover them, and darkness is a dust with blackness in it; ﴿nor humiliation﴾: nor any trace of disgrace or gloom.

The first attribute is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Faces that day will have dust upon them, covered by darkness﴾ [Abasa: 40-41].

The second attribute is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Faces that day will be humbled, toiling and weary﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 2-3]. The purpose of negating these two attributes is to negate from them the causes of fear, sorrow and abasement, so that it is known that their bliss which Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned is pure, unmixed with disagreeable things, and that there cannot befall them anything which, if it occurred, would alter the surface of the face and remove what is in it of radiance and brightness. Then He explained that they abide in Paradise eternally, not fearing cessation.

Know that the scholars of usul said: reward is a pure, lasting benefit combined with honour. His saying: ﴿And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace﴾ [Yunus: 25] indicates the utmost honour; His saying: ﴿For those who have done good is the best (reward) and more﴾ indicates the attainment of benefit; His saying: ﴿Neither darkness nor humiliation shall cover their faces﴾ indicates that it is pure; and His saying: ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally﴾ is an indication that it is lasting, secure from cessation. And Allah knows best.

[Page 65]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who earned evil deeds – the recompense of an evil deed is an equivalent thereof, and humiliation will cover them. They will have from Allah no protector. It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

The first issue: Know that just as He described the state of the believers in the preceding verse, He describes in this verse the state of those who committed evil deeds. Almighty Allah mentions four of their conditions.

The first is His saying: ﴿the recompense of an evil deed is an equivalent thereof.﴾ The purpose of this qualification is to draw attention to the difference between good deeds and evil deeds. Allah mentioned that for acts of righteousness He gives those who engage in them a reward with an increase, whereas for evil deeds He mentioned that He does not repay except with the equivalent. The difference is that an increase over the reward is an act of grace, which is good and serves to strengthen the encouragement to obedience. But an increase beyond what is deserved in the case of evil deeds would be injustice, and if He did it, the promise, the threat, the warning, and the admonition would all be nullified, because trust in them is only established when His wisdom is established, and if He committed injustice, His wisdom would be voided, exalted is Allah above that. This is how al-Qadi (the judge) established it, as a consequence of his school of thought.

The second is His saying: ﴿and humiliation will cover them.﴾ This is a metaphor for disgrace and contempt. Know that perfection is loved for its own sake and deficiency is hated for its own sake. So when a deficient person dies, his soul remains deficient, empty of perfections, and his awareness of being deficient becomes a cause of humiliation, abasement, shame, and torment.

The third is His saying: ﴿They will have from Allah no protector.﴾ Know that there is no protector from Allah, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter, for His decree encompasses all beings and His power is executed in all created things. However, the predominant state of disobedient natures is that in the immediate life they are occupied with their deeds and desires. After death, however, everyone acknowledges that they have no protector from Allah.

The fourth is His saying: ﴿It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night.⁠﴾ The purpose of this statement is to affirm what He negated for the blessed, when He said: ﴿Neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces.﴾

Know that the sages of Islam said: the blackness mentioned here is the blackness of ignorance and the darkness of error, for knowledge by its nature is light and ignorance by its nature is darkness. So His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be bright, laughing and joyful⁠﴾ [Abasa: 38] means the light of knowledge, its spirit, its cheerfulness, and its good tidings. And His saying: ﴿And other faces that Day will be dust-covered, with darkness covering them⁠﴾ [Abasa: 40] means the darkness of ignorance and the murkiness of error.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿And those who earned evil deeds⁠﴾ has two possible readings:

One: it is joined (in grammatical construction) to His saying: ﴿for those who did good⁠﴾, as if it were said: for those who did good is the best reward, and for those who earned evil deeds is the recompense of an evil deed, an equivalent thereof.

The second: the implied sense is: And the recompense of those who earned evil deeds is the recompense of an evil deed, an equivalent thereof, meaning that their recompense is that one evil deed is repaid with an equal evil deed, with no addition to it. This indicates that Allah's judgment regarding the good-doers is nothing but grace, and regarding the evildoers is nothing but justice.

The third issue: Some said that what is meant by His saying: ﴿And those who earned evil deeds⁠﴾ is the disbelievers. They argued for this by the fact that blackness of the face is a sign of disbelief, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿As for those whose faces turn black, [it will be said]: Did you disbelieve after your belief?⁠﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 106]. Likewise His saying: ﴿And other faces that Day will be dust-covered, with darkness covering them. Those are the disbelievers, the wicked⁠﴾ [Abasa: 40–42]. Also, because He said after this verse: ﴿And the Day We gather them all⁠﴾, and the pronoun in His saying "them" refers to these people; then He described them with association (of partners with Allah), which indicates that these are the disbelievers. And because knowledge is light, and the authority of all sciences and cognitions is the knowledge of Allah the Exalted, so every heart in which the knowledge of Allah the Exalted has come into being, darkness does not arise in it at all. Al-Shibli, may Allah have mercy on him, used to recite this and say:

"Every house you dwell in
needs no lamps.
Your face, the one we hope for, is our proof
on the Day people come with their proofs."

The Qadi said: His saying ﴿And those who earned evil deeds⁠﴾ is general, encompassing the disbeliever and the sinner. However, we say: although the wording is general, the proofs we have mentioned specify it.

The fourth issue: al-Farra' said: concerning His saying: ﴿the recompense of an evil deed is an equivalent thereof⁠﴾ there are two possibilities:

The first: the implied sense is: then for them is the recompense of an evil deed, an equivalent thereof, just as He said: ﴿then a ransom of fasting⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], meaning: then upon him is.

The second: the recompense is linked to the preposition bi (with) in His saying: ﴿an equivalent thereof⁠﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: on this second reading there must be a returning pronoun for the relative clause, and the implied sense is: so the recompense of an evil deed from them is with its equivalent.

As for His saying: ﴿and humiliation will cover them⁠﴾, it is conjoined to "yujazi" (is recompensed), because His saying: ﴿the recompense of an evil deed is an equivalent thereof⁠﴾ is understood as: He recompenses an evil deed with its equivalent. It has also been read as (yarhaquhum dhillatun) with the letter ya'.

As for His saying: ﴿It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night⁠﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: ﴿were covered⁠﴾ means were clothed, ﴿their faces⁠﴾ ﴿pieces⁠﴾. Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read "qit'an" with a sukun on the ta' (ṭāʾ), while the rest read it with a fatḥah on the ta'. Qit' with a sukun on the ta' means a piece, a portion, and from it is His saying: ﴿So travel with your family during a portion of the night⁠﴾ [Hud: 81], meaning a piece of the night. As for qiṭaʿ with a fatḥah on the ta', it is the plural of qiṭʿah. The meaning of the verse is: He described their faces as black, to the point that it is as if they were clothed in a blackness from the night, like His saying: ﴿You will see those who lied against Allah with faces blackened⁠﴾ [al-Zumar: 60], and like His saying: ﴿As for those whose faces turn black, [it will be said]: Did you disbelieve after your belief?⁠﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 106], and like His saying: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks⁠﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. That mark is the blackness of the face and the blueness of the eyes.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿murdlim⁠﴾ (dark). Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: it is an adjective of "qiṭaʿan" (pieces). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it may also be made a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), as if it were said: their faces were covered with pieces of the night in a state of its darkness.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 28–29:**

﴿On the Day We gather them all together, We will say to those who associated others with Allah: "Stay in your place, you and your partners." Then We will separate them, and their partners will say: "You did not worship us."﴾ ﴿Allah suffices as a witness between us and you; we were indeed unaware of your worship.﴾

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿On the Day We gather them all together, We will say to those who associated others with Allah: "Stay in your place, you and your partners." Then We will separate them, and their partners will say: "You did not worship us."﴾ ﴿Allah suffices as a witness between us and you; we were indeed unaware of your worship.﴾

And in this passage there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that this is another aspect of the exposure of those disbelievers. The pronoun in His words ﴿On the Day We gather them﴾ refers to what was mentioned earlier, namely His words: ﴿And those who earned evil deeds﴾ [Yunus: 27]. Since Allah described these people whom He gathers as associators and disbelievers, this shows that what is meant by ﴿those who earned evil deeds﴾ is the disbelievers. The summary of the matter is that He, the Exalted, gathers the worshipper and the worshipped. Then the worshipped disowns the worshipper, and it becomes clear to him that he did not do that by his knowledge or will. The purpose of this is that the people used to say: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus: 18], so Allah the Exalted made clear that they will not intercede for these disbelievers, but rather will disown them. This indicates the utmost degradation and punishment for these disbelievers. Similar to this are verses, among them His words, the Exalted: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166], and among them His words, the Exalted: ﴿Then He will say to the angels: "Did these people worship you?" They will say: "Glory be to You, You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn"﴾ [Saba': 40–41].

Know that this statement points, by way of symbolism, to a subtle rational truth: that everything other than the One, the Unique, the Real, is possible in its own essence (mumkin li-dhatihi), and that which is possible in its essence is in need by its very quiddity. A single thing cannot be both receptive and an agent at the same time. Therefore, whatever is other than the One, the Unique, the Real, has no influence in bringing into existence and in creating. Thus, a possible created thing is not fitting to be worshipped by others; rather, the true object of worship is none other than the True Originator, and that is none other than the True Existent, who is necessary in existence by His essence (wajib al-wujud li-dhatihi). So the disowning of the worshipped from the worshippers may mean what we have mentioned, and Allah knows best His intent.

**The second issue:** "Al-hashr" (gathering) is bringing together from every direction to one place of standing. ﴿Jami'an﴾ (all together) is in the accusative as a state (ḥal), meaning: We gather all of them while they are gathered. ﴿Makanakum﴾ (your place) is in the accusative by an implied verb, "Remain" (ilzamū), and the sense is: "Remain in your place." ﴿Antum﴾ (you) is an emphatic pronoun for the pronoun, and ﴿wa-shurakāʾukum﴾ (and your partners) is conjoined to it. Know that His words ﴿makānakum﴾ are a term specific to threat and warning. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, says to the worshippers and the worshipped: "Makānakum", that is: "Remain in your places until you are questioned." A similar verse is His words, the Exalted: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, and their wives, and what they used to worship﴾ ﴿besides Allah, and guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ ﴿and stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 22–24].

As for His words ﴿fa-zayyalnā baynahum﴾ (then We separated them), there are two discussions:

**The first discussion:** This word came in the past tense (al-madi) after His words ﴿Then We will say﴾, though the event is yet to come. The reason is that what Allah has decided will happen has become as if it is occurring now. A similar example is His words, the Exalted: ﴿And the companions of Paradise will call out﴾ [al-A'raf: 44].

**The second discussion:** Zayyalnā means "We separated" and "We distinguished." Al-Farra' said: "His words ﴿fa-zayyalnā﴾ are not from azaltu (I removed); rather, they are from ziltu, when one separates. The Arabs say: ziltu al-ḍa'na min al-ma'zi, fa-lam tazil (I separated the sheep from the goats, and they did not separate)," meaning: I distinguished them, but they did not become distinct. Then al-Wahidi said: "Al-zayl, al-tazyil, and al-muzayala are distinguishing and separating." Al-Wahidi said: "It was also read as ﴿fa-zāyalnā baynahum﴾, which is like fa-zayyalnā." Al-Wahidi related from Ibn Qutayba that he said regarding this verse: "It is from zāla yazūlu, and azaltuhu (I removed it) is by me." Then he related from al-Azhari that he said: "This is an error, because he did not distinguish between zāla yazūlu and zāla yazīlu, and between them there is a great difference. The correct view is what al-Farra' said." Then the commentators said: ﴿fa-zayyalnā﴾ means: We separated between the polytheists and their partners from the gods and idols, and the connection that existed between them in the world was cut off.

* * *

[Page 68]

As for His words ﴿And their partners will say: "You did not worship us"﴾, there are several discussions:

**The first discussion:** He attributed the partners to them for several reasons:

First: They set aside a portion of their wealth for those idols, thereby making them partners to themselves in that wealth. For this reason, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And their partners will say﴾.

Second: A slight connection suffices for attribution. Since the disbelievers were the ones who established this partnership, it was indeed proper to attribute the partners to them.

Third: When Allah the Exalted addressed the worshippers and the worshipped with His words ﴿makānakum﴾, they became partners in this address.

**The second discussion:** They differed about who is meant by these partners.

Some said: They are the angels, and they cited His words, the Exalted: ﴿And on the Day He will gather them all together, then He will say to the angels: "Did these people worship you?"﴾ [Saba': 40]. Others said: Rather, they are the idols. The evidence for this is that this address contains threat and warning, and that is not fitting for the near angels. Then they differed about how these idols spoke this statement. Some said: Allah the Exalted will create life, reason, and speech in them, so they are indeed able to say this statement. Others said: He will create speech in them without creating life in them, so that this speech is heard from them. This view is weak, because the apparent meaning of His words ﴿And their partners will say﴾ requires that the agent of that saying be the partners.

If it is said: When Allah revives them, will He keep them or annihilate them?

We say: All of this is possible, and there is no objection against Allah regarding any of His actions. The conditions of the Resurrection are unknown, except for the little that Allah the Exalted has informed us of in the Qur'an.

The third view: What is meant by these partners is everyone who was worshipped besides Allah the Exalted: idols, the sun, the moon, humans, jinn, and angels.

**The third discussion:** This address is undoubtedly a threat concerning the worshippers. Is it also a threat concerning the worshipped? As for the Mu'tazila, they definitively asserted that this is not permissible. They said: Because the worshipped has no sin, and whoever has no sin, it is ugly for Allah the Exalted to direct fear, threat, and warning at him.

As for our companions (the Ash'aris), they said: He, the Exalted, is not questioned about what He does.

**The fourth discussion:** The partners said: ﴿You did not worship us﴾, while they had indeed been worshipped. So this was a lie. We have mentioned in the commentary on Surah al-An'am the disagreement among people about whether the people of the Resurrection lie or not, and this matter has been treated thoroughly before. What we mention here is that some of them said: What is meant by their words ﴿You did not worship us by our command and will﴾ is that you did not worship us by our order and our will.

They said: The evidence that what we have mentioned is the meaning consists of two points:

First: They called Allah as a witness in this, when they said: ﴿Allah suffices as a witness between us and you﴾.

Second: They said: ﴿We were indeed unaware of your worship﴾. So they affirmed that they had been worshipped, but claimed that they were unaware of that worship. They were truthful in this, because one of the greatest causes of unawareness is that they are inanimate objects with no sense of anything and no awareness at all.

Among the people, some took the verse at its apparent meaning and said: The partners reported that the disbelievers did not worship them.

Then they mentioned for this several explanations:

First: That place is a place of bewilderment and confusion, so that lie is like the lie of children and the lie of madmen and the bewildered.

[Page 69]

Second: They did not give any weight to the deeds of the disbelievers and regarded them as nothing because of their falsity; for this reason, they said: "They did not worship us."

Third: They imagined in the idols they worshipped many attributes, so in reality they worshipped essences described by those attributes. Since those essences were empty of those attributes, they did not worship them, but rather worshipped things they imagined that have no existence in reality. Those attributes which they imagined in their idols were that they harm, benefit, and intercede with Allah without His permission.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 30:

﴿There, every soul will know what it has sent forth before, and they will be returned to God, their true Master, and what they used to fabricate will have strayed from them.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿There, every soul will know what it has sent forth before, and they will be returned to God, their true Master, and what they used to fabricate will have strayed from them.﴾ Know that this verse is like a completion of what precedes it. His saying ﴿There﴾ means: in that station and in that position, or it may mean at that time, by way of using a noun of place for time. Regarding His saying ﴿will know﴾ (tabluu), there are several discussions:

The first discussion: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿tatlu﴾ with two taa's; ʿAsim read ﴿nabluu kull nafs﴾ with a nun and kull in the accusative; and the rest read ﴿tabluu﴾ with a taa and a baa.

As for the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, it has two aspects:

The first: that the meaning of ﴿tatlu﴾ is "it follows what it has sent forth," because its deed is what guides it to the path of Paradise and to the path of Hellfire.

The second: that the meaning is that every soul reads what is in its record of good or evil, and from this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Read your record; sufficient is your own soul against you today as a reckoner﴾ [al-Isra' 17:14], and He said: ﴿Then those will read their record﴾ [al-Isra' 17:71]. As for the reading of ʿAsim, its meaning is that God, may He be exalted, says that at that time We test every soul by means of the testing of what it has sent forth of deeds. The meaning is: We know its state through knowing the state of its deed; if it was good, it is happy, and if it was ugly, it is wretched. The meaning is that We treat it as one who tests, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud 11:7]. As for the well-known reading, its meaning is that We test every soul's deeds at that time.

The second discussion: al-ibtila' is an expression for testing, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We tested them with good and evil﴾ [al-A'raf 7:168]. It is said: al-bala' then al-ibtila', i.e., testing, must come before the test.

One may say: at that time the results of deeds are revealed and the effects of actions appear, so how is the occurrence of knowledge called testing?

Its answer: testing is a cause of the occurrence of knowledge, and applying the name of the cause to the effect is a well-known metaphor.

* * *
As for His saying, ﴿and they will be returned to God, their true Master﴾, know that "return" (radd) is an expression for turning a thing back to the place from which it came, and here there are possibilities:
The first: that the meaning of His saying ﴿and they will be returned to God﴾ is: they will be returned to the place where there is no judgment except God's, as has preceded in its similar instances.

The second: that the meaning is ﴿they will be returned﴾ to what appears to them from God of reward and punishment, alerting thereby to the fact that God's judgment regarding reward and punishment does not change.

The third: that the meaning of His saying ﴿and they will be returned to God﴾ is: they will be made compelled to acknowledge His divinity, after they were in the world worshipping other than God, the Exalted. For this reason He said:

Page 70
﴿their true Master⁠﴾, meaning: they turned away from the false master and returned to the true Master.
* * *
As for His saying ﴿their true Master﴾, its explanation has already passed in the surah of al-An'am.
* * *
As for His saying ﴿and what they used to fabricate will have strayed from them﴾, the meaning is that they used to claim, regarding what they worshipped, that they were intercessors and that their worship brought them near to God, the Exalted. So God, the Exalted, alerted that this will vanish in the Hereafter, and they will know that this was falsehood, fabrication and invention.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 31–33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Or who owns hearing and sight? And who brings out the living from the dead and brings out the dead from the living? And who arranges the affair?" They will say, "Allah." So say, "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ ﴿So that is Allah, your Lord, the Truth. Then what is there after the truth except error? Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 34:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Is there any of your associates who originates creation and then repeats it?  Say: Allah originates creation and then repeats it. So how are you turned away?﴾ Know that this is the second argument, and its explanation is what Allah, exalted is He, has explained in the other verses concerning the manner in which the creation of man begins from the drop (nutfah), the clinging clot (alaqah) and the lump of flesh (mudghah), and the manner of his return, and concerning the manner in which the creation of the heavens and the earth begins. Since He has detailed these stages, He, exalted is He, has therefore been satisfied here with mentioning them in summary. And here there are questions.

The first question: What is the benefit in presenting this argument in the form of a question and interrogation?

The answer: When a matter is manifest and clear, and it is then mentioned in the form of a question, with the answer left to the one being questioned, that is more eloquent and has a stronger effect on the heart.

The second question: The people were deniers of the return, the gathering and the resurrection, so how was the argument against them made by this?

The answer: He, exalted is He, mentioned earlier in this surah that which indicates it, namely the obligation to distinguish between the one who does good and the one who does evil. This indication is clear and strong, and the rational person cannot be able to refute it. Because of the completeness of its strength and clarity, He relied upon it, whether the opponent assists in it or does not assist.

The third question: Why did He command His Messenger to acknowledge this, when the obligation arises only if the opponent acknowledges it?

The answer: Since the proof is manifest and clear, when it is presented to the opponent in the form of a question, and then he himself says, "The matter is so," this is a notice that this statement has reached such clarity that there is no need for the opponent's acknowledgment of it, and that whether he acknowledges or denies it, the matter is established and manifest.

As for His words, ﴿So how are you turned away?﴾, the intended meaning is astonishment at them for departing from this clear matter, which desire, imitation, or weak doubt has urged them to oppose, because reporting that the idols are gods is a lie and a falsehood, and occupying oneself with worshipping them, while they do not deserve this worship, resembles falsehood.

[Page 73]

Almighty God says: ﴿Say: Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth? Say: Allah guides to the truth. Is He who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or he who does not find guidance unless he is guided? What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ ﴿And most of them follow nothing but conjecture. Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾

There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: Know that this is the third argument. Know also that proving the existence of the Creator first by creation and then by guidance is a consistent pattern in the Qur'an. Almighty God related that the Friend (al-Khalil, Abraham) (peace be upon him) mentioned this, saying: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:78]. He related that Moses (peace be upon him) mentioned it, saying: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its form and then guided﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:50]. He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) with it, saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who destined and then guided﴾ [al-A'la 87:1–3]. In reality, this is a noble proof, because a human being has a body and has a soul. Proving the existence of the Creator through the conditions of the body is creation, and proving it through the conditions of the soul is guidance. Here too, when He mentioned the proof of creation in the first verse, which is His saying: ﴿Is it not He who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ [Yunus 10:34], He followed it with the proof of guidance in this verse.

Know that the purpose of creating the body is the attainment of guidance for the soul, as Almighty God said: ﴿And Allah brought you out from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing, and made for you hearing and sight and hearts that you may be grateful﴾ [al-Nahl 16:78]. This is almost an explicit statement that He created the body and gave the senses only so that they would be instruments for acquiring knowledge and sciences. Furthermore, bodily conditions are base, their outcome returning to the enjoyment of tasting some flavors or touching some tangible qualities. As for spiritual conditions and divine knowledge, they are perfections that remain forever, preserved from coming into being and passing away. So we know that creation is subordinate to guidance, and the noblest and highest purpose is the attainment of guidance.

Given this established, we say: Minds are confused, the truth is difficult, thoughts are mixed, and only a few are free from error. Therefore it is necessary that guidance and the perception of the truth occur only through the help of Allah, glory be to Him, His guidance and His direction. Because of the difficulty of this matter, the Speaker (al-Kalim, Moses) (peace be upon him), after hearing the Eternal Speech, said: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:25]. All creatures seek guidance and guard against misguidance, yet most of them have fallen into misguidance. All of this indicates that the attainment of guidance, knowledge and recognition is nothing but from Almighty God.

Given that you know this, we say: Guidance is either an expression for calling to the truth, or an expression for the attainment of that knowledge. In either case, we have shown that it is the noblest of human ranks and the highest of true felicities, and we have shown that it is nothing but from Almighty God.

As for idols, they are inanimate objects that have no effect in calling to the truth nor in guiding to truthfulness. Thus it is established that He, Almighty, is the One who brings about all good in this world and the Hereafter, and the One who guides to all perfections of soul and body, and that idols have no effect in any of that. And since this is so, occupying oneself with worshipping them is pure ignorance and sheer foolishness. This is the gist of the discussion in this argument.

The second issue: Al-Zajjaj said: It is said "hadaytu ila al-haqq" and "hadaytu li-l-haqq" with one meaning, and Almighty God mentioned both usages in His saying: ﴿Allah guides to the truth (yahdi li-l-haqq). Is He who guides to the truth (yahdi ila al-haqq)…﴾.

[Page 74]

The third issue: Regarding His saying ﴿amman la yahiddi﴾ there are six readings (qira'at):

The first: Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Warsh, on the authority of Nafi', read ﴿yahaddi﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and the ha' and a shadda on the dal. This is the choice of Abu 'Ubaydah and Abu Hatim, because its origin is yahtadi; the ta' was assimilated into the dal and the fatha of the assimilated ta' was transferred to the ha'.

The second: Nafi' read with a sukun on the ha' and a shadda on the dal. The ta' was assimilated into the dal, and the ha' was left as it is, so in his reading he combined two sukun letters, just as they combined them in ﴿yakhussimun﴾. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: This is an error on Nafi'.

The third: Abu 'Amr read with an indication of the fatha on the ha' without full vocalization, so it is between fatha and jazm, weakened (mukhtalasah) according to the principle of his school, choosing lightness. 'Ali ibn 'Isa mentioned that this is the correct reading of Nafi'.

The fourth: 'Asim read with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ha' and a shadda on the dal, to flee from the meeting of two sukun letters, since the jazm is moved with a kasra.

The fifth: Hammad and Yahya ibn Adam, on the authority of Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read with a kasra on the ya' and the ha', making the kasra follow the kasra. It was said: this is the dialect of the one who read ﴿nasta'inu wa-na'budu﴾.

The sixth: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿man yahdi﴾ with a sukun on the ha' and a lightening of the dal, meaning yahtadi. The Arabs say yahdi in the sense of yahtadi. It is said: "hadaytuhu fa-hudiya," i.e., he was guided.

The fourth issue: There is a difficulty in the wording of the verse, namely that the intended "partners" in this verse are idols, and that they are inanimate objects that do not accept guidance, so His saying ﴿amman la yahiddi illa an yuhda﴾ does not befit them.

The answer comes in several ways:

The first: It is not far-fetched that what is intended by His saying ﴿Say: Is there any of your partners who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ is the idols. And what is intended by His saying ﴿Say: Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?﴾ is the leaders of disbelief and misguidance and those who call to it. The evidence for this is His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:31], up to His saying: ﴿There is no god but He; glory be to Him above what they associate﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:31]. What is meant is that Allah, glory be to Him and Exalted, guided creation to the true religion through the signs He manifested, both rational and transmitted. As for these callers and leaders, they cannot guide others unless Almighty God guides them. So holding fast to the religion of Almighty God is more fitting than accepting the word of these ignorant ones.

The second answer: It may be said that since the people took them as gods, they were, for this reason, referred to in the way one refers to those who know and understand. Do you not see that He, Almighty, said: ﴿Indeed, those whom you call upon besides Allah are servants like you﴾ [al-A'raf 7:194], even though they are inanimate objects? And He said: ﴿If you call upon them, they will not hear your call﴾ [Fatir 35:14]. So the wording was applied to the idols according to how it applies to one who understands and knows. Likewise here, Almighty God described them with the attribute of one who understands, even though the matter is not so.

The third: We take that as a hypothetical, meaning that even if they were such that they could guide, they would not guide others unless another had first guided them. When we take the statement under this supposition, the question disappears.

The fourth: In our view, bodily structure is not a condition for the validity of life and intellect. Those idols, while being wood and stone, are capable of life and intellect, and on this supposition it is valid for Almighty God to make them living and rational, and then they would occupy themselves with guiding others.

The fifth: Guidance (al-huda) is an expression for transfer and movement. It is said: "hudiyat al-mar'ah ila zawjiha huda," when the woman is transferred to her husband. Al-hady is what is sent to the Sacred Precinct of livestock, and the gift (al-hadiyyah) was so named because it passes from one man to another. And it is said: "Jā'a fulān yuhadi bayna ithnayn," when a man comes walking between two others, leaning on them out of his weakness and swaying.

Given this established, we say: His saying ﴿amman la yahiddi illa an yuhda﴾ may mean that he does not move to a place unless he is moved to it. On this supposition, the intention is to point out that these idols are inanimate objects, empty of life and power.

[Page 75]

Know that when Almighty God established this clear argument against the disbelievers, He said: ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾, expressing amazement to people of intellect at their corrupt doctrine and false saying.

* * *

Then Almighty God said: ﴿And most of them follow nothing but conjecture﴾. In it there are two views:

The first: "And most of them follow nothing but conjecture" in their affirmation of Allah, Almighty, because it is a statement not supported by proof in their view; rather, they merely heard it from their forefathers.

The second: "And most of them follow nothing but conjecture" in their saying that the idols are gods and that they are intercessors with Allah.

The first view is stronger, because in the second view we would need to interpret "most" as "all."

Then Almighty God said: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾. In it there are two issues:

The first issue: The opponents of analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy) use this verse as evidence. They said: Acting on analogy is acting on conjecture, so it must not be permitted, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾.

The proponents of analogy answered, saying: The proof that establishes the obligation to act on analogy is a decisive proof, so the obligation to act on analogy is known, and thus acting on analogy is not conjectural but known.

The one who argued answered this objection, saying: If the ruling derived from analogy were known to be a ruling of Almighty God, then abandoning acting on it would be disbelief, by His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:44]. But since that is not the case, its action is invalidated. Some have evaded this argument by saying: The ruling derived from analogy is either known to be a ruling of Almighty God, or is conjectured to be so, or is neither known nor conjectured. The first is false, since otherwise whoever did not judge by it would be a disbeliever, by His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:44], and by consensus this is not the case. The second is false, because acting on conjecture is not permitted, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾. The third is false, because if that ruling is neither known nor conjectured, it is mere caprice, and so it is invalid, by His saying: ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected prayer and followed desires﴾ [Maryam 19:59].

The proponents of analogy replied: The essence of this argument returns to holding by generalities, and holding by generalities yields only conjecture.

Since these generalities indicate the prohibition of holding by conjecture, it follows that they indicate the prohibition of holding by themselves; and whatever's establishment leads to its negation is to be abandoned.

The second issue: This verse indicates that whoever is conjectural in matters of the fundamentals (usul) of belief, and is not certain, is not a believer.

If it is said: The saying of the People of the Sunnah, "I am a believer, if Allah wills," prevents certainty, so it must be that they are obliged to be disbelievers.

We say: This is weak from several aspects:

The first: The view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that faith is an expression for the totality of belief, affirmation and action. Doubt is a matter of whether these actions conform to the command of Almighty God. And doubt in one component of the reality does not necessitate doubt in the whole reality.

The second: The purpose of His saying "if Allah wills" is the persistence of faith at the time of the end.

The third: Its purpose is the humbling and breaking of the self. And Allah knows best.

Proving the existence of the Creator through the conditions of the body is creation, and proving it through the conditions of the soul is guidance. This is almost an explicit statement that He created the body and gave the senses only so that they would be instruments for acquiring knowledge and sciences. Furthermore, bodily conditions are base, their outcome returning to the enjoyment of tasting some flavors or touching some tangible qualities. As for spiritual conditions and divine knowledge, they are perfections that remain forever, preserved from coming into being and passing away. So we know that creation is subordinate to guidance, and the noblest and highest purpose is the attainment of guidance.

Because of the difficulty of this matter, the Speaker (al-Kalim, Moses) (peace be upon him), after hearing the Eternal Speech, said: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:25]. All of this indicates that the attainment of guidance, knowledge and recognition is nothing but from Almighty God.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 37–39 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This Qur'an could not have been produced by other than Allah, but it is a confirmation of what lies between its hands and a detailed explanation of the Book, there being no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "Then bring a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation had not yet come to them. Thus did those before them deny. So see how was the end of the wrongdoers.﴾ In this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that when we began the tafsir (exegesis) of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ (Yunus 10:20), we mentioned that the people only said that because they believed the Qur'an was not miraculous (mu'jiz), and that Muhammad was producing it from himself by way of fabrication and invention. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned many answers concerning this speech, and those explanations extended, in the order we explained and detailed, to this place. Then He, exalted is He, clarified in this context that the bringing of this Qur'an by Muhammad (peace be upon him) was not a way of fabricating against Allah, exalted is He, but rather it is a revelation sent down to him from Allah. Then He, exalted is He, argued for the soundness of this speech with His saying: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "Then bring a surah like it."﴾ That indicates that it is a miracle sent down to him from Allah, exalted is He, and that it is free from fabrication and invention. This is the correct arrangement of the verses.

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This Qur'an could not have been produced...﴾ *Kana* ("could not have been") here has two interpretations:

The first: that His saying *an yuftara* ("that it be fabricated") is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), and the meaning is: "This Qur'an was not a fabrication other than from Allah," just as you say, "This speech was nothing but a lie."

The second: that it is said that the word *an* ("that") came here with the meaning of *li* ("for"), and the sense is: "This Qur'an was not such that it could be fabricated apart from Allah," like His saying: ﴿The believers should not go forth all together﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:122), and ﴿Allah would not leave the believers﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:179), and ﴿Nor would Allah give you knowledge of the unseen﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:179). That is, it was not fitting for them to do that. Likewise, it is not fitting for this Qur'an to be fabricated; that is, its description is not the description of a thing that could be fabricated against Allah, because the *muftara* (fabrication) is what humans produce, whereas the Qur'an is miraculous and humans cannot produce its like. *Al-iftira'* (fabrication) is a derivation from *faraytu al-adim* ("I cut the hide") when I measured it for cutting; then it came to be used for lying, just as they say, "So-and-so invented this story," meaning he lied. The result of this speech is that no one can produce this Qur'an except Allah, mighty and majestic. Then He, exalted is He, argued for this claim with several matters:

**The first argument:** His saying: ﴿but it is a confirmation of what lies between its hands﴾. The presentation of this argument is in several respects:

One of them: Muhammad (peace be upon him) was an unlettered man. He did not travel to a city for the sake of learning, and Mecca was not a city of scholars, and there was not in it any of the books of knowledge. Then he (peace be upon him) brought this Qur'an, and this Qur'an contained stories of the earlier peoples, and the people were in the utmost enmity toward him. Had these stories not agreed with what is in the Torah and the Gospel, they would have criticized him and exaggerated in attacking him, and they would have said to him, "You brought these stories not as they should be." But when no one said that, despite their intense eagerness to attack him and to disfigure his image, we know that he brought those stories in agreement with what is in the Torah and the Gospel, even though he had not studied either of them and had not been a disciple of anyone in them. This indicates that he (peace be upon him) reported these matters only by revelation from Allah, exalted is He.

The second argument: that the revealed books of Allah indicated the coming of Muhammad (peace be upon him), as we have thoroughly established in surah al-Baqarah in the tafsir of His saying: ﴿Fulfil My covenant, and I will fulfil your covenant﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:40). Since the matter is so, the coming of Muhammad (peace be upon him) is a confirmation of what is in those books, from the glad tidings of his coming (ﷺ). So this is an expression of "confirmation of what lies between its hands."

The third argument: that he (peace be upon him) reported in the Qur'an many unseen matters concerning the future, and they occurred in agreement with that report, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The Romans have been defeated﴾ (al-Rum 30:1–2), and the verse, and like His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth﴾ (al-Fath 48:27), and like His saying: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe among you and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth﴾ (al-Nur 24:55). That indicates that the reporting of these unseen future matters occurred only by revelation from Allah, exalted is He, and that was an expression of "confirmation of what lies between its hands." So the first two respects report past unseen matters, and the third respect reports future unseen matters, and all of them together are an expression of the confirmation of what lies between its hands.

**The second type** of the proofs mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿and a detailed explanation of every thing﴾. Know that people have differed as to in what respect the Qur'an is miraculous. Some said: it is miraculous because it includes reports of the unseen past and future, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿a confirmation of what lies between its hands﴾. Others said: it is miraculous because it includes many sciences, and to this the indication is His saying: ﴿and a detailed explanation of every thing﴾. The careful treatment of this topic is that the sciences are either religious or non-religious, and there is no doubt that the first category is higher in rank, greater in importance, and more perfect in degree than the second.

As for the religious sciences, they are either the science of beliefs and religions, or the science of works.

As for the science of beliefs and religions, it is an expression of knowing Allah, exalted is He, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day.

As for knowing Allah, exalted is He, it is an expression of knowing His essence, knowing the attributes of His majesty, knowing the attributes of His beneficence, knowing His acts, knowing His rulings, and knowing His names. The Qur'an includes the proofs of these matters, their branches, and their details, in a manner that nothing among the books equals, and nothing among the compositions even comes close to it.

As for the science of works, it is either an expression of the science of obligations related to outward acts, which is the science of *fiqh* (jurisprudence), and it is known that all the jurists derived their discussions from the Qur'an; or it is a science of purifying the inner self or disciplining the hearts (*riyada al-qulub*). The Qur'an contains from the topics of this science what is hardly found elsewhere, like His saying: ﴿Take what is easy, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant﴾ (al-A'raf 7:199), and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality and wrongdoing and oppression﴾ (al-Nahl 16:90). Thus it is established that the Qur'an includes the details of all noble sciences, rational and transmitted, in a way whose occurrence is impossible in the rest of the books, and so it is miraculous. To this the indication is His saying: ﴿and a detailed explanation of the Book﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿there being no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds﴾, its demonstration is: a long book containing these many sciences must include some kind of contradiction; and since this book is free of it, we know that it is from Allah and by His revelation and sending down. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ (al-Nisa 4:82).

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned at the beginning of this verse that this Qur'an is not suited, by its state and attribute, to be a speech fabricated against Allah, exalted is He, and established against that these two types of proofs mentioned, He returned once more with the interrogative form as a way of denial, saying: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ Then He, exalted is He, mentioned another argument to refute this claim, saying: ﴿Say, "Then bring a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ We have pursued this argument thoroughly in the tafsir of His saying in surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then bring a surah like it, and call your witnesses besides Allah, if you are truthful﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:23). Here there are questions:

**The first question:** Why did He say in surah al-Baqarah: ﴿like it﴾ (*min mithlihi*), and here He said: ﴿a surah like it﴾ (*bi-surah mithlihi*)?

The answer: Muhammad (peace be upon him) was an unlettered man, who was not a disciple of anyone, and did not study a book. So in surah al-Baqarah He said: ﴿then bring a surah like it﴾ (*min mithlihi*), meaning: let a person who is equal to Muhammad (peace be upon him) in not being a disciple, not studying books, and not occupying himself with the sciences, bring a surah equal to this surah. And since the inability became manifest, the miracle became manifest.

This does not indicate that the surah in itself is miraculous. Rather, it indicates that the appearance of a surah like this from a person like Muhammad (peace be upon him), in lacking discipleship and learning, is miraculous.
