In this hour the complete walaya is attained. And whenever this state is present, its possessor fears nothing and grieves over nothing. How can that be conceived, when fear of something and grief over something only arise after awareness of it, while the one immersed in the light of Allah's majesty is oblivious of all that is other than Allah the Exalted? So it is impossible for him to have fear or grief. This is a lofty rank, and whoever has not tasted it does not know it.

Then the possessor of this state may lose it, and at that time fear, grief, hope, desire and dread arise in him due to physical conditions, as they arise in others. I have heard that Ibrahim al-Khawwas was in the desert with a companion who accompanied him. One night a powerful state and complete unveiling came upon him, so he sat in his place, and wild beasts came and stood near him, while the disciple climbed to the top of a tree out of fear of them. The shaykh was not alarmed by those beasts. When morning came and that state had passed, on the following night a mosquito landed on his hand, and he showed distress because of that mosquito. The disciple said: How does this state fit with what came before it? The shaykh said: We endured last night what we endured because of the strength of the unseen inspiration (al-warid al-ghaybi). When that inspiration departed, I am the weakest of Allah's creatures.

The second issue: Most of the verifiers said: The people of reward will not experience fear in the assembly of the Resurrection. They argued for the soundness of their view by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the awliya' of Allah, there is no fear upon them, nor do they grieve﴾, and by His words: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103]. Also, the Resurrection is the abode of recompense, so it is not fitting to inflict fear upon them. Others said: Rather, various kinds of fear occur for them, and they cited reports indicating this, but the apparent meaning of the Qur'an takes precedence over a single report (khabar al-wahid).

* * *

[p. 103]

As for His words: ﴿Those who believed and used to be mindful of Allah﴾, there are three grammatical possibilities:

The first: It is in the accusative (nasb) as a qualifier (sifa) of the awliya'.

The second: It is in the accusative by way of praise (nasb 'ala al-madh).

The third: It is in the nominative (raf') as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and its predicate is: "for them is good news."

* * *

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾, there are several opinions:

The first: What is meant by it is the good dream. From the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Good news is the good dream which a Muslim sees or which is seen for him." And from him, peace be upon him: "Prophethood has departed, and the bearers of good news remain." And from him, peace be upon him: "The good dream is from Allah, and the nightmare is from Satan. So when one of you has a dream that frightens him, let him seek refuge from it, and let him spit three times to his left, for it will not harm him." And from him (ﷺ): "The good dream is one part of forty-six parts of prophethood." And from Ibn Mas'ud: Dreams are of three kinds: the concern a man has during the day and sees at night; the presence of Satan; and the dream which is the true dream.

And from Ibrahim: Dreams are three: the good tidings from Allah are one part of seventy parts of prophethood; the thing one of you is concerned with during the day, so he may see it at night; and the frightening from Satan. So when one of you sees what grieves him, let him say: "I seek refuge in what the angels of Allah sought refuge in, from the evil of my dream which I saw, that it may harm me in my world or in my Hereafter."

Know that if we interpret His words, ﴿for them is good news﴾, as the true dream, then the apparent meaning of this text requires that this state occurs only for them. Reason also indicates this, because the walī of Allah is the one whose heart and spirit are absorbed in the remembrance of Allah. Whoever is like this, when he sleeps, nothing remains in his spirit except the knowledge of Allah. It is known that the knowledge of Allah and the light of Allah's majesty yield only truth and sincerity. As for the one whose thought is scattered among the affairs of this turbid and dark world, when he sleeps he remains that way, so there is certainly no reliance on his visions. For this reason He said: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾, in an exclusive and restrictive manner.

The second opinion regarding the explanation of the good news: It is an expression for people's love for him and their mention of him with good praise. From Abu Dharr, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, a man does a deed for Allah and people love him! He said: 'That is the immediate good news of the believer.'"

Know that the rational investigations strengthen this meaning, because perfection is loved for its own sake, not for something else. Whoever is characterized by an attribute of perfection becomes beloved to everyone. And there is no perfection for the servant higher and more noble than being absorbed in heart with the knowledge of Allah, absorbed in tongue with the remembrance of Allah, and absorbed in limbs and members with the servitude of Allah. When something of this category appears upon him, tongues flow with praising him and hearts are inclined to love him. And whenever these noble attributes are greater, this love is stronger. Also, the light of the knowledge of Allah is served by its very nature, so in whatever heart it is present, that person becomes served by nature. Do you not see that beasts and predators may be stronger than a human, yet when they see a human they fear him and flee from him? That is only because of the awe of the rational soul (al-nafs al-natiqa).

The third opinion regarding the explanation of the good news: It is an expression for the good news they receive at death, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The angels descend upon them, saying: Do not fear and do not grieve, and rejoice in the Garden﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. As for the good news in the Hereafter, it is the angels' greeting upon them, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The angels will enter upon them from every gate. Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23], and Allah's greeting upon them, as He said: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. And included in this category is what Allah mentioned in this noble Book, of the whiteness of their faces and the giving of their records in their right hands, and the pleasant states they encounter in them. All of that is among the bearers of good news.

The fourth opinion: That this is an expression for what Allah gave good news of to His pious servants in His Book and through the tongues of His prophets, of His Garden and His generous reward. Its evidence is His words: ﴿Their Lord gives them good news of mercy from Him and of approval﴾ [al-Tawbah: 21].

Know that the word bishara (glad tidings) is derived from a joyful news whose effect appears on the surface of the face (bashara al-wajh). Therefore, whatever is of this kind enters into this verse, and the aforementioned matters all share this attribute, so all of them are included in it. Whatever among these aspects relates to the worldly life is included under His saying: ﴿For them is good news in the worldly life﴾, and whatever relates to the Hereafter is included under His saying: ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾.

Then, when He, exalted is He, mentioned the attribute of the friends of God and explained their conditions, He said: ﴿There is no alteration in the words of God﴾. The meaning is that there is no failure in them, and "the word" (kalima) and "the saying" (qawl) are the same. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿The word is not changed before Me﴾ [Qaf: 29]. This is one of the things that strengthens the view that what is meant by the glad tidings is God's promise of reward and honor for those who obey Him, by His saying: ﴿Their Lord gives them glad tidings of mercy from Him and good pleasure﴾. Then He explained that: ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, and it is like His saying: ﴿And when you look there, you see bliss and a great dominion﴾ [al-Insan: 20].

Then al-Qadi said: His saying ﴿There is no alteration in the words of God﴾ indicates that they are capable of alteration, and whatever is capable of non-existence cannot be eternal. A parallel to this argument is the inference from the occurrence of abrogation (naskh) that the ruling of God, exalted is He, cannot be eternal. The discussion of such aspects has already preceded.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 62–64 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the awliya' (close friends) of Allah, there is no fear upon them, nor do they grieve.﴾ ﴿Those who believed and used to be mindful of Allah.﴾ ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. There is no alteration to the words of Allah. That is the great triumph.﴾

Know that we have explained that the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter, nor do you recite from it any Qur'an﴾ [Yunus: 61], strengthen the hearts of the obedient and break the hearts of the wicked. Then Allah the Exalted followed it with a description of the states of the sincere, truthful and steadfast in truth (siddiqin), which is what is mentioned in this verse. In it there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that to interpret this verse we need to explain who the walī is, and then explain what is meant by the negation of fear and grief from him.

We say: As for who the walī is, the Qur'an, the report (khabar), the transmitted narration (athar) and reason (ma'qul) all indicate it.

As for the Qur'an, it is His words in this verse: ﴿Those who believed and used to be mindful of Allah.﴾ His words "believed" point to the perfection of the theoretical faculty (al-quwwa al-nazariyya), and His words "used to be mindful" point to the perfection of the practical faculty (al-quwwa al-'amaliyya).

There is another position in this matter, which is to take faith as the totality of belief and action, and then to describe the walī as one who was mindful in everything.

As for mindfulness in the realm of knowledge, it is because the majesty of Allah is too exalted for human intellect to encompass. So when the truthful one describes Allah the Glorified with an attribute of majesty, he sanctifies Allah from His perfection and majesty being limited to that measure which he knew and described Him with. And when he worships Allah the Exalted, he sanctifies Allah the Exalted from the service fitting to His greatness being measured by that extent. Thus it is established that he is always in a state of fear and mindfulness.

As for the reports, they are numerous. 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They are a people who loved one another for the sake of Allah, not because of kinship between them nor because of wealth they exchange. By Allah, their faces are light, and indeed they are upon pulpits of light. They do not fear when people fear, and they do not grieve when people grieve." Then he recited this verse.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "They are those whom Allah the Exalted is remembered by seeing them."

The people of verification (ahl al-tahqiq) said: The reason for this is that their being seen reminds one of the matter of the Hereafter, because there are visible signs of humility and submission in them, and because of what Allah the Exalted mentioned in His words: ﴿Their mark is on their faces, from the trace of prostration﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

As for the athar: Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: The awliya' of Allah are those whose guidance Allah the Exalted undertook through clear proof, and who undertook to carry out the true servitude to Allah the Exalted and the call to Him.

As for reason (al-ma'qul), we say: It is established in the science of etymology (ilm al-ishtiqaq) that the root waw-lam-ya' indicates the meaning of nearness. So the walī of everything is the one who is close to it. Nearness to Allah the Exalted in terms of place and direction is impossible. Nearness to Him occurs only when the heart is immersed in the light of knowledge of Allah the Exalted, the Glorified. If it sees, it sees the proofs of Allah's power; if it hears, it hears the signs of Allah; if it speaks, it speaks in praise of Allah; if it moves, it moves in the service of Allah; if it strives, it strives in the obedience of Allah. There, it is in the utmost nearness to Allah. This person is a walī of Allah the Exalted. And when he is like this, Allah the Exalted is also a walī to him, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah is the walī of those who believe; He brings them out from darkness into light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. And it must be so, because nearness does not arise except from both sides.

The theologians (al-mutakallimun) said: The walī of Allah is the one who holds correct belief founded upon evidence and who performs righteous deeds in accordance with what the Sharia has brought. This is a concise statement on the interpretation of the walī.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 65–66:

The Exalted said: ﴿And let not their speech grieve you. Indeed, all might belongs to Allah. He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth. And those who call upon other than Allah do not follow partners. They follow only assumption, and they are only guessing.﴾

Know that when the people brought forth various kinds of doubts, which Allah related from them in what preceded in this surah, and Allah answered them with the answers we have explained and established, they turned to another path. They threatened and intimidated him, and claimed that we are the possessors of followers and wealth, so we will strive to subdue you and to nullify your affair. Allah, glorified is He, answered this path with His saying: ﴿And let not their speech grieve you. Indeed, all might belongs to Allah.﴾

Know that a person only grieves over the threat, menace, plotting and scheming of another if he deems it possible that it could affect his condition. When he knows from the One who knows the unseen that this will not have an effect, it ceases to be a cause for his grief.

Then, just as He removed from the Messenger the grief of the Hereafter through His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the friends of Allah—no fear shall be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62], likewise He removed the grief of this world through His saying: ﴿And let not their speech grieve you. Indeed, all might belongs to Allah.﴾ So, since Allah, exalted is He, is the One who sent him to the creation and the One who commanded him to call them to this religion, He would inevitably be his supporter and helper. And since it is established that might, domination and victory belong only to Him, security has been achieved and fear has been removed.

Page 105

If it is said: How then did He grant him security from that when he remained fearful, to the point that he needed to migrate and flee, and after that he feared from one state to another?

We say: Allah, exalted is He, promised him victory and support absolutely, and the time was not specified. So at every time he feared that this might not be that specified time, and then defeat and retreat would occur at that time.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, all might belongs to Allah﴾, there are discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: The judge (al-Qadi) said: "Indeed" (inna) is with a kasra on the alif, and opening it (anna) would be corruption approaching disbelief, because it would lead to the people saying: "All might belongs to Allah," and that the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, was being grieved by that.

If you read the alif with a kasra, it becomes a resumption (isti'naf), and this indicates the excellence of the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis).

The author of al-Kashshaf said: Abu Haywa read "anna al-izzata" with a fatha, by deleting the lam of causation (lam al-'illah), meaning: "because might belongs to Allah," which is an explicit causal construction.

The second discussion: The benefits of "Indeed, all might belongs to Allah" in this context are several:

The first: What is meant is that all might and power belong to Allah, the Exalted, who gives to His servants whatever He wills. The purpose is that He does not give the disbelievers power over him; rather, He gives him power over them, so that he becomes mightier than them. Thus Allah granted him security through this statement from the harm of the disbelievers by killing and harming. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21], and ﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51].

The second: Al-Asamm said: What is meant is that the polytheists gain strength through the abundance of their servants and wealth, and they threaten you with them. All those things belong to Allah, the Exalted, so He is able to strip them of all those things, to support you, and to transfer their wealth and their homes to you.

If it is said: His saying "Indeed, all might belongs to Allah" appears to contradict His saying: ﴿And might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8].

We say: There is no contradiction, because the might of the Messenger and the believers is entirely through Allah, so it belongs to Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: He hears what they say and knows what they resolve upon, and He will requite them for that.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾, there are two aspects:

The first: The Exalted mentioned in the preceding verses ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, which indicates that everything that does not reason is a possession of Allah and belongs to Him. Here, however, the word "man" (whoever) is specific to rational beings, indicating that all rational beings are included under the dominion and ownership of Allah. So the two verses together indicate that all of it is His dominion and His possession.

The second: What is meant by "whoever is in the heavens" is the discerning rational beings, namely the angels and the two weighty creatures (jinn and humankind).

He singled them out for mention to indicate that if these, being rational, belong to Him and are under His dominion, then inanimate things are more fitting for this servitude, and this is a refutation of making idols partners with Allah, the Exalted.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And those who call upon other than Allah do not follow partners. They follow only assumption﴾. Regarding the word "ma" (what/those who not) there are two views:

The first: It is a negation and denial, and the meaning is that they did not follow a partner of Allah, the Exalted; they only followed something they assumed to be a partner of Allah, the Exalted.

An example of this: if one of us assumed that Zayd was in the house when he was not there, and then addressed a person in the house whom he thought was Zayd, it would not be said that he addressed Zayd; rather, it would be said he addressed the one he thought was Zayd.

The second: That "ma" is interrogative, as if it were said: "What is it that those who call upon other than Allah as partners follow?" The intent is to disparage their action, meaning that they are not upon anything.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿They follow only assumption﴾. The meaning is that they only followed their false assumptions and their corrupt illusions. Then He clarified that this assumption has no ruling: ﴿And they are only guessing﴾. We have mentioned the meaning of "kharṣ" (guessing) in Surat al-An'am at His saying: ﴿They follow only assumption, and they are only guessing﴾ [al-An'am: 116].

They follow only assumption, and they are only guessing.﴾

They threatened and intimidated him, and claimed that we are the possessors of followers and wealth, so we will strive to subdue you and to nullify your affair. Allah, glorified is He, answered this path with His saying: ﴿And let not their speech grieve you. Indeed, all might belongs to Allah.﴾

Know that a person only grieves over the threat, menace, plotting and scheming of another if he deems it possible that it could affect his condition. When he knows from the One who knows the unseen that this will not have an effect, it ceases to be a cause for his grief.

Then, just as He removed from the Messenger the grief of the Hereafter through His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the friends of Allah—no fear shall be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62], likewise He removed the grief of this world through His saying: ﴿And let not their speech grieve you. Indeed, all might belongs to Allah.﴾ So, since Allah, exalted is He, is the One who sent him to the creation and the One who commanded him to call them to this religion, He would inevitably be his supporter and helper. And since it is established that might, domination and victory belong only to Him, security has been achieved and fear has been removed.

Page 105

If it is said: How then did He grant him security from that when he remained fearful, to the point that he needed to migrate and flee, and after that he feared from one state to another?

We say: Allah, exalted is He, promised him victory and support absolutely, and the time was not specified. So at every time he feared that this might not be that specified time, and then defeat and retreat would occur at that time.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, all might belongs to Allah﴾, there are discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: The judge (al-Qadi) said: "Indeed" (inna) is with a kasra on the alif, and opening it (anna) would be corruption approaching disbelief, because it would lead to the people saying: "All might belongs to Allah," and that the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, was being grieved by that.

If you read the alif with a kasra, it becomes a resumption (isti'naf), and this indicates the excellence of the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis).

The author of al-Kashshaf said: Abu Haywa read "anna al-izzata" with a fatha, by deleting the lam of causation (lam al-'illah), meaning: "because might belongs to Allah," which is an explicit causal construction.

The second discussion: The benefits of "Indeed, all might belongs to Allah" in this context are several:

The first: What is meant is that all might and power belong to Allah, the Exalted, who gives to His servants whatever He wills. The purpose is that He does not give the disbelievers power over him; rather, He gives him power over them, so that he becomes mightier than them. Thus Allah granted him security through this statement from the harm of the disbelievers by killing and harming. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21], and ﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51].

The second: Al-Asamm said: What is meant is that the polytheists gain strength through the abundance of their servants and wealth, and they threaten you with them. All those things belong to Allah, the Exalted, so He is able to strip them of all those things, to support you, and to transfer their wealth and their homes to you.

If it is said: His saying "Indeed, all might belongs to Allah" appears to contradict His saying: ﴿And might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8].

We say: There is no contradiction, because the might of the Messenger and the believers is entirely through Allah, so it belongs to Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: He hears what they say and knows what they resolve upon, and He will requite them for that.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾, there are two aspects:

The first: The Exalted mentioned in the preceding verses ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, which indicates that everything that does not reason is a possession of Allah and belongs to Him. Here, however, the word "man" (whoever) is specific to rational beings, indicating that all rational beings are included under the dominion and ownership of Allah. So the two verses together indicate that all of it is His dominion and His possession.

The second: What is meant by "whoever is in the heavens" is the discerning rational beings, namely the angels and the two weighty creatures (jinn and humankind).

He singled them out for mention to indicate that if these, being rational, belong to Him and are under His dominion, then inanimate things are more fitting for this servitude, and this is a refutation of making idols partners with Allah, the Exalted.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And those who call upon other than Allah do not follow partners. They follow only assumption﴾. Regarding the word "ma" (what/those who not) there are two views:

The first: It is a negation and denial, and the meaning is that they did not follow a partner of Allah, the Exalted; they only followed something they assumed to be a partner of Allah, the Exalted.

An example of this: if one of us assumed that Zayd was in the house when he was not there, and then addressed a person in the house whom he thought was Zayd, it would not be said that he addressed Zayd; rather, it would be said he addressed the one he thought was Zayd.

The second: That "ma" is interrogative, as if it were said: "What is it that those who call upon other than Allah as partners follow?" The intent is to disparage their action, meaning that they are not upon anything.

Page 106

Then the Exalted said: ﴿They follow only assumption﴾. The meaning is that they only followed their false assumptions and their corrupt illusions. Then He clarified that this assumption has no ruling: ﴿And they are only guessing﴾. We have mentioned the meaning of "kharṣ" (guessing) in Surat al-An'am at His saying: ﴿They follow only assumption, and they are only guessing﴾ [al-An'am: 116].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 67:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who made for you the night that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight. Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned His saying: ﴿Indeed, all honour belongs to Allah﴾, He argued for it with this verse. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, made the night so that fatigue and weariness might pass away through resting therein, and made the day "mubsiran" (giving sight), that is, illuminating, so that you may be guided by it in your needs through sight. The "mubsir" is that which gives sight, and the day is one in which sight occurs. He made it "mubsir" by way of transferring the name from the cause to the effect.

If it is said: His saying, ﴿It is He who made for you the night that you may rest therein﴾, indicates that He did not create it except for this purpose, and His saying, ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen﴾, indicates that He, exalted is He, intended by creating the night and the day many kinds of proofs.

We say: His saying, exalted is He, "li-taskunu" (that you may rest), does not indicate that there is no wisdom in it other than that; rather, it requires the occurrence of that wisdom.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen﴾, what is meant is that they reflect upon what they hear and take lesson from it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 68:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They say, "God has taken a son." Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. You have no authority for this. Do you say about God what you do not know?﴾

Know that this is another type of the falsehoods which God, exalted is He, related from the disbelievers, namely their saying: ﴿God has taken a son.﴾ It is possible that what is meant is the recounting of the saying of those who say: the angels are God's daughters. It is possible that what is meant is the saying of those who say: the idols are God's children. It is possible that there were among them a group of Christians who said that.

Then, when He, exalted is He, denounced this saying, He said after it: ﴿He is the Self-Sufficient. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾

Know that His being, exalted is He, self-sufficient and the owner of everything in the heavens and the earth indicates that it is impossible for Him to have a son. The explanation of this is from several aspects:

The first: He, glorified is He, is absolutely self-sufficient in what is in this verse, and reason also indicates this, for if He were in need, He would require another creator, which is impossible. Everyone who is self-sufficient must necessarily be a single being, free from parts and components. Whoever is like this, it is impossible that a part of his parts should separate from him, whereas a son means that a part of a human's parts separates and then from that part there is generated something like him. If this is impossible, it is established that His being self-sufficient prevents a son from being attributed to Him.

The second argument: He, exalted is He, is self-sufficient, and whoever is self-sufficient is eternal, without beginning, everlasting, and perpetual. Whoever is like this cannot be subject to extinction or termination, whereas a son comes into being only for a thing that passes away and perishes, so that his son stands in his place. Thus it is established that His being, exalted is He, self-sufficient, indicates that it is impossible for Him to have a son.

The third argument: He, exalted is He, is self-sufficient, and whoever is self-sufficient is impossible to be described with desire and pleasure. When that is impossible, it is impossible for Him to have a spouse and a son.

The fourth argument: He, exalted is He, is self-sufficient, and whoever is self-sufficient cannot have a son, because taking a son happens only with regard to one who is in need, so that his son may help him with the benefits that have been realized and those that are anticipated. So whoever is absolutely self-sufficient, taking a son is impossible for him.

The fifth argument: The offspring of an animal is its son only under two conditions: that it is equal to it in nature and reality, and that its beginning of existence and coming into being is from it. This is impossible with regard to God, exalted is He, because He is absolutely self-sufficient, and whoever is absolutely self-sufficient is necessarily existent in His essence. So if the Necessarily Existent had a son, his son would be equal to Him, and it would follow that the son of the Necessarily Existent is also necessarily existent. But His being necessarily existent prevents Him from being generated from another, and if He is not generated from another, He is not a son. Thus it is established that His being, exalted is He, self-sufficient is among the strongest proofs that He, exalted is He, has no son. These three together with the first three are of the utmost strength.

The sixth argument: He, exalted is He, is self-sufficient, and whoever is self-sufficient cannot have a father and a mother, and whoever is sanctified above having parents must be sanctified above having children.

If it is said: Does this not present a difficulty with the first parent?

We say: The first parent is not impossible to be a son of another, because He, glorified and exalted is He, is able to create the first parent from two parents who precede him. As for the Truth, glorified is He, it is impossible that He be in need of two parents, for otherwise He would not be absolutely self-sufficient.

The seventh argument: He, exalted is He, is absolutely self-sufficient, and whoever is absolutely self-sufficient cannot need another in bringing things into existence.

Having established this, we say: This son is either eternal or originated. If he is eternal, then he is necessarily existent in his essence, for if he were possibly existent he would need an agent; and the eternal's need for an agent would entail bringing into existence what already exists, which is impossible. And if he is necessarily existent in his essence, he is not a son of another, but rather an independently existent being in himself. As for if this son is originated, and the Truth, glorified is He, is absolutely self-sufficient, then He was able to bring him into existence from the beginning without associating anything else, so this would be an absolute servant, and not a son. This is the totality of the aspects derived from His saying: ﴿He is the Self-Sufficient﴾, which indicate that it is impossible for Him to have a son.

As for His saying: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, know that it is similar to His saying: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93]. Its summary reduces to this: whatever is other than the One, the Unique, the Real, is possible; every possible thing is needy; every needy thing is originated. So everything other than the One, the Unique, the Real, is originated, and God, exalted is He, is its originator, its creator, and its bringer into existence.

This indicates the invalidity of the claim affirming a spouse and a son. When He, exalted is He, has clarified by clear proof the impossibility of what they attributed to Him, He turned to them with denunciation and rebuke, saying: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾, drawing attention by this to the fact that they have no proof at all in that matter.

Then he intensified this denunciation, saying: ﴿Do you say about God what you do not know?﴾ We have mentioned that this verse is cited in refuting taqlid (blind imitation) in the foundations of religious belief. And those who deny analogy (qiyas) and solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad) may cite it in refuting these two principles, and the discussion of that has already passed.

God Most High says, **"Say: Indeed, those who invent lies against God will not prosper. [They have] a brief enjoyment in this world; then to Us is their return; then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve."** (10:69–70)

Know that when God Most High clarified, by a decisive proof, that ascribing a son to God is a false claim, and then clarified that this claimant has no proof for the soundness of his claim, it became clear that this doctrine is a fabrication against God and an attribution to Him of what does not befit Him. So He stated that whoever is in this condition will never prosper. Do you not see that He said at the beginning of Surat al-Mu'minun: **"The believers have certainly prospered"** (23:1), and said at the end of this same surah: **"Indeed, the disbelievers will not prosper"** (23:117)?

Know also that His saying, **"Indeed, those who invent lies against God will not prosper,"** includes this case, but it is not restricted to this case. Rather, everyone who speaks about the Essence of God Most High and His attributes without knowledge and without clear evidence falls under this threat. The meaning of **"will not prosper"** (la yufliḥ) has been mentioned by us at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah in His saying, **"And it is those who are the successful"** (3:104). In sum, *falāḥ* (success) is an expression for reaching the sought-after aim and objective. So the meaning of "he will not prosper" is that he will not succeed in his endeavour and will not attain his objective; rather, he is lost and ruined.

Among people there are those who, when they gain some of the immediate objectives and base aims, imagine that they have attained the ultimate goal. God, glorified is He, removed this illusion by saying that this base aim is only a little enjoyment in this world. Then death is inevitable, and at death there must be a return to God; and at this return He will certainly make him taste the severe punishment because of that earlier disbelief. This is a discourse of utmost coherence, and of the highest excellence and eloquence. And God knows best.

[Page 109]

**His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And recite to them the news of Noah, when he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing [among you] and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then in God I have put my trust. So resolve upon your affair with your associates, then let not your affair be obscure to you; then carry it out against me and give me no respite. And if you turn away, I have not asked you for any reward. My reward is only from God, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims."﴾**

Know that when He, glorified is He, had gone to great lengths in establishing the proofs and clear evidences, and in answering doubts and questions, He then began, after that, to explain the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, for several reasons:

The first: when speech goes on at length in establishing one kind of knowledge, a kind of weariness may arise. When a person moves from that branch of knowledge to another branch, his chest is expanded, his heart is delighted, and he finds in himself a renewed desire, a fresh energy, and a strong inclination.

The second: so that the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and his companions, may have an example in those prophets who came before. When the Messenger hears that the treatment these disbelievers gave to all the messengers was no different from this, it lightens the burden on his heart, as it is said: "When a calamity becomes general, it becomes lighter."

The third: when the disbelievers hear these stories and know that the ignorant ones, though they exaggerated in harming the earlier prophets, were nonetheless helped in the end by God, who aided them, gave them victory, supported them, and overcame their enemies, the hearing of such stories by these disbelievers becomes a cause of the breaking of their hearts and the falling of fear and dread into their breasts. At that point, they reduce their kinds of harm and foolishness.

The fourth: we have shown that Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, did not learn any knowledge and did not study any book, yet he related these narratives without any discrepancy, without any addition, and without any deficiency. This indicates that he, upon him be blessings and peace, knew them only through revelation and sending down.

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned in this surah three of the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them.

The first story is the story of Noah, peace be upon him, which is mentioned in this verse, and in it there are two benefits:

The first: when the people of Noah, peace be upon him, persisted in disbelief and denial, God hastened their destruction by drowning. God mentioned their story so that this story would be a lesson for these disbelievers and a call to abandon denial in favor of monotheism and prophethood.

The second: the disbelievers of Makkah used to ask for the punishment that the Messenger, peace be upon him, warned them of, and they would say to him: "You are lying, for this punishment has not come to us." So God mentioned to them the story of Noah, peace be upon him, because he, peace be upon him, used to warn them of this punishment and they used to deny him regarding it; then in the end it happened as he had informed. So it is likewise here.

The second issue: Noah, peace be upon him, said to his people: ﴿If my standing [among you] and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then in God I have put my trust﴾. This is a sentence of conditional and consequent. As for the condition, it is composed of two restrictions:

The first restriction: his saying ﴿If my standing [among you] is burdensome to you﴾. Al-Wahidi said in *al-Basit*: it is said *kabura* (it became great/burdensome) *yakburu kibaran* in reference to age, and *kabura al-amr wa al-shay'* when the matter or thing became great, *yakburu kibaran wa kabaratan*.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was heavy upon you, it was difficult for you, and his matter became great in your eyes. The word *al-maqām*, with a fatḥah on the *mīm*, is a verbal noun like *al-iqāmah*. It is said: "He stayed among them, a stay (*maqāman*) and a residence (*iqāmah*)." And *al-muqām*, with a ḍammah on the *mīm*, is the place where one stays. Here he meant by *al-maqām* his remaining and his lingering among them. In sum, his saying ﴿my standing is burdensome to you﴾ follows the pattern of their saying: "So-and-so is heavy-shadowed," meaning heavy in presence.

Know that the cause of this heaviness is two things:

One of them: he, peace be upon him, remained among them for a thousand years less fifty years.

The second: those disbelievers had become accustomed to those corrupt creeds and false ways, and it is generally the case that whoever has become accustomed to a way in religion finds it heavy to be called away from it and to have its weakness pointed out to him. If this is coupled with the long duration of the calling, it becomes even heavier and more hateful. If it is further coupled with presenting compelling proofs against the corruption of that creed, the aversion becomes even stronger. This is the cause of the occurrence of that heaviness.

The second restriction is his saying ﴿and my reminding you of the signs of God﴾.

Know that natures absorbed in this world and greedy for the pursuit of immediate pleasures are very averse to commanding acts of obedience and forbidding sins and wrongs, and strongly repelled by hearing mention of death and the disparagement of the world's condition. Whoever is like this finds the person who commands him to good and forbids him from evil burdensome. There is another meaning in the verse: that his saying ﴿If my standing [among you] and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you﴾ means that when they used to admonish the group, they would stand on their feet to admonish them, so that their place would be elevated and their speech audible, just as it is related of Jesus, peace be upon him, that he used to admonish the disciples while standing, and they were seated. Know that this is the condition mentioned in this verse.

As for the consequent, there are two views:

The first view: the consequent is his saying ﴿then in God I have put my trust﴾, meaning: the intensity of your hatred toward me drives you to harm me, and I meet that evil only with trust in God.

Know that he, peace be upon him, was always entrusting himself to God, exalted is He. This expression may give the impression that he placed his trust in God at this very moment, but the meaning is that he placed his trust in God for the repelling of this evil at this moment.

The second view, which is the view of the majority, is that the consequent of the condition is his saying ﴿resolve upon your affair with your associates﴾. His saying ﴿then in God I have put my trust﴾ is a statement inserted between the condition and its consequent, as you would say in speech: "If you have denounced something of mine, then God is sufficient for me; so do what you wish." Know that the consequent of this condition contains five restrictions in order.

The first restriction: his saying ﴿resolve upon your affair﴾, and in it there are two discussions:

The first discussion: al-Farra' said: *al-ijmāʿ* means preparing and determination upon a matter, and he recited:

*"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit: will I ever go forth one day while my affair is resolved?"*

When you want to gather what is scattered, you say: "I gathered the people, so they are gathered." Abu al-Haytham said: *ajmaʿa amrahu* means he made it whole after it had been scattered. He said: *wa tafarraqahu* means he kept pondering it, saying one time "I will do this" and another time "I will do that." When he resolved upon one matter, he had gathered it, that is, made it whole. This is the origin of *ijmāʿ*. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you were not with them when they resolved upon their affair﴾ [Yusuf: 102]. Then it came to mean resolve, to the point that it was connected with *ʿalā*, so it is said *ajmaʿtu ʿalā al-amr*, meaning I resolved upon it, while the original is *ajmaʿtu al-amr*.

The second discussion: al-Asma'i narrated from Nafi' the reading *fa-jmaʿū* ("gather") with the alif of the verb of gathering being connected (*wasl*). There are two views on this: The first: Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: the meaning is "gather the holders of the affair among you," so the governing noun was omitted, and what would apply to the governed noun if it remained applied to the genitive noun.

The second: Ibn al-Anbari said: what is meant by *al-amr* here is the stratagems and schemes of their plotting, so the sense is: "Do not leave out of your affair anything except that you bring it forward."

The second restriction: his saying ﴿and your associates﴾, and in it there are discussions:

The first discussion: the *wāw* here means *maʿa* ("together with"), and the meaning is: "Resolve upon your affair together with your associates." A parallel of this is their saying: "If the she-camel and her young are left, she will suckle it," and "If you leave yourself and the lion, it will eat you."

The second discussion: it is possible that by "associates" is meant the idols they called gods, and it is possible that what is meant is those who were of the same mind and religion as them. If the first is meant, then he only urged the disbelievers to seek help from the idols on the basis of their own belief that they harm and benefit. If the second is meant, then the reason for seeking help from them is evident.

The third discussion: al-Hasan and a group of readers read *wa-shurakāʾukum* with a *rafʿ* (nominative), as a conjunction upon the pronoun in the nominative, the sense being: "Resolve, you and your associates." Al-Wahidi said: this is permissible without emphasizing the pronoun, as in His saying: ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35], because His saying ﴿your affair﴾ is a separation between the pronoun and what is conjoined to it, so it served as a substitute for emphasis. Al-Farra' used to find this reading objectionable, because it would necessitate that *wa-shurakāʾukum* be written with a *wāw*, and this letter is not present in the codices.

The third restriction: his saying ﴿then let not your affair be obscure to you﴾. Abu al-Haytham said: meaning "ambiguous," from their saying: "The crescent was obscured for us (*ghumma ʿalaynā al-hilāl*), so it is *maghmūm*," when it became unclear. Tarafa said:

*"By my life, my affair is not obscure to me, my day nor my night is unclear to me, nor is it perpetual."*

Al-Layth said: "He is in obscurity regarding his affair" when he is not guided to it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: let your affair be manifest and uncovered.

The fourth restriction: his saying ﴿then carry it out against me﴾, and in it there are two discussions:

The first discussion: Ibn al-Anbari said its meaning is: "then proceed against me with your harm and what you threaten me with." The Arabs say: "So-and-so *qaḍā*," meaning he died and passed away. Some of them said: *qaḍāʾ* of a thing is its firm establishment, its execution, and its completion, and from this the judge is called *qāḍī*, because when he decides he has finished. So His saying ﴿then carry it out against me﴾ means: finish your affair, carry out what is in your hearts, and sever what is between me and you. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ [al-Isra': 4], meaning We informed them with a decisive announcement. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We decreed that matter to him﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]. Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: the figurative use of the word *ilā* in this context is from their saying: "I have cleared myself to you (*barītu ilayka*)" and "I have come out to you from the covenant (*kharajtu ilayka min al-ʿahd*)," in which there is the sense of informing. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "Then carry out what your opinion settles upon, firm and finalized."

The second discussion: it has been read as ﴿then afḍū ilayya﴾ with the *fāʾ*, meaning "then reach your evil." It was also said that it is from *afḍā al-rajul*, when a man went out into the open space, meaning: "Bring it out in the open to me and reveal it to me."

The fifth restriction: his saying ﴿and give me no respite﴾, meaning: do not delay after you have informed me of what you have agreed upon. This is the explanation of these expressions. The judge (al-Qadi) has arranged this statement in the finest manner, saying: At the outset he, peace be upon him, said: "Then in God I have put my trust, for I am certain of God's promise and firmly convinced that He does not break His appointment. Do not think that your threat to me of killing and harm will prevent me from calling to God, exalted is He." Then he, peace be upon him, presented what indicates the soundness of his call, saying: ﴿So resolve upon your affair﴾, as if he were saying to them: "Resolve every means you have power over that would bring about the attainment of your aim." Then he did not limit himself to these two, but added a third to them, which is his saying ﴿then let not your affair be obscure to you﴾, intending that they should go to every extreme in openness and public declaration. Then he did not limit himself to that, but added a fourth, saying: ﴿then carry it out against me﴾, meaning: direct all those evils at me. Then he added a fifth to that, which is his saying ﴿and give me no respite﴾, meaning: hasten that with the utmost of what you are able to do, without granting respite. This is the end of this discourse. It is known that such a discourse indicates that he, peace be upon him, had reached the furthest degree in trust in God, exalted is He, and that he was certain that their scheme would not reach him and their plotting would not penetrate him.

As for His saying, ﴿But if you turn away, then I have not asked you for any wage﴾, the exegetes said: this is an indication that he did not take wealth from them in return for calling them to the religion of God, Exalted is He, and whenever a person is free of greed, his words have a stronger effect on the heart.

Yet I have another view on it, which is to say: he (peace be upon him) made clear that he does not fear them in any way whatsoever. This is because fear arises from only one of two things: either the infliction of harm, or the cutting off of benefits. [Page 109]

**His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And recite to them the news of Noah, when he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing [among you] and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then in God I have put my trust. So resolve upon your affair with your associates, then let not your affair be obscure to you; then carry it out against me and give me no respite. And if you turn away, I have not asked you for any reward. My reward is only from God, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims."﴾**

Know that when He, glorified is He, had gone to great lengths in establishing the proofs and clear evidences, and in answering doubts and questions, He then began, after that, to explain the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, for several reasons:

The first: when speech goes on at length in establishing one kind of knowledge, a kind of weariness may arise. When a person moves from that branch of knowledge to another branch, his chest is expanded, his heart is delighted, and he finds in himself a renewed desire, a fresh energy, and a strong inclination.

The second: so that the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and his companions, may have an example in those prophets who came before. When the Messenger hears that the treatment these disbelievers gave to all the messengers was no different from this, it lightens the burden on his heart, as it is said: "When a calamity becomes general, it becomes lighter."

The third: when the disbelievers hear these stories and know that the ignorant ones, though they exaggerated in harming the earlier prophets, were nonetheless helped in the end by God, who aided them, gave them victory, supported them, and overcame their enemies, the hearing of such stories by these disbelievers becomes a cause of the breaking of their hearts and the falling of fear and dread into their breasts. At that point, they reduce their kinds of harm and foolishness.

The fourth: we have shown that Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, did not learn any knowledge and did not study any book, yet he related these narratives without any discrepancy, without any addition, and without any deficiency. This indicates that he, upon him be blessings and peace, knew them only through revelation and sending down.

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned in this surah three of the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them.

The first story is the story of Noah, peace be upon him, which is mentioned in this verse, and in it there are two benefits:

The first: when the people of Noah, peace be upon him, persisted in disbelief and denial, God hastened their destruction by drowning. God mentioned their story so that this story would be a lesson for these disbelievers and a call to abandon denial in favor of monotheism and prophethood.

The second: the disbelievers of Makkah used to ask for the punishment that the Messenger, peace be upon him, warned them of, and they would say to him: "You are lying, for this punishment has not come to us." So God mentioned to them the story of Noah, peace be upon him, because he, peace be upon him, used to warn them of this punishment and they used to deny him regarding it; then in the end it happened as he had informed. So it is likewise here.

The second issue: Noah, peace be upon him, said to his people: ﴿If my standing [among you] and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then in God I have put my trust﴾. This is a sentence of conditional and consequent. As for the condition, it is composed of two restrictions:

The first restriction: his saying ﴿If my standing [among you] is burdensome to you﴾. Al-Wahidi said in *al-Basit*: it is said *kabura* (it became great/burdensome) *yakburu kibaran* in reference to age, and *kabura al-amr wa al-shay'* when the matter or thing became great, *yakburu kibaran wa kabaratan*.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was heavy upon you, it was difficult for you, and his matter became great in your eyes. The word *al-maqām*, with a fatḥah on the *mīm*, is a verbal noun like *al-iqāmah*. It is said: "He stayed among them, a stay (*maqāman*) and a residence (*iqāmah*)." And *al-muqām*, with a ḍammah on the *mīm*, is the place where one stays. Here he meant by *al-maqām* his remaining and his lingering among them. In sum, his saying ﴿my standing is burdensome to you﴾ follows the pattern of their saying: "So-and-so is heavy-shadowed," meaning heavy in presence.

Know that the cause of this heaviness is two things:

One of them: he, peace be upon him, remained among them for a thousand years less fifty years.

The second: those disbelievers had become accustomed to those corrupt creeds and false ways, and it is generally the case that whoever has become accustomed to a way in religion finds it heavy to be called away from it and to have its weakness pointed out to him. If this is coupled with the long duration of the calling, it becomes even heavier and more hateful. If it is further coupled with presenting compelling proofs against the corruption of that creed, the aversion becomes even stronger. This is the cause of the occurrence of that heaviness.

The second restriction is his saying ﴿and my reminding you of the signs of God﴾.

Know that natures absorbed in this world and greedy for the pursuit of immediate pleasures are very averse to commanding acts of obedience and forbidding sins and wrongs, and strongly repelled by hearing mention of death and the disparagement of the world's condition. Whoever is like this finds the person who commands him to good and forbids him from evil burdensome. There is another meaning in the verse: that his saying ﴿If my standing [among you] and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you﴾ means that when they used to admonish the group, they would stand on their feet to admonish them, so that their place would be elevated and their speech audible, just as it is related of Jesus, peace be upon him, that he used to admonish the disciples while standing, and they were seated. Know that this is the condition mentioned in this verse.

As for the consequent, there are two views:

The first view: the consequent is his saying ﴿then in God I have put my trust﴾, meaning: the intensity of your hatred toward me drives you to harm me, and I meet that evil only with trust in God.

Know that he, peace be upon him, was always entrusting himself to God, exalted is He. This expression may give the impression that he placed his trust in God at this very moment, but the meaning is that he placed his trust in God for the repelling of this evil at this moment.

The second view, which is the view of the majority, is that the consequent of the condition is his saying ﴿resolve upon your affair with your associates﴾. His saying ﴿then in God I have put my trust﴾ is a statement inserted between the condition and its consequent, as you would say in speech: "If you have denounced something of mine, then God is sufficient for me; so do what you wish." Know that the consequent of this condition contains five restrictions in order.

The first restriction: his saying ﴿resolve upon your affair﴾, and in it there are two discussions:

The first discussion: al-Farra' said: *al-ijmāʿ* means preparing and determination upon a matter, and he recited:

*"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit: will I ever go forth one day while my affair is resolved?"*

When you want to gather what is scattered, you say: "I gathered the people, so they are gathered." Abu al-Haytham said: *ajmaʿa amrahu* means he made it whole after it had been scattered. He said: *wa tafarraqahu* means he kept pondering it, saying one time "I will do this" and another time "I will do that." When he resolved upon one matter, he had gathered it, that is, made it whole. This is the origin of *ijmāʿ*. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you were not with them when they resolved upon their affair﴾ [Yusuf: 102]. Then it came to mean resolve, to the point that it was connected with *ʿalā*, so it is said *ajmaʿtu ʿalā al-amr*, meaning I resolved upon it, while the original is *ajmaʿtu al-amr*.

The second discussion: al-Asma'i narrated from Nafi' the reading *fa-jmaʿū* ("gather") with the alif of the verb of gathering being connected (*wasl*). There are two views on this: The first: Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: the meaning is "gather the holders of the affair among you," so the governing noun was omitted, and what would apply to the governed noun if it remained applied to the genitive noun.

The second: Ibn al-Anbari said: what is meant by *al-amr* here is the stratagems and schemes of their plotting, so the sense is: "Do not leave out of your affair anything except that you bring it forward."

The second restriction: his saying ﴿and your associates﴾, and in it there are discussions:

The first discussion: the *wāw* here means *maʿa* ("together with"), and the meaning is: "Resolve upon your affair together with your associates." A parallel of this is their saying: "If the she-camel and her young are left, she will suckle it," and "If you leave yourself and the lion, it will eat you."

The second discussion: it is possible that by "associates" is meant the idols they called gods, and it is possible that what is meant is those who were of the same mind and religion as them. If the first is meant, then he only urged the disbelievers to seek help from the idols on the basis of their own belief that they harm and benefit. If the second is meant, then the reason for seeking help from them is evident.

The third discussion: al-Hasan and a group of readers read *wa-shurakāʾukum* with a *rafʿ* (nominative), as a conjunction upon the pronoun in the nominative, the sense being: "Resolve, you and your associates." Al-Wahidi said: this is permissible without emphasizing the pronoun, as in His saying: ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35], because His saying ﴿your affair﴾ is a separation between the pronoun and what is conjoined to it, so it served as a substitute for emphasis. Al-Farra' used to find this reading objectionable, because it would necessitate that *wa-shurakāʾukum* be written with a *wāw*, and this letter is not present in the codices.

The third restriction: his saying ﴿then let not your affair be obscure to you﴾. Abu al-Haytham said: meaning "ambiguous," from their saying: "The crescent was obscured for us (*ghumma ʿalaynā al-hilāl*), so it is *maghmūm*," when it became unclear. Tarafa said:

*"By my life, my affair is not obscure to me, my day nor my night is unclear to me, nor is it perpetual."*

Al-Layth said: "He is in obscurity regarding his affair" when he is not guided to it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: let your affair be manifest and uncovered.

The fourth restriction: his saying ﴿then carry it out against me﴾, and in it there are two discussions:

The first discussion: Ibn al-Anbari said its meaning is: "then proceed against me with your harm and what you threaten me with." The Arabs say: "So-and-so *qaḍā*," meaning he died and passed away. Some of them said: *qaḍāʾ* of a thing is its firm establishment, its execution, and its completion, and from this the judge is called *qāḍī*, because when he decides he has finished. So His saying ﴿then carry it out against me﴾ means: finish your affair, carry out what is in your hearts, and sever what is between me and you. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ [al-Isra': 4], meaning We informed them with a decisive announcement. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We decreed that matter to him﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]. Al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: the figurative use of the word *ilā* in this context is from their saying: "I have cleared myself to you (*barītu ilayka*)" and "I have come out to you from the covenant (*kharajtu ilayka min al-ʿahd*)," in which there is the sense of informing. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "Then carry out what your opinion settles upon, firm and finalized."

The second discussion: it has been read as ﴿then afḍū ilayya﴾ with the *fāʾ*, meaning "then reach your evil." It was also said that it is from *afḍā al-rajul*, when a man went out into the open space, meaning: "Bring it out in the open to me and reveal it to me."

The fifth restriction: his saying ﴿and give me no respite﴾, meaning: do not delay after you have informed me of what you have agreed upon. This is the explanation of these expressions. The judge (al-Qadi) has arranged this statement in the finest manner, saying: At the outset he, peace be upon him, said: "Then in God I have put my trust, for I am certain of God's promise and firmly convinced that He does not break His appointment. Do not think that your threat to me of killing and harm will prevent me from calling to God, exalted is He." Then he, peace be upon him, presented what indicates the soundness of his call, saying: ﴿So resolve upon your affair﴾, as if he were saying to them: "Resolve every means you have power over that would bring about the attainment of your aim." Then he did not limit himself to that, but commanded them to add to themselves their associates whom they claimed would strengthen their position through their standing and through drawing near to them. Then he did not limit himself to these two, but added a third to them, which is his saying ﴿then let not your affair be obscure to you﴾, intending that they should go to every extreme in openness and public declaration. Then he did not limit himself to that, but added a fourth, saying: ﴿then carry it out against me﴾, meaning: direct all those evils at me. Then he added a fifth to that, which is his saying ﴿and give me no respite﴾, meaning: hasten that with the utmost of what you are able to do, without granting respite. This is the end of this discourse. It is known that such a discourse indicates that he, peace be upon him, had reached the furthest degree in trust in God, exalted is He, and that he was certain that their scheme would not reach him and their plotting would not penetrate him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they denied him, and We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We made them successors, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. So look how was the end of those who were warned.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, related the words that passed between Noah and those disbelievers, He mentioned what the outcome of that event led to. As for Noah and his companions, there are two matters:

The first: He, may He be exalted, saved them from the disbelievers.

The second: He made them successors (khalaif), meaning that they succeeded those who perished by drowning.

As for the disbelievers, He, may He be exalted, drowned them and destroyed them.

When this story is heard by those who affirmed the Messenger and those who denied him, it is a deterrent for the responsible (mukallafin), inasmuch as they fear that there may befall them the like of what befell the people of Noah. It is also a summons to the believers to remain steadfast in faith, so that they may reach what the people of Noah reached. This method of encouragement and warning, when it is conveyed in the form of narration about those who came before, is more eloquent than a warning given directly (al-wa'id al-mubtada'). On this basis, He, may He be exalted, mentioned the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them.

As for the details of this story, they are mentioned in other surahs.

Know that the intended meaning is: "Then We sent after him messengers, [each] to his people, and they brought them clear proofs." He did not name them, but among them were Hud, Salih, Abraham, Lot, and Shu'ayb, may the blessings of God be upon them all. "Clear proofs" (al-bayyinat) means the overpowering miracles. God informs us that these peoples followed the path of Noah's people in denying their messengers, and that what reached them of God's destruction of the deniers among Noah's people did not deter them from this. For this reason He said: ﴿So they were not going to believe in what they had denied before﴾. The intended meaning is not the very same thing they denied, because that did not occur in their time. Rather, what is meant is something like the clear proofs they denied, since the manifest proofs given to the prophets, peace be upon them all, are as if they were one thing.

* * *

Then God said: ﴿Thus We seal upon the hearts of the transgressors.﴾ Our companions (al-Ash'ariyya) have argued from this verse that God may prevent the mukallaf (the person charged with religious obligations) from faith, and the argument is clear.

Al-Qadi said: Sealing does not prevent faith, as is proven by God's words: ﴿Rather, God set a seal upon them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except a few﴾ [An-Nisa: 155]. Had this sealing been a prevention, this exception would not be valid.

The answer: the discussion of this question has already been thoroughly covered in the commentary on God's words: ﴿God has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 7], so there is no benefit in repeating it.

Story of Musa (peace be upon him)

﴿Then after them We sent Musa and Harun to Fir'awn and his chiefs with Our signs, but they acted arrogantly, for they were a criminal people.﴾ ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Indeed, this is clear magic."﴾ ﴿Musa said, "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, 'Is this magic?' And magicians do not succeed."﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then after them We sent Musa and Harun to Fir'awn and his chiefs with Our signs, but they acted arrogantly, for they were a criminal people.﴾ ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Indeed, this is clear magic."﴾ ﴿Musa said, "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, 'Is this magic?' And magicians do not succeed."﴾ Know that this statement needs no explanation, but it contains one question: when the people said, "﴿Indeed, this is clear magic﴾," how did Musa (peace be upon him) relate that they said, ﴿Is this magic?﴾ in the form of a question?

Its answer: Musa (peace be upon him) did not relate of them that they said, ﴿Is this magic?﴾ Rather he said, ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you﴾ what you say; then he omitted the object of "Do you say" because the context indicates it. Then he said again, ﴿Is this magic?﴾, and this is a question in the manner of denial. Then he argued that it is not magic, saying: ﴿And magicians do not succeed.﴾ meaning that the outcome of their work is imagination and deception, and magicians do not succeed. As for turning the staff into a serpent and splitting the sea, it is known by necessity that these are not of the category of imagination and deception, so it is established that it is not magic.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 10, verses 78–82:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away from that upon which we found our fathers, and that greatness may be yours two in the land? We will not be believers in you two."﴾ ﴿And Pharaoh said: "Bring to me every learned sorcerer."﴾ ﴿So when the sorcerers came, Moses said to them: "Throw what you are going to throw."﴾ ﴿So when they threw, Moses said: "What you have brought is magic. Indeed, Allah will render it void. Indeed, Allah does not reform the work of the corrupters."﴾ ﴿And Allah establishes the truth by His words, even if the criminals dislike it.﴾ In this are issues:

**The First Issue:** Know that He, may He be exalted, related that Pharaoh and his people did not accept the call of Moses, peace be upon him, and they gave two reasons for non-acceptance:

The first is His saying: ﴿Have you come to us to turn us away from that upon which we found our fathers?﴾ Al-Wahidi said: *al-laft* (turning away) in the basic sense of the language is diverting from a matter, and its root is *al-layy* (twisting). It is said: *lafata 'unuqahu* (he twisted his neck) when he twisted it. From this one says *iltafata ilayhi*, meaning he inclined his face toward him.

Al-Azhari said: *lafata al-shay'* and *fataluhu* means he twisted it, and this is from the transposed (*maqlub*) forms.

Know that the sum of this statement is that they said: "We will not abandon the religion upon which we are, because we found our fathers upon it." Thus they held fast to imitation (*taqlid*) and repelled the manifest proof merely by persistence.

The second reason for non-acceptance is His saying: ﴿and that greatness may be yours two in the land.﴾ The exegetes said: the meaning is "and that kingship and honour may be yours two in the land of Egypt," and the address is to Moses and Harun. Al-Zajjaj said: he called kingship *kibriya'* (greatness) because it is the greatest thing sought of worldly affairs. Also, when the people acknowledge the truthfulness of a prophet, the reins of his community's affairs come to him, and so he becomes the greatest of the people.

Know that the first reason indicates adherence to imitation, and the second reason indicates greed for seeking this world and striving to preserve leadership. When these people mentioned these two reasons, they stated the judgment explicitly and said: ﴿We will not be believers in you two.﴾

Know that when these people mentioned these meanings, they then sought, and intended, to oppose the miracle of Moses, peace be upon him, with kinds of magic, so that they might show the people that what Moses brought was of the category of magic. So Pharaoh gathered the sorcerers and summoned them, and ﴿Moses said to them: "Throw what you are going to throw."﴾

[Page 115]

If it is said: How did he command them to disbelief and sorcery, when commanding disbelief is itself disbelief?

We say: He, peace be upon him, commanded them to throw their ropes and staves, so that he might make clear to the creation that what they had brought was corrupt work and vain striving, not in the sense that he commanded them to practise sorcery. When they threw their ropes and staves, Moses said to them: "What you have brought is the vain magic." The point is that the people said to Moses: "What you have brought is sorcery." Moses, peace be upon him, mentioned that what you have mentioned is false; rather, the truth is that what you have brought is sorcery and deception, whose falsehood becomes apparent.
