Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 83:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But none believed in Moses, except some of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs, lest he should persecute them. Indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land, and indeed he was one of the extravagant.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, explained in what preceded what came from Moses, peace be upon him, of the great miracles, and what appeared of the swallowing of the staff of all that they had brought of the implements of magic. Then He, exalted is He, explained that, despite witnessing the great miracles, none of them believed in him except some of his people. Almighty God mentioned this as consolation for Muhammad (ﷺ), because he used to grieve over the people's turning away from him and their persistence in disbelief. So He made clear that in this matter he has an example in all the prophets, for what appeared from Moses, peace be upon him, was greater in its miraculous nature in the sight of the eye, and yet none believed in him except some.

They differed over what is meant by "some" (dhurriyyah) in several respects:

The first: that dhurriyyah here means a small number. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the word dhurriyyah is used to refer to a people in a sense of belittling and diminishing. There is no way to take it in the sense of disparagement in this place, so it must be taken in the sense of diminutiveness, meaning a small number.

The second: some said: what is meant is the children of those who were called, because the fathers persisted in disbelief; either because the hearts of the children are softer, or because their motives to remain steadfast in disbelief are lighter.

The third: that dhurriyyah are a people whose fathers were from the people of Pharaoh and whose mothers were from the Children of Israel.

The fourth: dhurriyyah from the family of Pharaoh: Asiyah, the wife of Pharaoh, and his treasurer, and the wife of his treasurer, and her hairdresser.

As for the pronoun in His saying ﴿from his people﴾, they differed as to whether what is meant is the people of Moses or the people of Pharaoh, since both have been mentioned previously. The more apparent view is that it refers back to Moses, because he is the nearer of the two mentioned, and because it is related that those who believed in him were from the Children of Israel.

As for His saying ﴿out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs, lest he should persecute them﴾, there are discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: those who believed in Moses were greatly fearful of Pharaoh, because he was severe in punishment, and he had openly shown enmity toward Moses. So whenever he learned of the people's inclination toward Moses, he would exaggerate in harming them; for this reason they were fearful of him.

The second discussion: He said ﴿and their chiefs﴾ although Pharaoh is one person, for several reasons:

The first: one may refer to a single person with a plural expression, and the intention is glorification, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Hijr: 9].

The second: that what is meant by Pharaoh is the family of Pharaoh.

The third: that this is from the category of omitting the modifier (ḥadhf al-muḍāf), as if what was intended by Pharaoh was the family of Pharaoh.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿lest he should persecute them﴾, that is, to turn them away from their religion by imposing various kinds of trials upon them.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿Indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land﴾, that is, he was dominant and overpowering in it, ﴿and indeed he was one of the extravagant﴾. It was said: what is meant is that he was greatly given to killing and greatly given to torturing whoever opposed him in any matter. The purpose of this is to explain the cause of those believers being fearful. It was also said: he was extravagant only because he was among the most base of slaves, and so he claimed divinity.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 84–86:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Moses said, "O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims."﴾ ﴿So they said, "In Allah we have put our trust. Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people,﴾ ﴿and save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people."﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿If you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him﴾, is a conditional response (jaza', the consequent clause) dependent on two conditions. One of them comes first and the other comes later. The jurists (fuqaha') said: the later element must be placed first, and the earlier element must be placed later. An example of this is when a man says to his wife: "If you enter the house, then you are divorced, if you speak to Zayd." The matter is indeed so, because the whole of his statement, "If you enter the house, then you are divorced," becomes conditional upon his saying, "if you speak to Zayd." What is conditional comes after the condition, and this requires that what is later in wording is earlier in meaning, and what is earlier in wording is later in meaning. The sense is as if he says to his wife, at the time you speak to Zayd, "If you enter the house, then you are divorced." So if this suspension occurred before "if you speak to Zayd," the divorce would not take effect.

Now that you know this, we say: His saying, ﴿And Moses said, "O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims."﴾ requires that their being Muslims be a condition for them to become those addressed by His saying, ﴿if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him﴾. So it is as if the Exalted says to the Muslim, at the time of his Islam: "If you are among those who believe in Allah, then rely upon Allah." The matter is indeed so, because Islam is an expression of submission, and it points to yielding to the obligations issued by Allah the Exalted, showing humility, and abandoning rebellion. As for faith (iman), it is an expression of the heart becoming aware that the Necessarily Existent in Himself is One, and that everything other than Him is originated and created, under His management, subjugation and disposal. When these two states are attained, the servant entrusts all his affairs to Allah the Exalted, and the light of reliance upon Allah arises in the heart. This verse is therefore among the subtle secrets. Reliance upon Allah is an expression of entrusting affairs entirely to Allah the Exalted, and depending upon Allah the Exalted in all circumstances.

Know that whoever relies upon Allah in all important matters, Allah the Exalted will suffice him for all afflictions, by His saying: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq: 3].

**The second issue:** This which Moses commanded his people, namely reliance upon Allah, is what Allah the Exalted related about Noah, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Upon Allah I have relied﴾ [Yunus: 71]. At this point the difference between the two ranks becomes apparent, because Noah, peace be upon him, described himself as relying upon Allah the Exalted, while Moses, peace be upon him, commanded his people to do so. Thus Noah, peace be upon him, was complete, and Moses, peace be upon him, was beyond completeness.

**The third issue:** He said, ﴿then rely upon Him﴾, and did not say "rely upon Him" (tawakkalu 'alayhi), because the first (fa-'alayhi tawakkalu, with the object placed first) conveys restriction (hasr). It is as if he, peace be upon him, commanded them to rely upon Him alone, and forbade them from relying upon others. The matter is indeed so, because once it is established that everything other than Him belongs to Him, is His possession, is under His control, subjugation, rule and management, it is rationally impossible for a person to rely upon someone other than Him. For this reason, this expression came in this form.

Then Allah the Exalted explained that when Moses, peace be upon him, commanded them to do this, they accepted his word: ﴿So they said, "In Allah we have put our trust,"﴾ that is, "we have relied upon Him, and we do not turn to anyone besides Him." Then, when they did this, they occupied themselves with supplication, and they asked Allah the Exalted for two things:

The first of them: they said, ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾. On this there are several interpretations:

The first: the meaning is, "Do not make us a trial through which Pharaoh and his people are tested." For if You empowered them over us, it would enter their hearts that if we were upon the truth, You would not have empowered them over us. That would become a strong doubt in their persistence in disbelief, and their domination over us would become a trial for them.

The second: if You empowered them over us, they would deserve severe punishment in the Hereafter, and that would be a trial for them.

The third: ﴿Do not make us a trial﴾, that is, do not make us a place of trial for them, that is, a place of punishment for them.

The fourth: the meaning of "trial" (fitnah) may be "the one being tried" (maftun), because using a verbal noun to mean the object is permissible, like "creation" (khalq) meaning "the created thing" and "bringing into being" (takwin) meaning "the thing brought into being." The meaning is: "Do not make us ones who are tried," that is, do not enable them to compel us through oppression and coercion to turn away from this true religion which we have accepted. This interpretation is strengthened by what Allah the Exalted mentioned before this verse, namely His saying: ﴿But none believed in Moses except a few of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs, that he would try them﴾ [Yunus: 83].

As for the second request in this supplication, it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people﴾.

Know that this order indicates that the concern of these people for the affairs of their religion was greater than their concern for the affairs of their worldly life. This is because if we take their saying, ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾ to mean that if they were empowered over the Muslims, that would become a doubt for them that this religion is false, so they humbly implored Allah the Exalted to protect those disbelievers from this doubt, and they put this supplication before the request for their own salvation. That indicates that their care for the welfare of their enemies' religion was greater than their care for the welfare of themselves. And if we take it to mean that Allah the Exalted would not enable those disbelievers to compel them to abandon this religion, that would also be evidence that their concern for the welfare of their religions was greater than their concern for the welfare of their bodies. In all interpretations, this is a delicate and noble subtlety.

The Almighty said: ﴿And We revealed to Moses and his brother: "Settle your people in Egypt in houses, and make your houses a qiblah (direction of prayer), and establish the prayer, and give good tidings to the believers."﴾

Know that when He had described the fear of the believers from the disbelievers, and the reliance upon God that appeared from them, He followed this with commanding Moses and Aaron to take mosques and to devote themselves to the prayers. It is said: *tabawwa'a al-makan*, meaning he took the place as a dwelling (*mubawwa'*), just as one says *tawattana*, meaning he took it as a homeland (*mawtin*). The meaning is: make in Egypt houses for your people, and a place of return to which you come back for worship and prayer.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And make your houses a qiblah﴾. Concerning this there are several points of discussion:

The first point: Some people said that the "houses" means the mosques, as in the saying of the Almighty: ﴿in houses which God has permitted to be raised, and in which His name is mentioned﴾ [al-Nur 24:36]. Others said that the meaning is houses in general. As for the first group, they interpreted the qiblah as the side that one faces in prayer. Then they said: the meaning of His saying ﴿And make your houses a qiblah﴾ is: make your houses mosques which you face for the sake of prayer. Al-Farra' said: "And make your houses a qiblah" means toward the qiblah. Ibn al-Anbari said: "And make your houses a qiblah" means *qibalan*, that is, mosques; the singular is used while the plural is meant. They differed as to where this qiblah was. It is evident that the wording of the Qur'an does not indicate its specific location. However, it is reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: the Ka'bah was the qiblah of Moses, peace be upon him. And al-Hasan used to say: the Ka'bah is the qiblah of all the prophets, and the turning away from it by the command of God occurred in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, after the Hijrah.

Others said: that qiblah was in the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

As for those who said that the word "houses" mentioned in this verse means houses in general, they have two interpretations of His saying "qiblah":

The first: the meaning of making those houses a qiblah is that they should face one another, and the purpose of this is the attainment of unity and the mutual strengthening of one another.

Others said: the meaning is "make your homes a qiblah," that is, pray in your houses.

[p. 119]

The second point: The Almighty, at the beginning of this verse, addressed Moses and Aaron specifically, saying ﴿to settle your people in Egypt in houses﴾, then generalized this address, saying ﴿And make your houses a qiblah﴾. The reason for this is that the Almighty commanded Moses and Aaron to settle houses for their people for worship, and that is something entrusted to the prophets. Then the address came after that in general terms to both of them and to their people, concerning taking mosques and praying in them, because that is obligatory upon all. Then at the end of the speech He addressed Moses, peace be upon him, specifically, saying ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾. This is because the primary purpose of all acts of worship is the attainment of this good tiding; so God the Exalted singled out Moses for it, to indicate that the principal one in the prophethood is Moses, peace be upon him, and that Aaron is a follower of him.

The third point: The commentators mentioned three ways concerning the manner of this event:

The first: that Moses, peace be upon him, and those with him were at the beginning of their affair commanded to pray in their houses secretly, away from the disbelievers, so that they would not be exposed to them and be harmed and tempted away from their religion, just as the believers were in this state at the beginning of Islam in Mecca.

The second: It was said that when God sent Moses to them, Pharaoh ordered the destruction of the mosques of the Children of Israel and prevented them from praying, so God the Exalted commanded them to take mosques in their houses and pray in them out of fear of Pharaoh.

The third: that when God the Exalted sent Moses to them and Pharaoh showed that intense enmity, God the Exalted commanded Moses, Aaron, and their people to take mosques in defiance of the enemies, and He guaranteed that He would protect them from the evil of the enemies.

[Page 120]

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Moses said, "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world. Our Lord, that they may lead [others] astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment."﴾ ﴿He said, "The supplication of you both has been answered, so remain steadfast and do not follow the way of those who do not know."﴾

Know that when Moses had shown the clear and overpowering miracles, and saw the people persisting in denial, obstinacy and rejection, he began to invoke [punishment] against them. It is required of one who invokes against others that he first mention the reason for his action against them. Their offence was that, out of their love for this world, they abandoned the religion. For this reason, Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth.﴾ "Adornment" is an expression for health, beauty, clothing, mounts, household furnishings and wealth, and whatever exceeds these things of gold, silver and other goods.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿that they may lead [others] astray from Your way.﴾ On this there are two issues:

The first issue: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read *liyudillu* (لِيُضِلُّوا) with a *damma* on the *ya'* (i.e., *liyudillū*, "that they may lead astray"), while the rest read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'* (*liyadillū*, "that they may go astray").

[Page 120]

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'ari theologians) have used this verse as evidence that Allah, the Exalted, leads people astray and wills their misguidance. Its explanation is in two ways:

The first: the *lam* in His words ﴿liyudillū﴾ is the *lam* of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*), and the meaning is: Moses said, "O Lord of Majesty, You gave them this adornment and wealth so that they might go astray." This indicates that Allah, the Exalted, may will the misguidance of the responsible persons.

The second: He said ﴿and harden their hearts﴾, and Allah, the Exalted, said ﴿The supplication of you both has been answered﴾, and this also indicates the intended meaning.

The Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: It is not permissible that the meaning of this verse be what you have mentioned, and the following points show this:

The first: It has been established that Allah, the Exalted, is far removed from doing evil, and willing disbelief is evil.

The second: If He willed that, the disbelievers would be obedient to Allah, the Exalted, by means of their disbelief, because obedience has no meaning except performing what agrees with the will. And if they were like that, they would not deserve to be invoked against with the obliteration of their wealth and the hardening of their hearts.

The third: If we allowed that He wills the misguidance of His servants, we would allow that He sends the prophets, peace be upon them, to call to error, and it would be permissible that He strengthen the lying, misguided, misleading liars by manifesting miracles through them, and in this is the demolition of the religion and the nullification of trust in the Qur'an.

The fourth: It is not permissible that He say to Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both: ﴿But speak to him with gentle speech that perhaps he may be reminded or fear [Allah]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44], and that He say: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought] and a shortage of fruits that perhaps they would be reminded﴾ [al-A'raf: 130], and then that He intend misguidance for them and give them blessings so that they go astray; for that is like a contradiction, so one of the two must be interpreted in agreement with the other.

The fifth: It is not permissible to say that Moses, peace be upon him, invoked his Lord to obliterate their wealth so that they would not believe, while he was so earnest in desiring their faith.

Know that we have elaborated these points at length in many places of this book.

He meant: "Did your eye deceive you?" So it is likewise here.

[Page 121]

* * *

Given that this is established, we say: His words ﴿Our Lord, that they may lead [others] astray from Your way﴾ mean: "that they may perish and die." We say: In that case, his undertaking to acquire this ignorance would be due to a prior ignorance. If the occurrence of that prior ignorance were due to another ignorance, an infinite regress would follow, which is impossible. It is established that these ignorances and misguidances must end in a first ignorance and a first misguidance, and that cannot come about by the servant's origination and creation, because he hated it and only willed its opposite. Therefore it must be from Allah, the Exalted.

These things lead one to another by way of necessary consequence, so it must be that the doer of this disbelief is the One who created man disposed to love wealth and status.

If that is so, then guidance and misguidance are from Allah, the Exalted.

Thus it has been established by rational proof that Allah, the Exalted, giving Pharaoh and his people the adornment of this world and the wealth of this world must necessarily be the cause of their misguidance. It has therefore been established that what the apparent wording indicates has been proven sound by clear reason. How, then, is it possible to abandon the apparent wording in such a situation, and how is it fitting to take the speech to far-fetched and very weak interpretations?

Having understood this, we say:

As for the first point, namely reading the *lam* as the *lam* of consequence, it is weak, because Moses, peace be upon him, did not know the outcomes.

We reply: When Allah informed him that they would not believe, it would be impossible that faith proceed from them, because that would entail the reversal of Allah's report into falsehood, which is impossible; and what leads to the impossible is impossible.

[Page 122]

He went to great lengths in rejecting that reading. Yet this point he mentions here is worse than that, because it turns negation into affirmation and affirmation into negation. Permitting it opens the door to the Qur'an not remaining reliable, neither in its negation nor in its affirmation, and then the Qur'an is entirely nullified. This very same answer applies to his statement that the meaning is an interrogative with the sense of denial, for permitting that entails permitting the like of it in all other contexts. Perhaps He said: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110] as a denial and astonishment. As for the rest of the answers, their weakness is not hidden.

* * *

* * *

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 90–92 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh and his soldiers followed them in tyranny and enmity, until, when drowning overtook him, he said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who submit."﴾ ﴿"Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters."﴾ ﴿So today We will save you in your body, that you may be a sign for those who come after you. Indeed, many of the people are heedless of Our signs.﴾

Know that the explanation of the expression in His words ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾ is mentioned in Surat al-A'raf. The meaning is that when Allah, the Exalted, answered the supplication of the two (Musa and Harun), He commanded the Children of Israel to leave Egypt at the appointed time and facilitated its means for them. Pharaoh was unaware of this. When he heard that they had gone out and resolved to leave his kingdom, he set out after them. His words ﴿then Pharaoh followed them﴾ mean that he caught up with them; it is said: "atba'ahu" (he followed him) until he overtook him. His words ﴿in tyranny and enmity﴾: "al-baghy" is the seeking of superiority without right, and "al-'adw" is injustice. It is related that when Musa (peace be upon him) left with his people and they reached the edge of the sea, and Pharaoh with his army drew near to them, they fell into severe fear, because they were between a sea that drowns and an army that destroys. Then Allah bestowed His favour upon them by making a path appear for them in the sea, as Allah the Exalted has related this story in its entirety in other surahs. Then Musa (peace be upon him) and his companions entered and came out, and Allah left that path dry so that Pharaoh and his soldiers would be tempted to cross it. When he entered with his host, Allah drowned him by joining the parts of the water together with one another and removing the parting. This is the meaning of His words ﴿then Pharaoh followed them with his soldiers﴾. And He made clear what was in their hearts of tyranny, which is the desire to excess in killing and oppressing them, and enmity, which is transgressing the limit. The first aspect: he believed only at the descent of the punishment, and belief at this time is not accepted, because when punishment descends the situation becomes one of compulsion, and in this state repentance is not accepted. On this assumption, the mention of this word was not accompanied by sincerity, and for this reason it was not accepted.

Such a foul belief does not lose its darkness except by the light of decisive proofs and certain evidences. As for pure imitation, it is of no benefit, because it is merely adding the darkness of imitation to the darkness of prior ignorance.

* * *

Second question: the apparent wording indicates that his repentance was not accepted only because of the earlier disobedience and prior corruption, and the soundness of this reasoning does not prevent the acceptance of repentance.

The answer: the position of our companions (the Ash'aris) is that accepting repentance is not obligatory by reason ('aql), and one of their proofs for the soundness of this is this verse. Also, the cause was not merely the earlier disobedience, but that disobedience together with his being among the corrupters.

* * *

The third: some reciters read "li-man khalaqaka" with a qaf (li-man khalaqaka), meaning that you may be a sign for your Creator, like the rest of His signs.

So what is the reason for non-acceptance, when Allah, the Exalted, is far above being subject to anger and rancour, so that it could be said that because of that rancour He did not accept this confession from him?

The answer: the scholars have mentioned several aspects regarding this.

The first aspect: he believed only at the descent of the punishment, and belief at this time is not accepted, because when punishment descends the situation becomes one of compulsion, and in this state repentance is not accepted. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then their belief did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 85].

The second aspect: he uttered this word only in order to use it as a means to remove that present calamity and immediate trial. Thus his aim from this word was not the affirmation of Allah's oneness nor the acknowledgment of the might of Lordship and the humility of servanthood. On this assumption, the mention of this word was not accompanied by sincerity, and for this reason it was not accepted.

The third aspect: that confession was based on pure imitation (taqlid). Do you not see that he said: ﴿that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾? So it is as if he acknowledged that he did not know Allah, but he had heard from the Children of Israel that the world has a god. So he affirmed that god which he had heard the Children of Israel affirm the existence of. Thus this was pure imitation, and for this reason the word was not accepted from him. A further clarification of this is that Pharaoh, as we explained in Surat Ta-Ha, was one of the Dahriyya (materialists), and was among those who denied the existence of the Creator, the Exalted. Such a foul belief does not lose its darkness except by the light of decisive proofs and certain evidences. As for pure imitation, it is of no benefit, because it is merely adding the darkness of imitation to the darkness of prior ignorance.

The fourth aspect: I saw in some books that some groups of the Children of Israel, when they crossed the sea, occupied themselves with worshipping the calf. So when Pharaoh said: ﴿I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾, that was directed to the calf which they believed in worshipping at that time. So this word, in his case, became a cause for an increase in disbelief.

The fifth aspect: the Jews had hearts inclined to anthropomorphism (tashbih) and corporealism (tajsim). For this reason they occupied themselves with worshipping the calf, supposing that He, the Exalted, had indwelt the body of that calf and descended into it. Since this was the case, and Pharaoh said ﴿I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾, it is as if he believed in a god described with corporeality, indwelling and descent, and whoever believes that is a disbeliever. For this reason Pharaoh's belief was not valid.

The sixth aspect: perhaps belief is only completed by acknowledging the oneness of Allah, the Exalted, and acknowledging the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him). Here, when Pharaoh acknowledged the oneness but did not acknowledge the prophethood, it was inevitable that his belief was not valid.

A parallel to this: if one of the disbelievers said a thousand times, "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah," his belief would not be valid unless he said with it, "and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." So it is the same here.

The seventh aspect: the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) related that Jibril (peace be upon him) came to Pharaoh with a legal opinion (fatwa) in which was: "What is the view of the Amir concerning a slave who grew up in the wealth and favour of his master, then disbelieved his favour, denied his right, and claimed lordship over him?" Pharaoh wrote on it—Abu al-'Abbas al-Walid ibn Mus'ab says—: "The recompense of a slave who rebels against his master who is ungrateful for his favour is that he be drowned in the sea." Then when Pharaoh drowned, Jibril (peace be upon him) raised his fatwa to him.

* * *

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾, there are questions regarding it:

First question: who is the one who said to him: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before﴾?

The answer: the reports indicate that the speaker of this statement is Jibril. He mentioned his words ﴿and were among the corrupters﴾ in response to his words ﴿and I am of those who submit﴾. Some people said: the speaker of this statement is Allah, the Exalted, because after it He mentioned ﴿So today We will save you in your body﴾ up to His words ﴿Indeed, many of the people are heedless of Our signs﴾, and this speech is nothing but the speech of Allah, the Exalted.

Second question: the apparent wording indicates that his repentance was not accepted only because of the earlier disobedience and prior corruption, and the soundness of this reasoning does not prevent the acceptance of repentance.

The answer: the position of our companions (the Ash'aris) is that accepting repentance is not obligatory by reason ('aql), and one of their proofs for the soundness of this is this verse. Also, the cause was not merely the earlier disobedience, but that disobedience together with his being among the corrupters.

Third question: is it valid that Jibril (peace be upon him) began filling his mouth with mud, so that he would not repent out of anger toward him?

The answer: the closer view is that this is not valid, because in that situation either it is said that the obligation (taklif) was established, or it was not established. If it was established, it is not permissible for Jibril (peace be upon him) to prevent him from repentance; rather it is obligatory for him to help him to repent and to every act of obedience, because of His words, the Exalted: ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. Also, if he prevented him by what they mention, repentance would still be possible, because the mute may repent by regretting in his heart and resolving to abandon returning to the ugly deed, and then what Jibril (peace be upon him) did would have no benefit. Also, if he prevented him from repentance, he would have been content with his remaining in disbelief, and contentment with disbelief is disbelief. Also, how is it fitting for Allah, the Exalted, to say to Musa and Harun (peace be upon them both): ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech; perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44], and then command Jibril (peace be upon him) to prevent him from faith? And if it is said that Jibril (peace be upon him) did that on his own initiative and not by the command of Allah, the Exalted, this is refuted by Jibril's words: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64], and His description of them: ﴿And they are fearful of His awe﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28], and His words: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya': 27]. As for if it is said that the obligation had ceased for Pharaoh at that time, then this action attributed to Jibril would have no benefit at all.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So today We will save you in your body﴾, and there are aspects regarding it:

The first: ﴿We will save you in your body﴾, meaning We will cast you onto a najwa of the earth, which is an elevated place.

The second: We will bring you out of the sea and rescue you from what your people fell into, from the bottom of the sea, but after you have drowned. His words ﴿in your body﴾ are in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning in the state you are in at that time, having no spirit in you.

The third: this is a promise to him of salvation in the manner of mockery (tahakkum), as in His words: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21]. It is as if it were said to him: We will save you, but this salvation will only be for your body, not for your spirit. Such a statement may be made in the manner of ridicule, as one says: "We will free you, but after death," and "We will release you from prison, but after you die."

The fourth: some reciters read "nunahhika" with an unpointed ḥā' (nunaḥḥīka), meaning We will cast you to a side on the shore of the sea, because after drowning he was thrown to one side of the sea. Ka'b said: The water threw him onto the shore like a bull.

* * *

As for His words ﴿in your body﴾, there are aspects regarding it:

The first: what we mentioned, that it is in the place of a circumstantial clause, meaning in the state in which you were a mere body without a spirit.

The second: the intended meaning is: We will save you in your body complete, sound, unchanged.

The third: ﴿We will save you in your body﴾ means We will bring you out of the sea naked, without clothing.

The fourth: ﴿We will save you in your body﴾ means with your armour (bidr'ika). Al-Layth said: "al-badan" is the armour which is short in the sleeves; so His words ﴿in your body﴾ mean in your armour. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: He had on him a golden armour by which he was recognised, so Allah brought him out of the water with that armour so that he would be recognised. I say: if this is authentic, then it was a miracle for Musa (peace be upon him).

* * *

As for His words ﴿that you may be a sign for those who come after you﴾, there are aspects regarding it:

The first: a group among those who believed in his divinity, when they did not witness his drowning, denied it and claimed that one like him does not die. So Allah, the Exalted, made His affair manifest by bringing him out of the water in his own form until they saw him, and the doubt was removed from their hearts. It was said that his place of casting was on the route of the Children of Israel.

The second: it is not far-fetched that He, the Exalted, intended that creation should see him in that humiliation and abasement, after they had heard from him His words: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24], so that this would be a deterrent to creation from following a path like his, and so that they would know that he had been yesterday at the height of majesty and greatness, and then his affair ended in what they see.

The third: some reciters read "li-man khalaqaka" with a qaf (li-man khalaqaka), meaning that you may be a sign for your Creator, like the rest of His signs.

[Page 124]
[Page 125]
[Page 126]

Fourth: When He drowned him along with all his people, and He did not bring any of them out from the bottom of the sea but singled him out for bringing out, his being singled out in this wondrous state indicates the perfection of Allah's power and the truthfulness of Musa (peace be upon him) in his claim to prophethood.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, many of the people are heedless of Our signs﴾, the most evident view is that when He mentioned the story of Musa and Fir'awn, and mentioned the outcome of Fir'awn's situation, and concluded with this statement, and addressed it to Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), this serves as a warning to his community against turning away from the proofs, and as an incentive for them to reflect upon them and take lessons from them. For the purpose of mentioning these stories is to attain lessons, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, in their stories there is a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf: 111].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement and provided them with good things. And they did not differ until knowledge came to them. Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.﴾

Page 127
Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned what the seal had fallen upon in the matter of Pharaoh and his soldiers, He also mentioned in this verse what the seal had fallen upon in the matter of the Children of Israel. Here there are two discussions.

The first discussion: His saying, ﴿We settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement﴾, meaning, We made them dwell in a place of truthfulness, that is, a praiseworthy place. His saying, ﴿a good settlement﴾, has two interpretations:

The first: it is permissible that "mubawwa' sidq" be a verbal noun (masdar), meaning, We settled them in a settlement of truthfulness.

The second: the meaning is a suitable, pleasing dwelling. The settlement was described as "sidq" (truthful) because it is the habit of the Arabs that when they praise something they attribute it to truthfulness. They say: "rajul sidq" (a true man) and "qadam sidq" (a true foot/standing). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a true entrance and cause me to exit a true exit﴾ [al-Isra' 17:80]. The reason for this is that when a thing is complete in its time and suitable for the purpose required of it, then whatever good is presumed in it must indeed be borne out by that presumption.

The second discussion: They differed concerning whether the intended "Children of Israel" in this verse are the Jews who were in the time of Musa, peace be upon him, or those who were in the time of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

As for the first view: a group held it, and their evidence is that when He, exalted is He, mentioned this verse following the story of Musa, peace be upon him, it was more appropriate to apply this verse to their conditions. On this reckoning, what was meant by His saying, ﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement﴾ is al-Sham and Egypt, and those lands are lands abundant in fertility. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed﴾ [al-Isra' 17:1]. What is meant by His saying, ﴿and provided them with good things﴾ is those benefits. Also, what is meant by it is that He, exalted is He, made the Children of Israel inherit everything that was under the hands of the people of Pharaoh of speaking and silent [property], tillage and livestock, as He said: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land﴾ [al-A'raf 7:137].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they did not differ until knowledge came to them.﴾ What is meant is that the people of Musa, peace be upon him, remained upon one religion and one saying without difference until they read the Torah. Then, at that point, they became alert to the questions and matters, and difference arose among them. Then He, exalted is He, explained that this kind of difference must remain in the abode of this world, and that He, exalted is He, will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection.

As for the second view, namely that what is meant by the Children of Israel in this verse are the Jews who were in the time of Muhammad, peace be upon him, this was held by a great group of exegetes. Ibn 'Abbas said: They are Qurayzah, al-Nadir, and Banu Qaynuqa'. "We settled them in a good settlement" means between Medina and al-Sham, and "and provided them with good things" means the fresh dates and dates in those lands, of which there is no equal in goodness in other lands. Then they remained upon their religion, and difference did not appear among them until knowledge came to them. What is meant by knowledge is the Qur'an revealed to Muhammad, peace be upon him. He named it knowledge because it is the cause of knowledge, and naming the cause by the name of the effect is a well-known figure of speech (majaz).

Regarding the Qur'an being a cause for the occurrence of difference, there are two interpretations:

The first: the Jews used to foretell the mission of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and boast of it over the rest of the people. When God, exalted is He, sent him, they denied him out of envy, rebellion, and preference for retaining leadership. A group of them believed in him. Thus by this route the revelation of the Qur'an became a cause for the occurrence of difference among them.

The second: it may be said that this group of the Children of Israel were, before the revelation of the Qur'an, utterly disbelievers, and remained in this state until knowledge came to them. At that point they differed: a people believed, and other peoples remained upon their disbelief.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾, what is meant by it is that this kind of difference has no remedy for its removal in the abode of this world, and that He, exalted is He, in the Hereafter will judge between them, so that the one who is right is distinguished from the one who is wrong, and the truthful from the heretic.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 94–97 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾ ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe.﴾ ﴿Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment.﴾

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, had earlier mentioned their disagreement after knowledge had come to them, He presented to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in this verse, what strengthens his heart regarding the soundness of the Qur'an and the prophethood. So He said: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: "Doubt (shakk), in the linguistic usage, means joining some of a thing to another. It is said: 'He strung the pearls on the necklace (shakk al-jawahir fi al-iqd)' when he joined some of them to others. It is said: 'I shakkaftu the game' when you shoot it and then join its foreleg or hind leg to its other leg. Al-shakaik of howdahs are those whose parts are bound to one another. Al-shikak are houses lined up side by side. Al-shakaik are the adopted sons, because they join themselves (yashukkuna anfusahum) to a people who are not of them, that is, they attach themselves. And a man shakka in the weapon when he enters into it, joins it to himself and binds it to himself. So when they say 'So-and-so is in doubt about matters', they mean that he has placed himself between two things, so that this is possible and that is possible; thus he joins to what he imagines something else opposite to it."

The second issue: The exegetes differed concerning who is addressed by this address. It was said: the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace. And it was said: someone other than him.

As for those who hold the first view, they differed in several respects:

The first aspect: The address is with the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, outwardly, but what is meant is others, like the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1], and like His saying: ﴿If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], and like His saying: ﴿O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. And among the well-known examples: "It is you I mean, but hear, O neighbour."

What indicates the soundness of what we have mentioned are several points:

The first: His saying, the Exalted, at the end of the surah: ﴿Say: O people, if you are in doubt about my religion...﴾ [Yunus: 104]. So He made clear that those mentioned at the beginning of the verse by way of allusion are those mentioned in this verse explicitly.

[Page 129]

The second: If the Messenger were in doubt about his own prophethood, then the doubt of others about his prophethood would be even more fitting, and this would necessitate the complete collapse of the Shari'ah.

The third: Suppose he were in doubt about his own prophethood. How then would that doubt be removed by the reports of the People of the Book about his prophethood, given that most of them are disbelievers? Even if some among them were believers, their word would not be a proof, especially since it has been established that what is in their hands of the Torah and the Gospel is all altered and distorted. Thus it is established that the truth is that the address, although outwardly with the Messenger ﷺ, is in fact meant for the community. Such a thing is common: when a great sultan has a commander, and a group is under that commander's banner, and he wishes to command the subjects with a specific matter, he does not direct his address to them, but directs that address to that commander whom he has appointed over them, so that it may have greater effect on their hearts.

The second aspect: Allah knew that the Messenger did not doubt this, but the intent is that whenever he heard this speech he would declare: "O Lord, I do not doubt, nor do I seek proof from the words of the People of the Book; rather, what You have sent down to me of clear evidences suffices me." A parallel to this is His saying to the angels: ﴿Did these people worship you?﴾ [Saba: 40], that they should state the true answer and say: ﴿Glory be to You! You are our Guardian, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ [Saba: 41]. And like His saying to Jesus, upon him be peace: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and the purpose of it is that Jesus, upon him be peace, should declare his innocence of that. So likewise here.

The third aspect: Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, was of the human race, and it is possible for disturbing thoughts and agitated notions to arise in his heart. Such thoughts are not dispelled except by presenting proofs and establishing clear evidences. So He, the Exalted, sent down this kind of confirmations, so that through them those whisperings would be removed from his mind. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Perhaps you will leave aside part of what is revealed to you, and your breast will be constricted by it﴾ [Hud: 12].

I say: The complete explanation in this matter is that His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾, then do such-and-such, is a conditional proposition (qadiyyah shartiyyah). A conditional proposition has no implication whatsoever as to whether the condition occurred or did not occur, nor as to whether the consequent occurred or did not occur. Rather, it contains only a statement that the quiddity of that condition necessitates the quiddity of that consequent, and nothing more. The proof of this is that when you say: "If five is even, then it is divisible into two equal parts," this is a true statement, because its meaning is that the evenness of five necessitates its divisibility into two equal parts. Yet this statement does not indicate that five is even, nor that it is divisible into two equal parts. Likewise here: this verse indicates that if this doubt had occurred, the obligatory response would be to do such-and-such. As for whether this doubt occurred or did not occur, the verse contains no indication of it. The benefit of sending down this verse to the Messenger is that multiplying proofs and strengthening them increases the strength of certainty, the tranquillity of the soul and the calm of the breast. For this reason Allah has multiplied in His Book the establishment of the proofs of monotheism and prophethood.

The fourth way of establishing this meaning is that you say: The purpose of mentioning this speech is to win over the hearts of the disbelievers and to bring them close to accepting faith. For they demanded from him again and again proofs confirming the soundness of his prophethood, and it was as if they were ashamed of those repeated demands and requests, and that shame became a barrier preventing them from accepting faith. So He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ about your prophethood, then hold fast to the few proofs; meaning, the most fitting of people not to doubt his prophethood is himself. Then, even if he himself seeks a proof for his own prophethood after the dazzling proofs and overwhelming clear evidences that have preceded, there is no fault in that, and no deficiency results from it. So if that is not regarded as disgraceful for himself, then it is all the more fitting that the seeking of proofs by others should not be regarded as disgraceful. Thus it is established that the purpose of this speech is to win over the people and to remove shame from them regarding the increase of disputations.

[Page 130]

The fifth way: The meaning is that you are not in doubt at all. And if you were in doubt, there would be many ways available to you to remove that doubt; like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. The meaning is that if that impossible thing were assumed to occur, such-and-such an impossibility would follow from it. So likewise here. And if we assume the occurrence of this doubt, then return to the Torah and the Gospel so that you may know through them that this doubt is removed and this objection is false.

The sixth way: al-Zajjaj said: "Allah addressed the Messenger in His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾, and it includes all of creation, just as His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]." He said: "This is the best of the sayings." Al-Qadi said: "This is far-fetched, because whenever the Messenger is included within this address, the question returns, whether or not others are meant along with him. If it is permissible that he be meant along with others, then what prevents that he be meant alone, as the apparent meaning requires?" Then he said: "A interpretation of this kind indicates scarcity of learning."

The seventh way: The word "in" (in) in His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ is for negation; that is: you were not in doubt before, meaning: We do not command you to ask because you are in doubt, but so that you may increase in certainty, just as Abraham, upon him be peace, increased in certainty by witnessing the reviving of the dead.

As for the second view, which says that this address is not with the Messenger, its explanation is that the people in his time were of three groups: those who affirmed him, those who denied him, and those who hesitated regarding his matter, the doubters concerning him. So Allah addressed them with this address, saying: "If you, O human being, are in doubt about what We have sent down to you of guidance through Muhammad, then ask the People of the Book so that they may guide you to the soundness of his prophethood." Allah expressed this in the singular while meaning the plural, as in His saying: ﴿O human being, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ ﴿Who created you...﴾ [al-Infitar: 6–7], and ﴿O human being, you are laboring toward your Lord﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6], and His saying: ﴿When harm touches a human being﴾ [al-Zumar: 49]. In none of these verses is a specific individual meant; rather the intended meaning is the group. So likewise here. And when Allah, the Exalted, mentioned to them what would remove that doubt from them, He warned them against being joined to the second category, namely the deniers, so He said: ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾

* * *

The third issue: They differed concerning who is meant by the one asked in His saying: ﴿ask those who have been reading the Scripture﴾. The verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said: They are those among the People of the Book who believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, Abdullah ibn Suriya, Tamim al-Dari, and Ka'b al-Ahbar, because they are the ones whose report is trusted. And some said: It is all of them, whether they were among the Muslims or among the disbelievers, because if they reached the number that constitutes mass transmission (tawatur), and then recited a verse from the Torah and the Gospel, and that verse indicates the good tidings of the coming of Muhammad ﷺ, then the purpose has been achieved.

If it is said: If your position is that these books have been subject to alteration and change, how is it possible to rely upon them?

We say: They altered them only by concealing the verses that indicate the prophethood of Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace. If there remained in them verses indicating his prophethood, that would be among the strongest proofs for the soundness of the prophethood of Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace. For since they remained despite the strong motives of those people to remove them, this shows that they were in the utmost clarity. As for the purpose of that

[Page 131]

question, it is knowledge of which things it concerns, and there are two opinions regarding this:

The first: It is the Qur'an and knowing the prophethood of the Messenger ﷺ.

The second: It refers back to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They did not differ until knowledge came to them﴾ [Yunus: 93]. The first is preferable, because it is the more important, and the need to know it is more complete.

Know that when He, the Exalted, had explained this path, He said after it: ﴿The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾ ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah.﴾ That is: remain steadfast and persist in what you are upon, of freedom from doubt and freedom from denying the signs of Allah. It is possible that this is by way of stirring up and displaying firmness; for this reason the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said when it was revealed: "I do not doubt, nor do I ask; rather I testify that it is the truth."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾

Know that the categories of the responsible are three: either one is among those who affirm the Messenger, or among those who suspend judgment regarding his truthfulness, or among those who deny. There is no doubt that the case of the one who suspends judgment is easier than the case of the denier. Therefore He mentioned the one who suspends judgment with His saying: ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾, then He followed it with mention of the denier, and made clear that he is among the losers. Then, when He, the Exalted, had detailed this division, He made clear that He has servants against whom He has decreed wretchedness, so they do not change, and servants for whom He has decreed honour, so they do not change. So He said: ﴿Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe.﴾ Concerning this there are several issues:

Issue 1: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *kalimat* in the plural, while the rest read *kalimah* in the singular. I say: it is *kalimat* according to the numerical plurality of kind or category, and *kalimah* (singular) according to the unity of genus.

Issue 2: The intended meaning of this *kalimah* is God's judgment concerning that and His informing of it, and His creating in the servant the totality of capacity and motive (*al-qudrah wa al-da'iyah*), which necessitates the occurrence of that effect. Then God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And even if every sign came to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾. The meaning is that they will absolutely not believe, even if there came to them proofs that have no limit or count; this is because proof does not guide except with the help of God, the Exalted, and when that help is not attained, those proofs are lost.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 94–97 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾ ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe.﴾ ﴿Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment.﴾

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, had earlier mentioned their disagreement after knowledge had come to them, He presented to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in this verse, what strengthens his heart regarding the soundness of the Qur'an and the prophethood. So He said: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: "Doubt (shakk), in the linguistic usage, means joining some of a thing to another. It is said: 'He strung the pearls on the necklace (shakk al-jawahir fi al-iqd)' when he joined some of them to others. It is said: 'I shakkaftu the game' when you shoot it and then join its foreleg or hind leg to its other leg. Al-shakaik of howdahs are those whose parts are bound to one another. Al-shikak are houses lined up side by side. Al-shakaik are the adopted sons, because they join themselves (yashukkuna anfusahum) to a people who are not of them, that is, they attach themselves. And a man shakka in the weapon when he enters into it, joins it to himself and binds it to himself. So when they say 'So-and-so is in doubt about matters', they mean that he has placed himself between two things, so that this is possible and that is possible; thus he joins to what he imagines something else opposite to it."

The second issue: The exegetes differed concerning who is addressed by this address. It was said: the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace. And it was said: someone other than him.

As for those who hold the first view, they differed in several respects:

The first aspect: The address is with the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, outwardly, but what is meant is others, like the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1], and like His saying: ﴿If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], and like His saying: ﴿O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. And among the well-known examples: "It is you I mean, but hear, O neighbour."

What indicates the soundness of what we have mentioned are several points:

The first: His saying, the Exalted, at the end of the surah: ﴿Say: O people, if you are in doubt about my religion...﴾ [Yunus: 104]. So He made clear that those mentioned at the beginning of the verse by way of allusion are those mentioned in this verse explicitly.

[Page 129]

The second: If the Messenger were in doubt about his own prophethood, then the doubt of others about his prophethood would be even more fitting, and this would necessitate the complete collapse of the Shari'ah.

The third: Suppose he were in doubt about his own prophethood. How then would that doubt be removed by the reports of the People of the Book about his prophethood, given that most of them are disbelievers? Even if some among them were believers, their word would not be a proof, especially since it has been established that what is in their hands of the Torah and the Gospel is all altered and distorted. Thus it is established that the truth is that the address, although outwardly with the Messenger ﷺ, is in fact meant for the community. Such a thing is common: when a great sultan has a commander, and a group is under that commander's banner, and he wishes to command the subjects with a specific matter, he does not direct his address to them, but directs that address to that commander whom he has appointed over them, so that it may have greater effect on their hearts.

The second aspect: Allah knew that the Messenger did not doubt this, but the intent is that whenever he heard this speech he would declare: "O Lord, I do not doubt, nor do I seek proof from the words of the People of the Book; rather, what You have sent down to me of clear evidences suffices me." A parallel to this is His saying to the angels: ﴿Did these people worship you?﴾ [Saba: 40], that they should state the true answer and say: ﴿Glory be to You! You are our Guardian, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ [Saba: 41]. And like His saying to Jesus, upon him be peace: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and the purpose of it is that Jesus, upon him be peace, should declare his innocence of that. So likewise here.

The third aspect: Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, was of the human race, and it is possible for disturbing thoughts and agitated notions to arise in his heart. Such thoughts are not dispelled except by presenting proofs and establishing clear evidences. So He, the Exalted, sent down this kind of confirmations, so that through them those whisperings would be removed from his mind. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Perhaps you will leave aside part of what is revealed to you, and your breast will be constricted by it﴾ [Hud: 12].

I say: The complete explanation in this matter is that His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾, then do such-and-such, is a conditional proposition (qadiyyah shartiyyah). A conditional proposition has no implication whatsoever as to whether the condition occurred or did not occur, nor as to whether the consequent occurred or did not occur. Rather, it contains only a statement that the quiddity of that condition necessitates the quiddity of that consequent, and nothing more. The proof of this is that when you say: "If five is even, then it is divisible into two equal parts," this is a true statement, because its meaning is that the evenness of five necessitates its divisibility into two equal parts. Yet this statement does not indicate that five is even, nor that it is divisible into two equal parts. Likewise here: this verse indicates that if this doubt had occurred, the obligatory response would be to do such-and-such. As for whether this doubt occurred or did not occur, the verse contains no indication of it. The benefit of sending down this verse to the Messenger is that multiplying proofs and strengthening them increases the strength of certainty, the tranquillity of the soul and the calm of the breast. For this reason Allah has multiplied in His Book the establishment of the proofs of monotheism and prophethood.

The fourth way of establishing this meaning is that you say: The purpose of mentioning this speech is to win over the hearts of the disbelievers and to bring them close to accepting faith. For they demanded from him again and again proofs confirming the soundness of his prophethood, and it was as if they were ashamed of those repeated demands and requests, and that shame became a barrier preventing them from accepting faith. So He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ about your prophethood, then hold fast to the few proofs; meaning, the most fitting of people not to doubt his prophethood is himself. Then, even if he himself seeks a proof for his own prophethood after the dazzling proofs and overwhelming clear evidences that have preceded, there is no fault in that, and no deficiency results from it. So if that is not regarded as disgraceful for himself, then it is all the more fitting that the seeking of proofs by others should not be regarded as disgraceful. Thus it is established that the purpose of this speech is to win over the people and to remove shame from them regarding the increase of disputations.

[Page 130]

The fifth way: The meaning is that you are not in doubt at all. And if you were in doubt, there would be many ways available to you to remove that doubt; like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. The meaning is that if that impossible thing were assumed to occur, such-and-such an impossibility would follow from it. So likewise here. And if we assume the occurrence of this doubt, then return to the Torah and the Gospel so that you may know through them that this doubt is removed and this objection is false.

The sixth way: al-Zajjaj said: "Allah addressed the Messenger in His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾, and it includes all of creation, just as His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]." He said: "This is the best of the sayings." Al-Qadi said: "This is far-fetched, because whenever the Messenger is included within this address, the question returns, whether or not others are meant along with him. If it is permissible that he be meant along with others, then what prevents that he be meant alone, as the apparent meaning requires?" Then he said: "A interpretation of this kind indicates scarcity of learning."

The seventh way: The word "in" (in) in His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ is for negation; that is: you were not in doubt before, meaning: We do not command you to ask because you are in doubt, but so that you may increase in certainty, just as Abraham, upon him be peace, increased in certainty by witnessing the reviving of the dead.

As for the second view, which says that this address is not with the Messenger, its explanation is that the people in his time were of three groups: those who affirmed him, those who denied him, and those who hesitated regarding his matter, the doubters concerning him. So Allah addressed them with this address, saying: "If you, O human being, are in doubt about what We have sent down to you of guidance through Muhammad, then ask the People of the Book so that they may guide you to the soundness of his prophethood." Allah expressed this in the singular while meaning the plural, as in His saying: ﴿O human being, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ ﴿Who created you...﴾ [al-Infitar: 6–7], and ﴿O human being, you are laboring toward your Lord﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6], and His saying: ﴿When harm touches a human being﴾ [al-Zumar: 49]. In none of these verses is a specific individual meant; rather the intended meaning is the group. So likewise here. And when Allah, the Exalted, mentioned to them what would remove that doubt from them, He warned them against being joined to the second category, namely the deniers, so He said: ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾
