Our companions (the Ash'arites) have argued with this verse in support of their position affirming the binding decree (*al-qada' al-lazim*) and the predetermined measure (*al-qadr al-wajib*), and it is the truth and certainty, and there is no escape from it.

* * *

Then God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And even if every sign came to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾. The meaning is that they will absolutely not believe, even if there came to them proofs that have no limit or count; this is because proof does not guide except with the help of God, the Exalted, and when that help is not attained, those proofs are lost.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 94–97 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾ ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe.﴾ ﴿Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment.﴾

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, had earlier mentioned their disagreement after knowledge had come to them, He presented to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in this verse, what strengthens his heart regarding the soundness of the Qur'an and the prophethood. So He said: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: "Doubt (shakk), in the linguistic usage, means joining some of a thing to another. It is said: 'He strung the pearls on the necklace (shakk al-jawahir fi al-iqd)' when he joined some of them to others. It is said: 'I shakkaftu the game' when you shoot it and then join its foreleg or hind leg to its other leg. Al-shakaik of howdahs are those whose parts are bound to one another. Al-shikak are houses lined up side by side. Al-shakaik are the adopted sons, because they join themselves (yashukkuna anfusahum) to a people who are not of them, that is, they attach themselves. And a man shakka in the weapon when he enters into it, joins it to himself and binds it to himself. So when they say 'So-and-so is in doubt about matters', they mean that he has placed himself between two things, so that this is possible and that is possible; thus he joins to what he imagines something else opposite to it."

The second issue: The exegetes differed concerning who is addressed by this address. It was said: the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace. And it was said: someone other than him.

As for those who hold the first view, they differed in several respects:

The first aspect: The address is with the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, outwardly, but what is meant is others, like the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1], and like His saying: ﴿If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], and like His saying: ﴿O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. And among the well-known examples: "It is you I mean, but hear, O neighbour."

What indicates the soundness of what we have mentioned are several points:

The first: His saying, the Exalted, at the end of the surah: ﴿Say: O people, if you are in doubt about my religion...﴾ [Yunus: 104]. So He made clear that those mentioned at the beginning of the verse by way of allusion are those mentioned in this verse explicitly.

[Page 129]

The second: If the Messenger were in doubt about his own prophethood, then the doubt of others about his prophethood would be even more fitting, and this would necessitate the complete collapse of the Shari'ah.

The third: Suppose he were in doubt about his own prophethood. How then would that doubt be removed by the reports of the People of the Book about his prophethood, given that most of them are disbelievers? Even if some among them were believers, their word would not be a proof, especially since it has been established that what is in their hands of the Torah and the Gospel is all altered and distorted. Thus it is established that the truth is that the address, although outwardly with the Messenger ﷺ, is in fact meant for the community. Such a thing is common: when a great sultan has a commander, and a group is under that commander's banner, and he wishes to command the subjects with a specific matter, he does not direct his address to them, but directs that address to that commander whom he has appointed over them, so that it may have greater effect on their hearts.

The second aspect: Allah knew that the Messenger did not doubt this, but the intent is that whenever he heard this speech he would declare: "O Lord, I do not doubt, nor do I seek proof from the words of the People of the Book; rather, what You have sent down to me of clear evidences suffices me." A parallel to this is His saying to the angels: ﴿Did these people worship you?﴾ [Saba: 40], that they should state the true answer and say: ﴿Glory be to You! You are our Guardian, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ [Saba: 41]. And like His saying to Jesus, upon him be peace: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and the purpose of it is that Jesus, upon him be peace, should declare his innocence of that. So likewise here.

The third aspect: Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, was of the human race, and it is possible for disturbing thoughts and agitated notions to arise in his heart. Such thoughts are not dispelled except by presenting proofs and establishing clear evidences. So He, the Exalted, sent down this kind of confirmations, so that through them those whisperings would be removed from his mind. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Perhaps you will leave aside part of what is revealed to you, and your breast will be constricted by it﴾ [Hud: 12].

I say: The complete explanation in this matter is that His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾, then do such-and-such, is a conditional proposition (qadiyyah shartiyyah). A conditional proposition has no implication whatsoever as to whether the condition occurred or did not occur, nor as to whether the consequent occurred or did not occur. Rather, it contains only a statement that the quiddity of that condition necessitates the quiddity of that consequent, and nothing more. The proof of this is that when you say: "If five is even, then it is divisible into two equal parts," this is a true statement, because its meaning is that the evenness of five necessitates its divisibility into two equal parts. Yet this statement does not indicate that five is even, nor that it is divisible into two equal parts. Likewise here: this verse indicates that if this doubt had occurred, the obligatory response would be to do such-and-such. As for whether this doubt occurred or did not occur, the verse contains no indication of it. The benefit of sending down this verse to the Messenger is that multiplying proofs and strengthening them increases the strength of certainty, the tranquillity of the soul and the calm of the breast. For this reason Allah has multiplied in His Book the establishment of the proofs of monotheism and prophethood.

The fourth way of establishing this meaning is that you say: The purpose of mentioning this speech is to win over the hearts of the disbelievers and to bring them close to accepting faith. For they demanded from him again and again proofs confirming the soundness of his prophethood, and it was as if they were ashamed of those repeated demands and requests, and that shame became a barrier preventing them from accepting faith. So He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ about your prophethood, then hold fast to the few proofs; meaning, the most fitting of people not to doubt his prophethood is himself. Then, even if he himself seeks a proof for his own prophethood after the dazzling proofs and overwhelming clear evidences that have preceded, there is no fault in that, and no deficiency results from it. So if that is not regarded as disgraceful for himself, then it is all the more fitting that the seeking of proofs by others should not be regarded as disgraceful. Thus it is established that the purpose of this speech is to win over the people and to remove shame from them regarding the increase of disputations.

[Page 130]

The fifth way: The meaning is that you are not in doubt at all. And if you were in doubt, there would be many ways available to you to remove that doubt; like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. The meaning is that if that impossible thing were assumed to occur, such-and-such an impossibility would follow from it. So likewise here. And if we assume the occurrence of this doubt, then return to the Torah and the Gospel so that you may know through them that this doubt is removed and this objection is false.

The sixth way: al-Zajjaj said: "Allah addressed the Messenger in His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾, and it includes all of creation, just as His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]." He said: "This is the best of the sayings." Al-Qadi said: "This is far-fetched, because whenever the Messenger is included within this address, the question returns, whether or not others are meant along with him. If it is permissible that he be meant along with others, then what prevents that he be meant alone, as the apparent meaning requires?" Then he said: "A interpretation of this kind indicates scarcity of learning."

The seventh way: The word "in" (in) in His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt﴾ is for negation; that is: you were not in doubt before, meaning: We do not command you to ask because you are in doubt, but so that you may increase in certainty, just as Abraham, upon him be peace, increased in certainty by witnessing the reviving of the dead.

As for the second view, which says that this address is not with the Messenger, its explanation is that the people in his time were of three groups: those who affirmed him, those who denied him, and those who hesitated regarding his matter, the doubters concerning him. So Allah addressed them with this address, saying: "If you, O human being, are in doubt about what We have sent down to you of guidance through Muhammad, then ask the People of the Book so that they may guide you to the soundness of his prophethood." Allah expressed this in the singular while meaning the plural, as in His saying: ﴿O human being, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ ﴿Who created you...﴾ [al-Infitar: 6–7], and ﴿O human being, you are laboring toward your Lord﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6], and His saying: ﴿When harm touches a human being﴾ [al-Zumar: 49]. In none of these verses is a specific individual meant; rather the intended meaning is the group. So likewise here. And when Allah, the Exalted, mentioned to them what would remove that doubt from them, He warned them against being joined to the second category, namely the deniers, so He said: ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾

* * *

The third issue: They differed concerning who is meant by the one asked in His saying: ﴿ask those who have been reading the Scripture﴾. The verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said: They are those among the People of the Book who believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, Abdullah ibn Suriya, Tamim al-Dari, and Ka'b al-Ahbar, because they are the ones whose report is trusted. And some said: It is all of them, whether they were among the Muslims or among the disbelievers, because if they reached the number that constitutes mass transmission (tawatur), and then recited a verse from the Torah and the Gospel, and that verse indicates the good tidings of the coming of Muhammad ﷺ, then the purpose has been achieved.

If it is said: If your position is that these books have been subject to alteration and change, how is it possible to rely upon them?

We say: They altered them only by concealing the verses that indicate the prophethood of Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace. If there remained in them verses indicating his prophethood, that would be among the strongest proofs for the soundness of the prophethood of Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace. For since they remained despite the strong motives of those people to remove them, this shows that they were in the utmost clarity. As for the purpose of that

[Page 131]

question, it is knowledge of which things it concerns, and there are two opinions regarding this:

The first: It is the Qur'an and knowing the prophethood of the Messenger ﷺ.

The second: It refers back to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They did not differ until knowledge came to them﴾ [Yunus: 93]. The first is preferable, because it is the more important, and the need to know it is more complete.

Know that when He, the Exalted, had explained this path, He said after it: ﴿The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾ ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah.﴾ That is: remain steadfast and persist in what you are upon, of freedom from doubt and freedom from denying the signs of Allah. It is possible that this is by way of stirring up and displaying firmness; for this reason the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said when it was revealed: "I do not doubt, nor do I ask; rather I testify that it is the truth."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾

Know that the categories of the responsible are three: either one is among those who affirm the Messenger, or among those who suspend judgment regarding his truthfulness, or among those who deny. There is no doubt that the case of the one who suspends judgment is easier than the case of the denier. Therefore He mentioned the one who suspends judgment with His saying: ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾, then He followed it with mention of the denier, and made clear that he is among the losers. Then, when He, the Exalted, had detailed this division, He made clear that He has servants against whom He has decreed wretchedness, so they do not change, and servants for whom He has decreed honour, so they do not change. So He said: ﴿Indeed, those against whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe.﴾ Concerning this there are several issues:

Issue 1: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *kalimat* in the plural, while the rest read *kalimah* in the singular. I say: it is *kalimat* according to the numerical plurality of kind or category, and *kalimah* (singular) according to the unity of genus.

Issue 2: The intended meaning of this *kalimah* is God's judgment concerning that and His informing of it, and His creating in the servant the totality of capacity and motive (*al-qudrah wa al-da'iyah*), which necessitates the occurrence of that effect. As for the judgment, the informing and the knowledge, this is evident; and as for the totality of capacity and motive, this is also evident, because capacity, when it is apt for both alternatives, does not favor one side over the other except by a determining factor (*murajjih*), and that determining factor comes from God, the Exalted, to put an end to infinite regress (*tasalsul*). When this totality is present, the act becomes necessary. Our companions (the Ash'arites) have argued with this verse in support of their position affirming the binding decree (*al-qada' al-lazim*) and the predetermined measure (*al-qadr al-wajib*), and it is the truth and certainty, and there is no escape from it.

* * *

Then God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And even if every sign came to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾. The meaning is that they will absolutely not believe, even if there came to them proofs that have no limit or count; this is because proof does not guide except with the help of God, the Exalted, and when that help is not attained, those proofs are lost.

THE THIRD STORY

Among the stories mentioned in this surah: the story of Yunus (peace be upon him).

﴿Why was there not a town that believed, so that its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and let them enjoy themselves for a time.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed, so that its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and let them enjoy themselves for a time.﴾

Page 132

Know that when He, may He be exalted, had explained earlier, ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾ and ﴿Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾, He followed it with this verse, because it indicates that the people of Yunus believed after their disbelief and benefited from that faith. This shows that disbelievers are of two kinds: among them are those for whom the decree of a disbelieving end was passed, and among them are those for whom the decree of a believing end was passed. And whatever Allah has decreed will come to pass. There are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: concerning the word "lawla" (why not / if only) in this verse, there are two views.

The first view: that it means negation. Al-Wahidi reported in "al-Basit" that Abu Malik, a companion of Ibn Abbas, said: "Everywhere in the Book of Allah where "lawla" is mentioned, it means "halla" (why not), except for two instances: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed, so that its faith benefited it﴾, meaning: "There was not a town that believed so that its faith benefited it," and likewise ﴿Why was there not among the generations before you﴾, meaning: "There was not among the generations." Accordingly, the sense of the verse is: "There was not a town that believed so that its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus." The phrase ﴿except the people of Yunus﴾ is in the accusative as a discontinuous exception from the first part, because the beginning of the speech concerned the town, though its intended meaning is its people. The exception of the people is made from the town, as in his saying:

". . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . And there was not in the enclosure any one
except the remnants. . . . . . . ∗∗∗ . . . . . . . . . ."

It is also read in the nominative as a substitute (badal).

The second view: that "lawla" means "halla" (why not), and the meaning is: "Why was there not one town among the towns that We destroyed which believed, being steadfast in disbelief and sincere in faith before seeing the punishment, except the people of Yunus?" The apparent wording requires that the people of Yunus be excepted from the towns, but the meaning is that the people of Yunus are excepted from the people of the towns, and it is a discontinuous exception in the sense of "but the people of Yunus, when they believed, We did such-and-such with them."

The second issue: It is reported that Yunus (peace be upon him) was sent to Nineveh in the land of Mosul, and they denied him. He left them in anger. When they lost him, they feared the descent of punishment, so they put on sackcloth and cried out for forty nights. Yunus had told them: "Your term is forty nights." They said: "If we see the signs of destruction, we will believe in you." When thirty-five nights had passed, a black cloud appeared in the sky, very intensely black, and from it a severe smoke emerged, and that smoke descended until it fell upon the city and blackened its roofs. They went out to the desert and separated the women and children from the animals and their young, so the animals yearned for one another, the cries rose, the supplications multiplied, and they displayed faith and repentance and humbly turned to Allah, may He be exalted, so He had mercy on them and removed it from them. That day was the day of Ashura, a Friday. It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud that their repentance reached the point that they returned wrongful gains; so much so that a man would pull out a stone after its foundation had been laid in a building and return it to its owner. It was also said: they went out to an elder among their remaining scholars and said: "The punishment has descended upon us; what do you see?" He said to them: "Say: O Living when there is no living, O Living who gives life to the dead, O Living, there is no god but You." They said it, and Allah removed the punishment from them. It is also reported from al-Fadl ibn Abbas that they said: "O Allah, indeed our sins have grown great and mighty, and You are greater and mightier than them. Deal with us in the way You are worthy of, and do not deal with us in the way we deserve."

The third issue: If someone says: He, may He be exalted, related that Pharaoh repented at the end of the matter but his repentance was not accepted, and He related that the people of Yunus repented and He accepted their repentance. What is the difference?

Page 133

The answer: Pharaoh repented only after he witnessed the punishment, whereas the people of Yunus repented before that, for when signs appeared to them indicating the nearness of the punishment, they repented before they witnessed it. Thus the difference becomes clear.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 99–100:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them entirely. Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ ﴿It is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah, and He places defilement upon those who do not reason.﴾ Know that this surah, from its beginning up to this place, is concerned with relating the doubts of the disbelievers in denying prophethood, together with the answer to them. One of their doubts was that the Prophet (ﷺ) would threaten them with the descent of punishment along with the disbelievers, and would promise his followers that Allah would grant them victory, elevate their status and strengthen their side. Then the disbelievers did not see this, so they made it a doubt with which to disparage his prophethood. They also exaggerated in seeking the hastening of that punishment as a form of mockery. Then Allah, glorified and exalted is He, explained that the delay of what was promised does not undermine the soundness of the promise. Then He set forth examples of this, namely the account of Noah and the account of Moses with Pharaoh, peace be upon them both, and these explanations extended to these stations. Then in this verse He explained that the Messenger's earnestness in bringing them into faith does not benefit, and his exertion in establishing the proofs and in answering the doubts does not avail; because faith is not attained except through Allah's creation, His will, His guidance and His guiding. So if this meaning is not realized, faith is not realized. And in the verse there are issues:

First issue: Our companions argued for the soundness of their position that all existing things occur by the will of Allah, the Exalted. They said: the particle (law, "if") indicates the negation of one thing due to the negation of another. So His saying: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them﴾ requires that that will did not occur, and the faith of all the people of the earth did not occur entirely. This indicates that He, exalted is He, did not intend the faith of all. Al-Jubba'i, al-Qadi and others answered that what is meant is the will of compulsion, i.e., if Allah had willed to compel them into faith, He would have been able to do so and it would have been valid from Him; but He did not do that, because faith that arises from the servant under compulsion neither benefits him nor yields any benefit. Then al-Jubba'i said: the meaning of Allah compelling them to that is that He makes them know by necessity that if they tried to abandon it, Allah would prevent them between themselves and that; and at this point they must do what they were compelled to. Just as one among us who knows that if he attempts to kill a king, he will be prevented from it by force, his abandoning that act does not become a cause for deserving praise and reward; so likewise here.

Know that this discourse is weak, and its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: the disbeliever was able to disbelieve; was he able to believe or not? If he was able to disbelieve but not able to believe, then the ability to disbelieve necessitates disbelief. If the one who created that ability is Allah, the Exalted, then it must be said that He created in him an ability necessitating disbelief, and so it must be said that He willed disbelief from him. But if the ability is capable of two opposites, as is the position of that group, then the preponderance of one of the two sides over the other, if it does not depend on a preponderant factor, then the preponderance has occurred without a preponderant factor, and this is false. And if it depends on a preponderant factor, that factor is either from the servant or from Allah. If it is from the servant, the division recurs concerning it and there follows an infinite regress, which is impossible. And if it is from Allah, the Exalted, then the totality of that ability together with that motive necessitates that disbelief; so if the creator of the ability and the motive is Allah, the Exalted, then the same objection returns.

The second: His saying ﴿And if your Lord had willed﴾ cannot be taken to mean the will of compulsion; because the Prophet (ﷺ) did not seek that there should come to them a faith that would not benefit them in the Hereafter. So Allah explained that the Messenger had no power to bring about this faith, then He said: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them﴾. Therefore the faith mentioned in this verse must be this beneficial faith, so that the discourse is coherent. As for taking the wording to mean the will of coercion and compulsion, it does not befit this place.

The third: this compulsion is meant either as: that He shows him terrifying signs, at the sight of which his fear greatly increases, and then he brings faith at that moment; or it means the creation of faith in them. The first is false, because Allah explained before this verse that the sending down of these signs does not benefit: His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been decreed will not believe, even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾, and He also said: ﴿Even if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered everything before them, they would not have believed unless Allah willed﴾ [al-An'am: 111]. And if what is meant is the second, then this compulsion to faith is not what is meant, but rather it is an expression for the creation of faith in them. Then it is said: but He did not create faith in them; so this shows that He did not intend the attainment of faith for them, and this is exactly our position.

Know that when He exalted mentioned this discourse, He said: ﴿Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ The meaning is that you have no power to act upon anyone; and the purpose of it is to show that irresistible power and executing will belong only to the Truth, glorified and exalted is He.

Second issue: Our companions argued for the soundness of their position—that there is no ruling for things before the revelation of the Shari'ah—by His saying: ﴿It is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah﴾. They said: the way of inference from it is that permission (idhn) is an expression for release in an act and the lifting of hardship. The plain sense of this verse indicates that before this meaning is realized, it is not permitted for him to proceed to this faith. Then they said: and what indicates this from the side of reason are several points:

The first: the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and occupying oneself with thanking Him and praising Him, reason does not indicate that any benefit results from it; therefore it must not be obligatory according to reason. The proof of the first: that benefit is either returning to the one thanked or to the thanker. The first is false, because among created beings the thanked one benefits from thanks, so thanks gladdens him and ingratitude grieves him; therefore thanks is good and ingratitude is ugly. As for Allah, subhanahu, thanks does not gladden Him nor does ingratitude grieve Him, so He gains no benefit from this thanks at all. The second is also false, because the thanker grows weary in the present by that thanking and expends service, while the one thanked gains nothing from it at all. And it cannot be said that this thanking is the cause of reward; because entitlement against Allah, the Exalted, is impossible, for entitlement against another is only conceivable if that other is such that were he not to give, his refraining from giving that right would cause a deficiency in his own right; and since the Truth, subhanahu, is exempt from deficiency and increase, that cannot be conceived regarding Him. Thus it is established that occupying oneself with faith and with thanks yields no benefit by pure reason, and what is like this cannot be something reason makes obligatory. By this decisive proof is established the soundness of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah.﴾ Al-Qadi said: what is meant is that faith does not proceed from him except by Allah's knowledge, or by His obligation, or by His empowering him to it.

Our reply: taking "permission" to mean what you have mentioned is abandoning the apparent sense, and that is not permissible, especially since we have shown that the decisive rational proof strengthens our view.

Third issue: Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "wa-najʿalu" with the nun, while the rest read it with the yā', as a reference to the name of Allah, the Exalted.

Fourth issue: Our companions argued for the soundness of their position that the creator of disbelief and faith is Allah, the Exalted, by His saying: ﴿And He places defilement upon those who do not reason﴾. Its exposition: al-rijs (defilement) may be used to mean an ugly deed; He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the defilement, O people of the house, and purify you with complete purification﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33]. The meaning of rijs here is an ugly deed, whether it is disbelief or disobedience; and by purification is meant the transfer of the servant from the defilement of disbelief and disobedience to the purity of faith and obedience. So when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in what precedes this verse that faith does not arise except by Allah's will and His creating, He mentioned after it that defilement does not arise except by His creating and bringing into being. And the defilement that stands opposite to faith is nothing but disbelief; thus the indication of this verse is established that disbelief and faith are from Allah, the Exalted.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi, the grammarian, answered this, saying: al-rijs admits of two other meanings:

One of them: that what is meant by it is punishment, so His saying: ﴿And He places defilement upon those who do not reason﴾ means He inflicts punishment upon them, as He said: ﴿And that He may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the polytheist men and polytheist women﴾ [al-Fath: 6].

The second: that He, exalted is He, judges them to be defiled, as He said: ﴿The polytheists are only impure (najas)﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], and the meaning is that the purity established for the Muslims has not been attained by them.

The reply: we have already shown by rational proof that ignorance cannot be an act of the servant, because he does not will it and does not intend to bring it about; rather he wills its opposite, and he intends only to attain its opposite. So if it were by him, nothing would come about except what he intended. We have raised the objections to this argument and answered them earlier in this book. As for taking al-rijs to mean punishment, that is false, because rijs is an expression for what is corrupt, loathsome and detested; so taking this word to mean their ignorance and disbelief is more fitting than taking it to mean the punishment of Allah, even though that punishment is true, right and proper. And as for taking the word rijs to mean Allah's judgment of their defilement, that is extremely remote, because Allah's judgment with that is His attribute, so how could it be said that the attribute of Allah is defilement? Thus it is established that the argument we have mentioned is evident.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 99–100:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them entirely. Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ ﴿It is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah, and He places defilement upon those who do not reason.﴾ Know that this surah, from its beginning up to this place, is concerned with relating the doubts of the disbelievers in denying prophethood, together with the answer to them. One of their doubts was that the Prophet (ﷺ) would threaten them with the descent of punishment along with the disbelievers, and would promise his followers that Allah would grant them victory, elevate their status and strengthen their side. Then the disbelievers did not see this, so they made it a doubt with which to disparage his prophethood. They also exaggerated in seeking the hastening of that punishment as a form of mockery. Then Allah, glorified and exalted is He, explained that the delay of what was promised does not undermine the soundness of the promise. Then He set forth examples of this, namely the account of Noah and the account of Moses with Pharaoh, peace be upon them both, and these explanations extended to these stations. Then in this verse He explained that the Messenger's earnestness in bringing them into faith does not benefit, and his exertion in establishing the proofs and in answering the doubts does not avail; because faith is not attained except through Allah's creation, His will, His guidance and His guiding. So if this meaning is not realized, faith is not realized. And in the verse there are issues:

First issue: Our companions argued for the soundness of their position that all existing things occur by the will of Allah, the Exalted. They said: the particle (law, "if") indicates the negation of one thing due to the negation of another. So His saying: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them﴾ requires that that will did not occur, and the faith of all the people of the earth did not occur entirely. This indicates that He, exalted is He, did not intend the faith of all. Al-Jubba'i, al-Qadi and others answered that what is meant is the will of compulsion, i.e., if Allah had willed to compel them into faith, He would have been able to do so and it would have been valid from Him; but He did not do that, because faith that arises from the servant under compulsion neither benefits him nor yields any benefit. Then al-Jubba'i said: the meaning of Allah compelling them to that is that He makes them know by necessity that if they tried to abandon it, Allah would prevent them between themselves and that; and at this point they must do what they were compelled to. Just as one among us who knows that if he attempts to kill a king, he will be prevented from it by force, his abandoning that act does not become a cause for deserving praise and reward; so likewise here.

Know that this discourse is weak, and its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: the disbeliever was able to disbelieve; was he able to believe or not? If he was able to disbelieve but not able to believe, then the ability to disbelieve necessitates disbelief. If the one who created that ability is Allah, the Exalted, then it must be said that He created in him an ability necessitating disbelief, and so it must be said that He willed disbelief from him. But if the ability is capable of two opposites, as is the position of that group, then the preponderance of one of the two sides over the other, if it does not depend on a preponderant factor, then the preponderance has occurred without a preponderant factor, and this is false. And if it depends on a preponderant factor, that factor is either from the servant or from Allah. If it is from the servant, the division recurs concerning it and there follows an infinite regress, which is impossible. And if it is from Allah, the Exalted, then the totality of that ability together with that motive necessitates that disbelief; so if the creator of the ability and the motive is Allah, the Exalted, then the same objection returns.

The second: His saying ﴿And if your Lord had willed﴾ cannot be taken to mean the will of compulsion; because the Prophet (ﷺ) did not seek that there should come to them a faith that would not benefit them in the Hereafter. So Allah explained that the Messenger had no power to bring about this faith, then He said: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them﴾. Therefore the faith mentioned in this verse must be this beneficial faith, so that the discourse is coherent. As for taking the wording to mean the will of coercion and compulsion, it does not befit this place.

The third: this compulsion is meant either as: that He shows him terrifying signs, at the sight of which his fear greatly increases, and then he brings faith at that moment; or it means the creation of faith in them. The first is false, because Allah explained before this verse that the sending down of these signs does not benefit: His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been decreed will not believe, even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾, and He also said: ﴿Even if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered everything before them, they would not have believed unless Allah willed﴾ [al-An'am: 111]. And if what is meant is the second, then this compulsion to faith is not what is meant, but rather it is an expression for the creation of faith in them. Then it is said: but He did not create faith in them; so this shows that He did not intend the attainment of faith for them, and this is exactly our position.

Know that when He exalted mentioned this discourse, He said: ﴿Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ The meaning is that you have no power to act upon anyone; and the purpose of it is to show that irresistible power and executing will belong only to the Truth, glorified and exalted is He.

Second issue: Our companions argued for the soundness of their position—that there is no ruling for things before the revelation of the Shari'ah—by His saying: ﴿It is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah﴾. They said: the way of inference from it is that permission (idhn) is an expression for release in an act and the lifting of hardship. The plain sense of this verse indicates that before this meaning is realized, it is not permitted for him to proceed to this faith. Then they said: and what indicates this from the side of reason are several points:

The first: the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and occupying oneself with thanking Him and praising Him, reason does not indicate that any benefit results from it; therefore it must not be obligatory according to reason. The proof of the first: that benefit is either returning to the one thanked or to the thanker. The first is false, because among created beings the thanked one benefits from thanks, so thanks gladdens him and ingratitude grieves him; therefore thanks is good and ingratitude is ugly. As for Allah, subhanahu, thanks does not gladden Him nor does ingratitude grieve Him, so He gains no benefit from this thanks at all. The second is also false, because the thanker grows weary in the present by that thanking and expends service, while the one thanked gains nothing from it at all. And it cannot be said that this thanking is the cause of reward; because entitlement against Allah, the Exalted, is impossible, for entitlement against another is only conceivable if that other is such that were he not to give, his refraining from giving that right would cause a deficiency in his own right; and since the Truth, subhanahu, is exempt from deficiency and increase, that cannot be conceived regarding Him. Thus it is established that occupying oneself with faith and with thanks yields no benefit by pure reason, and what is like this cannot be something reason makes obligatory. By this decisive proof is established the soundness of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah.﴾ Al-Qadi said: what is meant is that faith does not proceed from him except by Allah's knowledge, or by His obligation, or by His empowering him to it.

Our reply: taking "permission" to mean what you have mentioned is abandoning the apparent sense, and that is not permissible, especially since we have shown that the decisive rational proof strengthens our view.

Third issue: Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "wa-najʿalu" with the nun, while the rest read it with the yā', as a reference to the name of Allah, the Exalted.

Fourth issue: Our companions argued for the soundness of their position that the creator of disbelief and faith is Allah, the Exalted, by His saying: ﴿And He places defilement upon those who do not reason﴾. Its exposition: al-rijs (defilement) may be used to mean an ugly deed; He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the defilement, O people of the house, and purify you with complete purification﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33]. The meaning of rijs here is an ugly deed, whether it is disbelief or disobedience; and by purification is meant the transfer of the servant from the defilement of disbelief and disobedience to the purity of faith and obedience. So when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in what precedes this verse that faith does not arise except by Allah's will and His creating, He mentioned after it that defilement does not arise except by His creating and bringing into being. And the defilement that stands opposite to faith is nothing but disbelief; thus the indication of this verse is established that disbelief and faith are from Allah, the Exalted.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi, the grammarian, answered this, saying: al-rijs admits of two other meanings:

One of them: that what is meant by it is punishment, so His saying: ﴿And He places defilement upon those who do not reason﴾ means He inflicts punishment upon them, as He said: ﴿And that He may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the polytheist men and polytheist women﴾ [al-Fath: 6].

The second: that He, exalted is He, judges them to be defiled, as He said: ﴿The polytheists are only impure (najas)﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], and the meaning is that the purity established for the Muslims has not been attained by them.

The reply: we have already shown by rational proof that ignorance cannot be an act of the servant, because he does not will it and does not intend to bring it about; rather he wills its opposite, and he intends only to attain its opposite. So if it were by him, nothing would come about except what he intended. We have raised the objections to this argument and answered them earlier in this book. As for taking al-rijs to mean punishment, that is false, because rijs is an expression for what is corrupt, loathsome and detested; so taking this word to mean their ignorance and disbelief is more fitting than taking it to mean the punishment of Allah, even though that punishment is true, right and proper. And as for taking the word rijs to mean Allah's judgment of their defilement, that is extremely remote, because Allah's judgment with that is His attribute, so how could it be said that the attribute of Allah is defilement? Thus it is established that the argument we have mentioned is evident.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 101:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth. But signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe."﴾

Regarding the verse, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Asim and Hamzah recited ﴿qul unzuru﴾ with a kasra on the lam (ﷺ-less reading: *qul inzuru*), due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). The original form is with a kasra. The rest of the readers recited it with a damma, transferring the vowel of the hamza to the lam.

**The second issue:** Know that when Exalted is He had explained in the preceding verses that faith is not attained except by the creation and will of God, He commanded reflection and inference from the evidences, so that it would not be supposed that the truth is pure predestination. So He said: ﴿Say: "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth."﴾

Know that this indicates two objectives:

The first: there is no way to know God except by contemplating the evidences, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Reflect upon creation, but do not reflect upon the Creator."

The second: the evidences are either from the world of the heavens or from the world of the earth. As for the heavenly evidences, they are the movements of the celestial spheres, their measures, their positions, and what is in them of the sun, the moon, and the stars, and the benefits and advantages specific to each of them. As for the earthly evidences, they are the examination of the conditions of the upper elements, the conditions of minerals, the conditions of plants, and the conditions of humans in particular. Then each of these categories divides into types that have no end. Were a person to begin contemplating the manner of God's wisdom, exalted is He, in creating the wing of a mosquito, his intellect would be exhausted before reaching the least degree of those wisdoms and benefits. There is no doubt that God, exalted is He, is the one who mentioned these evidences most in the Glorious Qur'an. For this reason He said: ﴿Say: "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth,"﴾ without mentioning the details. It is as if He, exalted is He, drew attention to the general principle, such that the intelligent person becomes alert to its divisions, and then begins to detail the wisdom of each of them according to his intellectual and human capacity.

Then, when He, exalted is He, had commanded this reflection and contemplation, He explained afterward that this reflection and contemplation upon these signs does not benefit the one upon whom God, exalted is He, has decreed in eternity wretchedness and misguidance. So He said: ﴿But signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe.﴾ On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** The grammarians said that "ma" in this position may carry two meanings:

The first: that it is a negation, meaning that these signs and warnings do not produce benefit for the one whom God has decreed will not believe, like your saying: "Wealth avails you nothing if you do not spend it."

The second: that it is an interrogative, like your saying: "What thing avails them?", which is an interrogative in the sense of denial.

**The second issue:** The signs (*ayat*) are the evidences, and the warnings (*nudhur*) are the messengers who warn, or the warnings themselves.

**The third issue:** It was recited as (*wa-ma yughni*) with the ya' from below (i.e., with the verb in the third-person masculine form).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 102–103:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then do they await only the like of the days of those who passed away before them? Say: "Then wait; I am with you among those who wait."﴾ ﴿Then We shall deliver Our messengers and those who believe. Thus it is incumbent upon Us: We shall deliver the believers.﴾

Know that the meaning is: Do they await only days like the days of the past nations? The intended sense is that the earlier prophets, peace be upon them, used to threaten the disbelievers of their times with the coming of days containing various kinds of punishment, and they (the disbelievers) would deny them and mock them by hastening them. Likewise were the disbelievers who lived in the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, who did the same. Then He, exalted is He, commanded him to say to them: ﴿Then wait; I am with you among those who wait.﴾ Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then We shall deliver Our messengers and those who believe.﴾ And in this there are issues:

The first issue: al-Kisa'i, in the narration of Nusayr, read "nunji" (نُنْجِي) with a light (خَفِيفَة) pronunciation, while the rest read it with a doubled letter (مُشَدَّدَة). Both are dialects (لُغَتانِ), and likewise in His saying: ﴿We deliver the believers﴾.

The second issue: "thumma" (ثُمَّ) is a conjunction particle (حَرْفُ عَطْفٍ), and the sense of the speech is: "Our custom in the past was that We would destroy them swiftly, then We would deliver Our messengers."

The third issue: When He commanded the Messenger in the first verse to agree with the disbelievers in awaiting the punishment, He mentioned the detail, saying: The punishment descends only upon the disbelievers, while the Messenger and his followers are the people of salvation.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿Thus it is incumbent upon Us: We shall deliver the believers.﴾ In this there are two issues:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: That is, like that deliverance We give victory to the believers and destroy the polytheists; and "haqqan 'alayna" (حَقًّا عَلَيْنا) is a parenthetical clause (اعْتِراض), meaning: that is incumbent upon Us, truly incumbent.

The second issue: The judge (al-Qadi) said: His saying "haqqan 'alayna" is meant to denote obligation (الوُجُوب), because the rescue of the Messenger and the believers from punishment to reward is obligatory; and were it not so, it would not be good of Allah, exalted is He, to impose on them burdensome deeds. And when its obligation is established for this reason, it operates in the manner of settling a debt for a prior cause.

The answer: We say: It is a truth (haqq) by virtue of the promise and the decree, and we do not say it is a truth by virtue of entitlement (الِاسْتِحْقاق), because it is established that the servant has no entitlement against his Creator to anything.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verses 104–106:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "O mankind, if you are in doubt about my religion, then I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah, but I worship Allah, who causes you to die. And I have been commanded to be among the believers."﴾ ﴿And [I was commanded], "Direct your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, and never be among the polytheists."﴾ ﴿And do not invoke other than Allah that which neither benefits you nor harms you. For if you should do so, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers.﴾

Know that when the Exalted mentioned the proofs to the utmost ends and the most eloquent conclusions, He commanded His Messenger to make his religion manifest and to make clear his separation from the polytheists, so that doubts and suspicions about his matter would disappear and the worship of Allah would move from the way of secrecy to open manifestation. So He said: ﴿Say: "O mankind, if you are in doubt about my religion"﴾. Know that the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that these disbelievers did not know the religion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is reported that they used to say about him: "He has become a Sabian (ṣabaʾa)," and he is a Sabian. So Allah the Exalted commanded that He make clear to them that he is upon the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf (upright, inclining to truth), a Muslim, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, a ḥanīf﴾ [al-Nahl: 120], and because of His saying: ﴿I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth, as a ḥanīf﴾ [al-An'am: 79], and because of His saying: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 2]. The meaning is: if you do not know my religion, then I explain it to you in detail. Then he mentioned in it several matters:

The first condition is His saying: ﴿So I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah﴾. The reason this negation was necessarily placed first is what we have mentioned: the removal of corrupt inscriptions from the tablet must precede the affirmation of correct inscriptions on that tablet. This negation was obligatory because worship is the utmost form of veneration, and it befits only one who possesses the utmost majesty and nobility. As for idols, they are stones, and the human being is of higher rank than them. How could the noblest be fitting to occupy himself with the worship of the basest?

Page 138
The second condition is His saying: ﴿But I worship Allah, who causes you to die﴾. The purpose is that, since He had shown that it is obligatory to abandon the worship of other than Allah, He showed that it is obligatory to occupy oneself with the worship of Allah.
If it is said: What is the wisdom in mentioning the true object of worship in this place with this attribute, namely His saying: ﴿who causes you to die﴾?

We say: There are several aspects to this:

First: It is possible that the intended meaning is: "I worship Allah who created you first, then causes you to die second, then restores you third." These three stages have been established in the Qur'an many times and in various modes, so here He suffices with mentioning the causing of death from among them, because it alerts to the rest.

Second: Death is the most awe-inspiring of things, so we single out this attribute for mention in this place so that it will be stronger in admonition and deterrence.

Third: When they hastened the descent of the punishment, the Exalted said: ﴿Then do they await anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them? Say: "Then wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ ﴿Then We shall save Our messengers and those who believed﴾. This verse indicates that He destroys those disbelievers, preserves the believers, and strengthens their state. Since the mention of this statement was recent, it is therefore that He says here: ﴿But I worship Allah, who causes you to die﴾, which is an allusion to what He established and clarified in that verse, as if he says: "I worship He who promised me their destruction and my preservation."

The third of the matters mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾. Know that when He mentioned worship, which is of the kind of bodily acts, He moved from it to faith and knowledge, and this indicates that the outward does not become adorned with righteous deeds unless the light of faith and knowledge arises in the heart.

The fourth condition is His saying: ﴿And [I was commanded], "Direct your face toward the religion, inclining to truth"﴾. Concerning it are issues:

The first issue: The "wa" (and) in His saying ﴿And [I was commanded] to direct my face﴾ is a conjunctive particle, and regarding what it conjoins there are two views:

First: His saying ﴿I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾ stands in place of His saying: "It was said to me: Be among the believers," and then He conjoined to it ﴿and to direct your face﴾.

Second: His saying ﴿and to direct your face﴾ stands in place of His saying: "I have been commanded to direct the face," so the sense becomes: "I have been commanded to be among the believers and to direct the face to the religion, inclining to truth."

The second issue: Directing the face is a metaphor for turning the intellect entirely toward seeking the religion, because whoever wants to look at something with thorough investigation sets his face opposite it in such a way that he does not turn it away from it, neither slightly nor greatly; for if he turns it away even slightly, that opposition is broken, and when that opposition is broken, sight is impaired. For this reason it is fine to make directing the face toward the religion a metaphor for diverting the intellect entirely to seeking the religion. His saying ﴿ḥanīf﴾ means: inclining to it with a total inclination, turning away from everything else with a total turning away. The conclusion of this discourse is complete sincerity and abandoning attention to anything other than Him. Thus His saying first ﴿I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾ indicates the attainment of the essence of faith, and His saying ﴿and to direct my face to the religion, inclining to truth﴾ indicates absorption in the light of faith and total turning away from anything else.

The fifth condition is His saying: ﴿And never be among the polytheists﴾.

Know that it is not possible for this to be a prohibition against worshipping idols, because that has already been mentioned in His saying in this verse: ﴿So I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah﴾. Therefore this statement must be understood to carry an additional benefit: that whoever has recognized his Master, if after that he turns to other than Him, that is shirk. This is what the people of the hearts call hidden shirk.

Page 139
The sixth condition is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not invoke other than Allah that which neither benefits you nor harms you﴾. The possible in its essence is non-existent when considered in itself, and existent by the bringing-into-being of the Real. If that is the case, then whatever is other than the Real has no existence except by the bringing-into-being of the Real. Given this, there is no one who benefits except the Real, and no one who harms except the Real; "everything perishes except His face" [al-Qasas: 88]. If that is so, then there is no judgment except for Allah, and there is no return in both abodes except to Allah.
Then He said at the end of the verse: ﴿For if you should do so, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: if you occupy yourself with seeking benefit and harm from other than Allah, then you are among the wrongdoers, because injustice is an expression for placing a thing in other than its proper place. When what is other than the Real is removed from exercising disposal, then ascribing disposal to what is other than the Real is placing a thing in other than its place, and so it is injustice.

If it is said: Does seeking satiety through eating and quenching thirst through drinking detract from that sincerity?

We say: No, because the existence of bread and all its attributes is by Allah's bringing-into-being and creation, and seeking benefit from a thing which Allah created for benefit is not incompatible with returning wholly to Allah. However, the condition of this sincerity is that the gaze of his intellect should not fall upon any of these existents without his witnessing with the eye of his intellect that they are non-existent in their own essences, existent by the bringing-into-being of the Real, subsisting in themselves, and remaining by the sustaining of the Real. At that time he sees what is other than the Real as pure non-existence in terms of themselves, and he sees the light of His existence and the overflow of His beneficence high above all.

It is reported that they used to say about him: "He has become a Sabian (ṣabaʾa)," and he is a Sabian. So Allah the Exalted commanded that He make clear to them that he is upon the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf (upright, inclining to truth), a Muslim, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, a ḥanīf﴾ [al-Nahl: 120], and because of His saying: ﴿I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth, as a ḥanīf﴾ [al-An'am: 79], and because of His saying: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 2]. The meaning is: if you do not know my religion, then I explain it to you in detail. Then he mentioned in it several matters:

The first condition is His saying: ﴿So I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah﴾. The reason this negation was necessarily placed first is what we have mentioned: the removal of corrupt inscriptions from the tablet must precede the affirmation of correct inscriptions on that tablet. This negation was obligatory because worship is the utmost form of veneration, and it befits only one who possesses the utmost majesty and nobility. As for idols, they are stones, and the human being is of higher rank than them. How could the noblest be fitting to occupy himself with the worship of the basest?

Page 138
The second condition is His saying: ﴿But I worship Allah, who causes you to die﴾. The purpose is that, since He had shown that it is obligatory to abandon the worship of other than Allah, He showed that it is obligatory to occupy oneself with the worship of Allah.
If it is said: What is the wisdom in mentioning the true object of worship in this place with this attribute, namely His saying: ﴿who causes you to die﴾?

We say: There are several aspects to this:

First: It is possible that the intended meaning is: "I worship Allah who created you first, then causes you to die second, then restores you third." These three stages have been established in the Qur'an many times and in various modes, so here He suffices with mentioning the causing of death from among them, because it alerts to the rest.

Second: Death is the most awe-inspiring of things, so we single out this attribute for mention in this place so that it will be stronger in admonition and deterrence.

Third: When they hastened the descent of the punishment, the Exalted said: ﴿Then do they await anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them? Say: "Then wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ ﴿Then We shall save Our messengers and those who believed﴾. This verse indicates that He destroys those disbelievers, preserves the believers, and strengthens their state. Since the mention of this statement was recent, it is therefore that He says here: ﴿But I worship Allah, who causes you to die﴾, which is an allusion to what He established and clarified in that verse, as if he says: "I worship He who promised me their destruction and my preservation."

The third of the matters mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾. Know that when He mentioned worship, which is of the kind of bodily acts, He moved from it to faith and knowledge, and this indicates that the outward does not become adorned with righteous deeds unless the light of faith and knowledge arises in the heart.

The fourth condition is His saying: ﴿And [I was commanded], "Direct your face toward the religion, inclining to truth"﴾. Concerning it are issues:

The first issue: The "wa" (and) in His saying ﴿And [I was commanded] to direct my face﴾ is a conjunctive particle, and regarding what it conjoins there are two views:

First: His saying ﴿I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾ stands in place of His saying: "It was said to me: Be among the believers," and then He conjoined to it ﴿and to direct your face﴾.

Second: His saying ﴿and to direct your face﴾ stands in place of His saying: "I have been commanded to direct the face," so the sense becomes: "I have been commanded to be among the believers and to direct the face to the religion, inclining to truth."

The second issue: Directing the face is a metaphor for turning the intellect entirely toward seeking the religion, because whoever wants to look at something with thorough investigation sets his face opposite it in such a way that he does not turn it away from it, neither slightly nor greatly; for if he turns it away even slightly, that opposition is broken, and when that opposition is broken, sight is impaired. For this reason it is fine to make directing the face toward the religion a metaphor for diverting the intellect entirely to seeking the religion. His saying ﴿ḥanīf﴾ means: inclining to it with a total inclination, turning away from everything else with a total turning away. The conclusion of this discourse is complete sincerity and abandoning attention to anything other than Him. Thus His saying first ﴿I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾ indicates the attainment of the essence of faith, and His saying ﴿and to direct my face to the religion, inclining to truth﴾ indicates absorption in the light of faith and total turning away from anything else.

The fifth condition is His saying: ﴿And never be among the polytheists﴾.

Know that it is not possible for this to be a prohibition against worshipping idols, because that has already been mentioned in His saying in this verse: ﴿So I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah﴾. Therefore this statement must be understood to carry an additional benefit: that whoever has recognized his Master, if after that he turns to other than Him, that is shirk. This is what the people of the hearts call hidden shirk.

Page 139
The sixth condition is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not invoke other than Allah that which neither benefits you nor harms you﴾. The possible in its essence is non-existent when considered in itself, and existent by the bringing-into-being of the Real. If that is the case, then whatever is other than the Real has no existence except by the bringing-into-being of the Real. Given this, there is no one who benefits except the Real, and no one who harms except the Real; "everything perishes except His face" [al-Qasas: 88]. If that is so, then there is no judgment except for Allah, and there is no return in both abodes except to Allah.
Then He said at the end of the verse: ﴿For if you should do so, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: if you occupy yourself with seeking benefit and harm from other than Allah, then you are among the wrongdoers, because injustice is an expression for placing a thing in other than its proper place. When what is other than the Real is removed from exercising disposal, then ascribing disposal to what is other than the Real is placing a thing in other than its place, and so it is injustice.

If it is said: Does seeking satiety through eating and quenching thirst through drinking detract from that sincerity?

We say: No, because the existence of bread and all its attributes is by Allah's bringing-into-being and creation, and seeking benefit from a thing which Allah created for benefit is not incompatible with returning wholly to Allah. However, the condition of this sincerity is that the gaze of his intellect should not fall upon any of these existents without his witnessing with the eye of his intellect that they are non-existent in their own essences, existent by the bringing-into-being of the Real, subsisting in themselves, and remaining by the sustaining of the Real. At that time he sees what is other than the Real as pure non-existence in terms of themselves, and he sees the light of His existence and the overflow of His beneficence high above all.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 107:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but He; and if He intends you good, there is none to repel His bounty. He causes it to reach whomever He wills of His servants. And He is the All-Forgiving, the All-Merciful.﴾

On this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Know that He, glorified and exalted, established at the end of this surah that all possible beings (al-mumkinat) depend upon Him, all created things are in need of Him, intellects are bewildered concerning Him, and mercy, generosity and existence overflow from Him.

Know also that a thing is either harmful, or beneficial, or neither harmful nor beneficial. These two categories (harmful and beneficial) share the name "good." Since harm is something existential (wujudi), He said concerning it: ﴿If Allah touches you with harm﴾. Since good may be existential or may be non-existential (adami), He did not use the word "touch" concerning it, but said: ﴿and if He intends you good﴾. The verse indicates that harm and good both occur by the power of Allah, the Exalted, and by His decree. This includes disbelief and faith, obedience and disobedience, joy and calamities, good things and pains, pleasures and comforts, and wounds. So He, glorified and exalted, made clear that if He decrees evil for anyone, there is none to remove it but He; and if He decrees good for anyone, there is absolutely none to repel His bounty.

Then, in the verse there is another subtle point: He, exalted, gave preference to the side of good over the side of evil in three respects.

The first: when He mentioned the touching of harm, He made clear that there is none to remove it but He. This indicates that He removes harms, because an exception from a negation is an affirmation (istithna' min al-nafy ithbat). When He mentioned good, He did not say that He repels it, but said that there is no one who can repel His bounty. This indicates that good is desired in itself (matlub bi'l-dhat), and that evil is desired only incidentally (matlub bi'l-'arad),

(page 140)

as the Prophet (ﷺ) said, relating from the Lord of Might: "My mercy precedes My wrath."

The second: He, exalted, said concerning the attribute of good: ﴿He causes it to reach whomever He wills of His servants﴾, and this indicates that the side of good and mercy is stronger and more dominant.

The third: He said: ﴿And He is the All-Forgiving, the All-Merciful﴾, and this also indicates the strength of the side of mercy. The summary of the discussion on this verse is that He, glorified and exalted, made clear that He alone is the one who creates, brings into existence, shapes and originates, that there is no creator besides Him, and no one worthy of worship except Him. Then He drew attention to the fact that good is willed in itself, and evil is willed incidentally. Beneath this topic there are deep secrets. This is what we say concerning this verse.

**The second issue:** The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: When He, exalted, explained in the first verse, concerning the idols, that they neither harm nor benefit, He explained in this verse that they are also unable to repel harm coming from another, or to obtain good coming from another. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said concerning ﴿If Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but He﴾: meaning, with sickness or poverty, so there is no one to repel it but Him.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and if He intends you good﴾, al-Wahidi said: It is an inversion (maqlub, transposition of words). Its meaning is: "and if He intends good for you." However, since each of the two phrases is connected to the other, it is permissible to replace each of them with the other.

I say: Priority in wording indicates greater attention. So His saying ﴿and if He intends you good﴾ indicates that the intended one is the human being, and all other goods are created for his sake. This subtle point is derived only from this structure of the expression.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 108:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "O mankind, the truth has certainly come to you from your Lord. So whoever is guided, it is only for [the benefit of] his own soul that he is guided; and whoever goes astray, it is only against it that he goes astray. And I am not over you a manager."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had established the proofs mentioned concerning tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood and the return (ma'ad), and had adorned the end of this surah with these clear proofs that indicate that He, exalted is He, alone is the One who originates creation, innovates, brings into being and creates, He concluded it with this noble and exalted conclusion. In its interpretation there are two views:

The first: whoever He has decreed in eternity to be guided, that will certainly happen to him, and whoever He has decreed for misguidance, likewise; there is no way to avert it.

The second, which is the statement fitting for the Mu'tazilah: The judge (al-Qadi) said: He, exalted is He, has made clear that He has perfected the Sharia, removed the pretext, and cut off the excuse. ﴿So whoever is guided, it is only for [the benefit of] his own soul that he is guided; and whoever goes astray, it is only against it that he goes astray. And I am not over you a manager.﴾ Therefore it is not obligatory upon me to strive more than I have done in bringing you to the great reward and in rescuing you from the painful punishment. Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse is abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse of fighting.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 10, verse 109:

Then God, exalted is He, concluded this conclusion with another subtle conclusion, so He said: ﴿And follow what is revealed to you, and be patient until God judges, and He is the best of judges.﴾

The meaning is that God commanded him to follow the revelation and the Revelation (al-tanzil). If, as a result of that following, something disagreeable reaches him, then let him be patient with it

until God judges concerning it, and He is the best of judges. Some of them recited poetry on patience, saying:

I will be patient until patience itself is unable to match my patience, and I will be patient until God judges concerning my affair.
